MR. DOUGLAS    ALLEGED EXCESSIVE PROFITS OF SUGAR COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I will state my question of privilege, I will read a letter to substantiate that statement, and move a motion. For several months we have been told by ministers of the crown that the series of increases in the price of sugar has been due entirely to the rise in world prices and has not been due to any undue profiteering by the sugar companies of Canada. I have in my hand a letter from the British Columbia Sugar Refining Company dated November 29 and signed by the president. It says:
Due to the higher prices for sugar that prevailed through most of the past financial year, the profits of the over-all company have proven to be greater than normal. Under these circumstances, the directors of the company have decided that a special bonus be paid to all permanent employees.
The amount of each individual bonus has been determined by a formula which takes into account the length of service of each employee. Your bonus cheque is enclosed with this letter.
I wish to point out that this payment does not establish a precedent as it is being made as a result of most unusual circumstances that may not again arise in future years. It is hoped that it will be accepted in recognition of your years of service through both poor and good years.
The company has no wish to receive any publicity from making this payment and I would be obliged if each of you would keep it as confidential as possible.
Yours very truly,
Forrest Rogers, president.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fort Arthur:
That in the opinion of this house the government should investigate the excessive profits made by the sugar companies of Canada due to the price increases imposed in 1963.

speechtext: Once more I have to decide whether there is or is not a good question of privilege. speechtext: In view of the statements that are being made day by day regarding this whole incident, may I again ask the minister to reconsider his refusal to appoint a royal commission to look into this incredible series of disclosures?

subtopic: ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE IN COFFIN CASE
speechtext:
With reference to that question, Mr. Speaker, which the hon. member has posed on more than one occasion, I may say I have inquired from the officers of the department on the question whether the sentence should have been commuted or allowed to take its course. I find that it was painstakingly investigated and considered in the Department of Justice and the cabinet

in the ordinary way before a recommendation was made to the governor in council. The record does not, of course, disclose the considerations that moved the cabinet to its recommendation. That confirms what the former prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition, said with reference to the fact that there could be in his mind no question of matters of this nature being divulged in any way whatsoever, and I am convinced they were not.
However, I can say that the file indicates that representations were made to the department prior to consideration of the commutation issue, upon alleged new evidence relating to several of the matters now being raised, including the source of money spent by Coffin after the date of the murder, a rifle allegedly seen in Coffin's truck, other Americans in jeeps alleged to have been in the vicinity, and jeep tracks at the scene of the crime.

subtopic: ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE IN COFFIN CASE
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, in view of the latter part of the minister's statement, namely that these various matters were considered, does he not feel that in the public interest the suggestion which was made by the hon. member for Danforth should be considered? This is one of the most difficult problems a government faces; in view of the discussion that has been aroused and the books that have been written, would the minister, even if he did not appoint a royal commission, appoint a group of people to go into this matter? The administration of justice in connection with commutations is a heavy responsibility as it rests on the minister, and everything should be done to reassure the public that no miscarriage of justice took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE IN COFFIN CASE
speechtext:
I agree fully that nothing should be done in any department, more particularly the Department of Justice, which would lead to a miscarriage of justice, but I have to say at once that the moment these questions were raised, officers of the Department of Justice gave and are still giving consideration to them. They are, as I indicated earlier, reading the book. My right hon. friend shakes his head, but all this has arisen because of the book that has been written, and I am sure the book must be read and considered in the light of the information which is in the files of the Department of Justice.
What I want to say in answer to the question of the Leader of the Opposition is that until I have a report from them-and at this moment I must say I am not satisfied that there is cause for further action on the part of the government-none the less I am
Inquiries of the Ministry not closing the door to an investigation, and the director who is in charge of the criminal law section of the Department of Justice, together with several of the officers of the department, are devoting their time to a consideration of this matter.

subtopic: ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE IN COFFIN CASE
speechtext: As a supplementary question, in view of the fact that the controversy surrounding this matter is seriously calling into question the faith of a good many people in the whole administration of justice, would the minister urge the officials to hurry up their reading of the book so we could get a statement on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE IN COFFIN CASE
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this matter is so serious that it should not be considered by way of hurry up proceedings, and I think the time that should be taken to consider this will certainly be time well spent. I am not aware of all the assertions made in the hon. member's question, but I did see a newspaper item indicating that a contract for some of the preliminary construction was going to be let. It is perfectly obvious to anyone familiar with the situation that a crossing of the river in that general area is very much needed and wholly desirable; but it is also equally important to this country that the government should not stand idly by if in fact the reports are to the effect that the construction and location of the piers in the way proposed will materially affect shipping in the St. Lawrence system, and in addition damage the harbour of Three Rivers, which has a very good record as a harbour and one of which I am sure the hon. member who asked me the question would be very proud.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter to which the hon. gentleman refers has been one of
Inquiries of the Ministry very great concern to the government. As hon. members know, a bill passed the United States Senate and I believe is now in conference or perhaps has now been approved by congress which would require the marking of imported goods and particularly the marking of sawn lumber. We have already made strong representations to the United States authorities both on the bill as a whole and on the lumber amendment, pointing out the restrictive effects on trade which would flow from the enactment of this measure. We are continuing to be in close touch. Indeed, I believe our ambassador was in the state department, and I think in the White House, yesterday putting forward these representations.
We believe that the amendment which deals with sawn lumber in particular is contrary to obligations undertaken by the United States under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. We are hopeful, of course, that these representations will have the effect of there being non-approval of the legislation by the President, but it is too early to say whether we have been successful.
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister say whether the note remitted by the ambassador is in the nature of a note of protest?
Oh yes; the note is also one of protest, and we hope it will have the effect immediately of there being either the veto or non-approval of the legislation by the President.
Mr. Speaker, has the minister been in touch with his opposite number in the United States?
Mr. Speaker, we thought because of the great importance of this matter that our representations should be made at the highest level, which is higher than my opposite number in the United States.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FASTER UNLOADING OF GRAIN CARS
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Since there is only a two bushel wheat quota in existence at many points in Alberta, and in the light of the fact that in Vancouver there are many grain cars lined up waiting to be unloaded, would the minister look into this situation and try to speed up the handling of grain at this port in order that these cars might be unloaded and released for further movement of grain from the country elevators in Alberta and western Saskatchewan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FASTER UNLOADING OF GRAIN CARS
speechtext:
I have been in communication with the officials of the wheat board on a

number of occasions with regard to expediting shipments, particularly of wheat, and the movement of grain both east and west. The chairman of the wheat board told me today by telephone that now the St. Lawrence seaway has frozen over for the winter it will be the objective of the board to achieve as high a degree of equalization as possible until the opening of the navigation season next spring. This will include points in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FASTER UNLOADING OF GRAIN CARS
speechtext: I am afraid that does not answer the question I asked. My question was directed to these cars which are lined up in Vancouver waiting to be unloaded. This has nothing to do with equalization. The point is that these cars are not being moved out for reloading.

subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FASTER UNLOADING OF GRAIN CARS
speechtext: I meant to include that in my answer. I have been discussing this with the wheat board. They are conscious of the problem and they are doing everything they can to get a quicker turnaround.

subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FASTER UNLOADING OF GRAIN CARS
speechtext:
In
view of the fact that a question I asked two days ago is really supplementary to the one just put to the minister by my hon. friend, I wonder if I may address it now to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I addressed it originally on Wednesday to the Minister of Agriculture, who I see has now left the house.
My question was this. Are the minister or his departmental officials considering approaching, or making plans to approach, farm co-operative organizations, wheat pools and line elevator company officials to improve elevator and other facilities so that Canada, with a surplus of grain, could meet the demand for western wheat? That question was in line with what the minister said in reference to not being able to complete the contract with China. We have the wheat, but we do not have the facilities to deliver it.

subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FASTER UNLOADING OF GRAIN CARS
speechtext:
I have already been in touch with the groups mentioned by the hon. member, and I have consulted the wheat board in an effort to speed up movement out of Vancouver. However, even though we have experienced some of these difficulties-difficulties which have persisted for years and years under the administration of my predecessor and of his predecessor, too, in charge of the wheat board-I can assure the hon. gentleman that we shall achieve our targets, which involve the movement of tremendous quantities. Indeed, the chairman of the wheat board feels we shall exceed even the 550 million bushel figure which was originally cited. So any of these difficulties are relatively minor in comparison with the enormous movement which

is going on now, movement which is the result of very close and energetic co-operation among the railways, the elevator companies and all parties concerned.

speechtext:

Inquiries of the Ministry Minister with regard to charges that the R.C.M.P. were making security investigations at Regina college. The Prime Minister said he would make inquiries. I wonder if the Acting Prime Minister has any information to give the house.
Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Acting Prime

subtopic: REPORTED APPROACH TO STUDENT AT UNIVERSITY OF SASKATCHEWAN

subsubtopic: RESPECTING TRUSTEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MARITIME UNIONS
subsubtopic: RESPECTING TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question asked by my hon. friend gives me the opportunity to answer it and several others that have been raised in connection with the trusteeship. Inquiries of the Ministry
With respect to the desire that has been expressed to have an interim report from the trustees, I find that it is the wish of the trustees to be allowed to carry on for the present without making a report, with the assurance that they will make a report for presentation to parliament early in the new year, or as early in the new year as possible. subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege that affects me as a member and also as a member of the Queen's privy council. On page 5767 of Hansard for yesterday I find this sentence attributed to the hon. member for Medicine Hat:
Never before in our history has any member spent so much out of public funds in order to advertise a political party.

I must say, Mr. Speaker, that this is an imputation against my personal honour and against my activities as minister of agriculture. I have to ask not only for a complete withdrawal but, I would suggest, a very strong apology as well.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if anything I said yesterday can be construed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle as being offensive to him personally, I withdraw that. However, the statement he has quoted is my opinion, and I have a right to express my opinion in this house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
A very serious question of privilege has been raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. The words spoken by the hon. member for Medicine Hat in this house constitute a reflection on a member of this house. Let us look again at the sentence, sir:
Never before in our history has any member spent so much out of public funds in order to advertise a political party.
This is a most unusual statement to be made by any hon. member. The only recourse, sir, is a complete withdrawal.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: It just happens that I believe the remark is true. If it happens to be offensive to a particular member of this house, we could surely change the word "member" to "former minister" or something of that sort. However, I do not feel under any obligation to withdraw something I said which I still believe is true.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Prove it.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: I suggest that if the hon. member insists that he believes this statement, he has no choice but to move a substantive motion.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
In so far as the
question of privilege is concerned, when the remark was made yesterday by the hon. member for Medicine Hat I was quite astounded, because what he is saying is that the former minister of agriculture has misapplied public funds. In essence he is making a charge of fraud by misuse of public funds. Citation 108, paragraph 3 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, says in effect that libels on members have also been constantly punished and scandalous charges or imputations directed against members are equivalent to libelous charges.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has raised a substantial question of privilege, and not only should there be a complete withdrawal but a very strong apology as suggested. Certainly, in the brief time I have been in this house any
Question of Privilege
honourable member would withdraw such charges without any question at all.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Of course the hon. member who has just spoken has made an imputation that I am not honourable, so I could raise another question of privilege right now.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: That is a question.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: If the hon. member for Qu'Appelle takes definite objection to the word "member", I could withdraw that. The implication I intended, and which I think was clear to all hon. members in the house when the statement was made, was that he, along with his government, had spent a great deal of public funds to advertise the advantages the farmers of Canada would receive from the Conservative party, and I still believe it.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Unless some other hon. member has some really soothing remarks to offer at this time, it happens very often that in the course of debate members get overheated, get carried away with remarks, with the emotion of the situation, and with the argument they are trying to present. This morning the hon. member for Medicine Hat has certainly cut off any individual reference to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: At least that is the import of what I have understood.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: He has made it worse.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: But on the other hand it seems to me that the question having been raised, having been aired, it would be a very gracious act if the hon. member for Medicine Hat would care to rise and just soften the effect of some of the words he used this morning.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to withdraw anything that the hon. member can construe as having been an allegation directly against him personally.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but this goes beyond any allegations against me personally. He has intimated that I have misused public funds.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
That is your conscience
talking.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Withdraw that remark.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
I have no choice, Mr. Speaker, but to ask the hon. member for Medicine Hat not only to withdraw what he said about me in a personal way but to say without any equivocation that he removes

Question of Privilege
from me any imputation about the way I handled public funds in connection with my department.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I had made such a statement I would withdraw it, but I did not.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
May I point out that Beau-chesne, citation 108 (3), says:
Libels on members have also been constantly punished: but to constitute a breach of privilege they must concern the character or conduct of members in that capacity, and the libel must be based on matters arising in the actual transaction of the business of the house.
I would hope that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle would feel that the matter has been straightened out. If not, now is the time to say so.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: I have no choice but to say I am not satisfied on the second point, namely that I misused public funds of this country for the good of the Conservative party. The hon. member for Medicine Hat repeated that statement again this morning-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: He did not.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: -and I have to ask that it be completely withdrawn, and I would hope he would be gentleman enough to apologize for it.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this matter refers to something that happened in the house quite some time ago concerning the ARDA program, and before any decision is taken by Your Honour I think there would have to be some reference to the debates that took place some time ago. I think there was nothing personal in the remark that was made, but Your Honour will remember there were charges some years ago when the ARDA program was put forth, for example, that something was published and circulated in rural communities concerning the ARDA program before it had been passed by parliament. At that time charges were discussed in the house which in my opinion would warrant some of the implications in the remarks of the hon. member for Medicine Hat.
It also seems to me that we become very touchy in relation to party responsibilities in relation to points of privilege, and if the hon. member for Medicine Hat withdraws the personal implication, I think the party implication that was made at that time warranted the statement the hon. member made in the house yesterday.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just one brief word on citation 108 (3) which Your Honour has read. There obviously is a direct imputation by the hon. member for Medicine

Hat as to the misuse of government funds, and what the hon. member for Timiskaming has just said refers to the publication of an ARDA pamphlet. There is no difference between that kind of pamphlet and the pamphlet covering the $500 house bonus issued under the Minister of Labour. The imputation has not been made in that regard, and should not be made in this regard by the hon. member for Medicine Hat; but citation 108 (3) says that a libel on an hon. member to constitute a breach of privilege "must concern the character or conduct of members in that capacity, and the libel must be based on the matters arising in the actual transaction of the business of the house."
The business of the house in this instance concerned the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, on which the hon. member was speaking, and there is no doubt it affects the conduct and personal character of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I do not know why the hon. member for Medicine Hat cannot be gentleman enough to get up and withdraw the charges he made.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the last speaker has suggested that the hon. member for Medicine Hat had said that there was a misuse of public funds. I would like him to read that from what was reported in Hansard. I have not read that, and I would like him to read it where it says that. The hon. member is imputing something to the hon. member for Medicine Hat that is not in the record.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: I still have the question to decide, and I would like to hear from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle whether he is satisfied with the explanations given and with the statement of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. These things concern the privileges of all hon. members of the house and are indeed very serious in principle. In the present instance they may not be that serious, but generally speaking, in principle libels against members, and purported libels, are serious and must be attended to.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is because the subject is so serious that I cannot add anything more to what I have said. I would hope you would take this subject under advisement and come to a conclusion based on what has been said here today. I think the sentence I quoted out of Hansard is my complete case, both on my personal side and on my position as minister. I would ask, in view of the reluctance of the hon. member for Medicine Hat to withdraw the two charges, and in view of the charge made by the hon. member for Timiskaming who spoke in this debate today, that you consider the

evidence you have before you and decide your future course at your leisure.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that is an excellent suggestion, that the matter be taken under advisement and that no more time of the house be taken at present. Because it is a very serious matter, I hope, when Your Honour does so, Your Honour will also examine some speeches made in the house by the senior hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, also imputing motives to another privy councillor.

subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Acting on very sound advice, I will take the matter under advisement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. HAMILTON    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR MEDICINE HAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before we proceed with the orders of the day I have a question for the Secretary of State. I want to ask the Secretary of State what imputation he was placing on the hon. member for Queens, in his absence, when he suggested to Your Honour that you examine some statement the hon. member for Queens had made. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to spend a little time on this question of the national museum and the situation which exists there and has existed for some time. I think it is interesting to note that there has been trouble and dissension in this organization since 1956; at least it began to appear in 1956. I think it is also of interest that there have now been three different administrations involved, the St. Laurent, the Diefenbaker and the Pearson administrations. Therefore I do not think one can say that this is really a one party issue. I tend to feel it is not necessarily a weakness in the ministerial approach, because we have had a succession of ministers of northern affairs and national resources and the situation has kept on developing. In other words I think there is something inherent in the administration of the museum and the personalities within the permanent administration which is the cause of quite a few of the difficulties.
This tale of the national museum is one of the most complicated I know. It is not a very large organization as government organizations go, yet it has been filled with more malice and sensation than any other part of this department.

speechtext:
I have been asked by the parliamentary secretary whether I would give them the same break some time. I am sure the parliamentary secretary knows what a co-operative group of people we are. We have just had recent evidence of that during the question period.
This museum trouble has broken out into the open again with some opinions expressed by the former director, Dr. Loris Russell. The minister in a sense tried, I will not say to slur over the issues raised by Dr. Russell, but he did not really come to grips with the problem. I have a mass of material I could go into, everything from archaeologists' bibliographies to the whole question of the kind of administrative controls which have existed in the museum, but I should like to try to approach the subject from some distance.
It seems to me-this is an honest opinion which I should like to put before the minister-that in all the information I have been able to gather, the one weak point in the whole business in a personal way relates to the now deputy minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, Mr. Cote. In fairness I would like to explain why I think this is so. Ever since Dr. Rousseau was approached to come to the national museum, ever since it was decided that in order to bring Dr. Rousseau in, even though he was a botanist, and put him into the human history branch, thus effectively putting someone who should, from his background at least, have been on the natural history side, we have had two natural history types, Dr. Russell and Dr. Rousseau, heading two departments. Ever since that time the difficulties have developed. Mr. Cote was deeply involved in bringing Dr. Rousseau into the museum, and he was also deeply involved in all the recriminations which followed. As I understand it, I think the minister will acknowledge that although the previous deputy minister, Mr. Robertson, was not exactly at arms length with the museum, the main channel


through which the museum was administered by the department was Mr. Cote as acting deputy minister.
I suggest that a great many of the problems we have had with the museum must arise from some kind of inadequacy in the objectives and the kind of approach he has had to the museum. I am not sure that this situation has been cleaned up at all. Dr. Rousseau was, in a sense, given the gate. Dr. Russell has resigned, I take it from his account in the paper, to consider his situation because of the fact that he was not made over-all head. We have had a historian brought in from the University of Manitoba, for what good reason I am unable to fathom. Without being uncomplimentary to this gentleman's academic record, about which I have made some inquiries, there is nothing, it seems to me, in Dr. Glover's documents which would indicate he is the man we should have been looking for to fill this particular post. He has not, within an academic framework, had a career of the kind which would lead him to be the head of a department of even a relatively small university. The field in which he specializes has no more relevance to the museum and its purpose than a host of other studies.
Once again there seems to be a reaching out to get someone to come in without any real explanation of how his training and background would permit him to give the kind of leadership which this part of the museum will need. The move might be interpreted as being in response to the criticisms of the Canadian historical association; at least it is suggested by Dr. Russell that there were such criticisms. Dr. Russell seems to feel that it was criticism by the historians which prevented him from moving up into the top position.
I do not know what views the minister has, or may have, as to the role a museum should play; whether it should have a split capacity and deal with human history on the one hand and natural history on the other. I do not know whether he thinks the emphasis should be on research or on display. But I know there has to be a clear policy in this regard, a policy spelled out over a number of years in terms of dollars and cents in the estimates in order to achieve the desired objective, because there is bound to be competition.
We have the example of a similar situation in the federal civil service where the national library and the public archives are under one director. I have heard criticism of this arrangement because of the fact that the aims of the archives and the aims of the library are not on all fours; there are

differences in emphasis. It seems to me that if we cannot create a separate crown agency, a body with a genuine feeling for the subject matter itself, we should consider separating these two branches completely, that is the human history and the natural history branches. We might, on the one hand, have a natural history or a natural science museum, and on the other hand have the kind of museum which emphasizes human history and which is related to anthropology, archaeology, sociology and subjects such as those.
The pettiness involved in the situation we are considering is enormous. It so happens that one of the key figures involved in this museum question is a friendly acquaintance of mine. He has left the museum now. He is an archaeologist. I know from my contacts with him that the world of the archaeologist and the anthropologist is filled with controversy. There are different schools of thought. There are personality clashes entering into the field of scholarship. Their world is not a wide one, and in Canada we do not have a great number of people working in either of these two fields. We tend to bring into this country the controversies which split the academic world in the United States in these two fields of study.
This being the case, it does not seem to me there is any possibility of breaking out of the present rut unless we get an outstanding man, a world figure, to fill this particular post. It is apparent there will always be restiveness in the fields of anthropology and archaeology, particularly if work in the area of research has to be under the direction of a straight historian. I think only the most broadminded historian, someone with the highest of status in terms of international reputation, would be acceptable to the people working in anthropology and archaeology in this field.
I suggest to the minister that Dr. Glover, with all due respect to his accomplishments, hardly fills this role. He does not straddle the field of history in Canada or in North America with any genius. But, I should like to suggest, it is someone with a personality and reputation of this kind who is necessary if we are to bridge these other conflicts and establish a successful human history museum.
Another thing which disturbs me about the national museum is this. Dr. Russell suggests that politicians have been too much involved in this whole matter. I am trying to figure out who he means by "politicians". Is it Mr. Lesage, who in co-operation with Mr. Cote went to such lengths to get Dr. Rousseau into the museum? Is it the former minister of northern affairs, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who played politics with the museum? We do not know. Is it the present
Supply-Northern Affairs minister who is playing politics with the museum? Is there a suggestion that the appointment of Dr. Glover is a political appointment? We do not know. These are questions which the minister does not necessarily have to answer in terms of the past, but I think he should project a future in which no political interference will be brought to bear in connection with the museum's affairs.
There have been a number of appointments to the staff of the museum which intrigue me, particularly in the field of archaeology. I do not intend to discuss them at length because I have put a number of questions on the order paper in connection with them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been checking what I said before the lunch break, and I think it could be construed that I was unfair to Dr. Glover who was appointed to look after the human history aspect of the museum. I wanted to make it quite clear that when I said I had checked into his career I was informed by certain people that in historical circles he has not been one of the giants of the history profession in Canada, but he certainly has done good work and has at least several outstanding publications to his credit.
One other conclusion I came to was that I should have put on the record part of what Dr. Loris Russell said in his interview the other day in Toronto in order to put the thing in focus. I think it would look pretty scrambled on the basis alone of my preceding remarks. I am taking these quotations from the Ottawa Citizen of two days ago, December 11. This is Dr. Russell's story:
From 1930-37 I was at the national museum and I left to go to Toronto as a University of Toronto professor and a member of the Royal Ontario museum staff. In 1950 I was approached by the then chief curator of the national museum, Dr. F. J. Alcock. He said he was going to retire and wanted me to succeed him.
I came to Ottawa and while working at the national museum I learned in 1954 that there was a movement under way to make Dr. Jacques Rousseau the director. In fact, Dr. Rousseau had

Supply-Northern Affairs been promised the job by people who forgot it was a civil service position and would be awarded by competition.
I should like to interject here that I understand from information I have received from several sources that the deputy minister, Mr. Cote, was involved in this whole arrangement to bring Dr. Rousseau here. I do not know what were the main reasons for it. I do not know whether it was an attempt to strengthen French Canadian representation at one higher level in the civil service, but he was involved in it. As a matter of fact I understand he even helped Dr. Rousseau prepare his application to the civil service commission.
In 1956 the position came up for competition, and I won it.
I understand from information I have that Dr. Russell won it on the basis of the fact that he had the advantage of overseas service. All other things being equal, this gave him an advantage. Dr. Russell goes on to say:
There was a big hassle and the events that followed were slightly incredible. They were stuck with somebody they didn't want.
To get out of this mess they decided to split the national museum into two separate sections -the Canadian museum of human history with Dr. Rousseau as director and the Canadian museum of natural history with myself as director. They used the Massey commission report-
When he says "they" I presume he is talking about the senior administrators and the politicians of the day, which in this sense would be Jean Lesage who was minister of the department and, I would also assume, the deputy and assistant deputy ministers of the department.
They used the Massey commission report of 1951 to justify this act. The division would never have been made if I hadn't won the competition. It was an excuse to get themselves out of a mess. I found this out years later and I can't be contradicted-I know this to be a fact.
I also know it to be a fact. This is an example of what happens when you try to do something in order to achieve purposes that do not quite fit into the administrative structure. Dr. Russell goes on:
I protested this on grounds that you need a strong museum, not a lot of small uninfluential segments. I said this division was bad in 1956 and in 1957 the government could not get this bill creating two museums through the House of Commons. It was a piece of parliamentary clumsiness. They muffed it.
Again, I understand that by "they muffed it" he really means the minister and the senior officials.
So they created two branches of the national museum with both of them holding equal powers. We got along well for two years with no quarrels, no friction, although some people on the staff were working for us both.

I want to interject here that they created these two branches and put a man in charge of the human history branch who was not really experienced in that field. I think this is important to show how far the government and the administration of that time were prepared to wrench things to achieve, I suppose, although I am not exactly sure, a better French Canadian representation in the senior levels of government.
There is some poetic irony here because the people in most bitter and violent disagreement with Dr. Rousseau were the same people who used their power and influence for him in 1956.
I take it he means Mr. Cote, who helped to push Dr. Rousseau into this position and then was the main instrument in getting him out when things turned a few years later.
Dr. Rousseau was forced out and it was a bitter blow to him. As far as I know we parted friends and I hold no grudge.
The human history branch was in a dreadful state and deputy minister Gordon Robertson asked me to take over as a single director of a single museum. I agreed to act as director of natural history and acting director of human history.
But I was instructed to function as a single director-at no increase in pay-and I said I would not be bound to serve under a dual directorship again.
In the next few years I made it my main business to rebuild the human history branch. I added new staff, leaned over to assure the staff that I was not less interested in their work than the natural history branch. Finally we had a very nice organization flourishing with first class men on the staff.
But in 1960 I began to worry. The centennial year was coming and nothing was being done. There was a lot of talk but no concrete proposals.
I made it my centennial project to collect Canadiana on my own authority. We needed historical exhibits-ours were all anthropological. Everyone told me I was ten years late-now they say there wouldn't be anything if I hadn't started on my own authority.
To add to our problems the present national museum building was condemned in 1961 and public works said it would have to come down. We began to plan for a national museum with a great store of Canadian historical exhibits. The cabinet approved a series of yearly grants of $50,000 for this search for articles.
Now, in Ottawa, we have the greatest collection of Canadiana anywhere. It represents the history of the people-tells how they lived. I wasn't looking for bargains. I wanted to get the material before it had all gone into the United States.
It was all there-almost completely telling the story of Canadian life from the seventeenth to early twentieth century.
It was beginning to create a lot of excitement amongst historians. I had tried to get a historian on the staff-but I wanted one who would appreciate my point of view.
This is where I ran into trouble. The historians began to complain. They weren't interested in museums but they wanted a professional historian to run the historical section of the new museum.
Many of them were critical. I wanted to show people how Canadians lived.
I think it is interesting that Dr. Russell wanted to do this because this was not his

field primarily. His training was on the natural history side of things. I continue to quote from the article:
The historians wanted to show people relics from famous battles-they wanted to tell the military and political history all over again. I say this is best done in books.
Under their fire I became a little tactless and wrote a critical article saying historians were not interested in the museum. I said a historian must work with a qualified museum expert to create a great historical museum.
Apparently you do not talk to historians like this. It caused a great ruckus and one member of the Canadian historical association-
I have heard that this was Dr. Hilda Neatby.
-wrote the Prime Minister saying Russell must go. One letter was so abusive they wouldn't show it to me. I'd like to challenge that person to come out and say to my face what he said behind my back.
Great pressure was put on to get me out. An advisory committee to the minister was appointed and it appointed a subcommittee to advise it. These committees decided the new museum's historical section would be strictly military and political with only a passing reference to social history. I had lost that one.
In December of 1962 it was decided to appoint a new director of human history with equal power to mine-back to the old scheme which failed before. I hoped they would eventually appoint a director general and I decided to wait for a year.
Two qualified museum experts were among those who entered the competition for the job. When the smoke cleared-
I want to emphasize this phrasing.
When the smoke cleared Professor Richard Glover of the University of Manitoba won the job. He is a qualified historian but he has absolutely no museum experience and this was in the terms of reference for the job.
I should like the minister to explain to us something about that competition. I understand that a gentleman from Nova Scotia and another gentleman who was in the historical names section were also involved in the competition. I think in the light of the charges that have been made it would be a good idea if the minister indicated where these two people fell short and where Dr. Glover came through in this particular competition. I think it is especially fair that this should be done in the light of the things which happened between Dr. Russell and Dr. Rousseau and what that competition led to. I continue to quote:
This changed the situation. I met the new deputy minister Ernest Cote at the earliest opportunity. He has great enthusiasm and is a capable administrator but he is neither a scientist nor a museum man. His answers to me were frank but they were all wrong as far as I was concerned. I decided to resign,
I want that point to be remembered in connection with my suggestion that the root of much of the difficulty in the museum is the role played by Mr. Cote as administrator.
28902-5-370
Supply-Northern Affairs He is a capable administrator and he has great enthusiasm, as Dr. Russell says, but he is neither a scientist nor a museum man. I would judge from some of the things in which he has been involved that he has no clear idea where the museum should be going. I should like to continue reading:
I resigned because the situation had become impossible. You cannot have a museum of political and military history without arousing controversy. You have to pay homage to French Canada when you mention Canadian history and some segments do not concern French Canada.
Whether they like it or not they will have to use the material I have collected. And I personally do not think the new building will be ready in 1967.
The national museum must have unified direction and the director must have the status of the deputy minister and have access to the minister direct.
I should like to ask the minister whether these suggestions by Dr. Russell, which have already been put forward by other people, are not worth considering. If I understand correctly, Dr. Lamb who is head of the public archives and the national library, has the status of a deputy minister. It certainly seems to give him executive power, and this would be a means of having the control that has been missing in most cases. I continue to quote:
He must be a man with a blending of scholarly status and museum experience and he must have the confidence of the entire staff. The national museum should be a senior museum in Canada and people must be able to look up to it. They cannot look up to it now.
Political sniping at individual museum staff members must stop. Certain M.P.s have been doing this since the Rousseau incident. The best help the M.P.s can give the museum is to leave it alone. If individuals are not protected from outside political attack it will kill the museum as sure as an axe in the head of an ox.
I quite agree with him in connection with that last point. I probably have been one of those he is thinking about in terms of placing questions in order to find out what has been going on there. This is the reason I should like to close with the emphasis that we should, as much as possible, leave the past history of the museum alone.
However, I consider we cannot do that unless we get some fairly clear indication from the minister as to what he is going to do, for example, about putting the museum under a single head, or else making a completely clearcut situation as between the natural history section and the human history section. I think we need to know what the minister's feelings are, particularly in the field of archaeology and anthropology, about the difference that is envisaged in the research function and development of archaeology; whether there will be a research program right across the country which is

Supply-Northern Affairs led by the national museum's branch, or whether there is going to be a double function. Again, I do not believe he has given us as yet any clear answers.
I would hope that after the minister gives his policy, and the direction the museum is going, the political sniping will stop. We have a wonderful example here, over the years since 1956, of what a mess a place can get into when politicians and senior administrators at the top try to bend an institution in order to achieve objectives that have very little to do with the objectives of the institution itself. That is the way I read the Rousseau case and all the consequences that flowed from it.
I suggest that the minister has not had a great deal of time to determine what should be done with the museum and the kind of direction he is going to give it, but I would also suggest he has not got much time to make the decisions, because this is one of the responsibilities that rest upon him. For that reason I would ask him to be as clear and unequivocal as he can in response to these points and, further, if he cannot be definitive, that he undertake to do so within a certain period of time.
I have one final point. It seems to me Dr. Russell indicates he has no wish to come back but I still say, in view of the commendations I have heard with regard to his administration, that he should be kept in mind as someone who can still make a great contribution, and I would not assume that his role in the Royal Ontario museum is necessarily a die cast forever.

Mr. Chairman, I have known something about the museum and its operations for some time, particularly going back to the session of 1956-57, at which time I received information from a newspaperman, now deceased, as to the peculiar manoeuver-ing and finangling that was going on in so

far as the museum was concerned. As a result, when the bill was brought in to split the museum in two I opposed it, and we were able to block the passage of the bill because the election of 1957 was then about to be held. However, in spite of that fact they went ahead and split the museum into two parts without having any legislative authority to do so, and I think the troubles of the museum sprang from that action.
I do not propose to go back over the history of the matter and rake up a lot of old straw. However, I do think there is no question but that the difficulties in the museum, which have continued from that time, sprang from the attempt to divide it into two parts, and all the difficulties and jealousies came into being at that time. I do not think there is any point in attempting to attack officials, either past or present, over what took place.
We would like to see the museum put on a good, sound basis so there will be no continuation of the troubles in future. In order to accomplish that I think it is essential to restore the museum as one united organization with one head, a director general; and we must get the right man for that job, a man who knows museum work and who has the personality and ability to handle the job. We should then give him the authority to go ahead and organize the museum in an effective manner. There will be trouble in the museum until action along that line is taken. I do not want to take up any more time of the committee in discussion, but I hope that course of action will be followed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to take advantage of this item to say a few words, because I have been interested in this subject and problem for a number of years. Anyone who has any knowledge of the affairs of the museum knows there has been a very unsatisfactory state of affairs in it for a good number of years, under the former Liberal government and under the previous government, and unfortunately this state of affairs continues.
My interest has been prompted as the result of conversations with a good number of people in Ottawa who are interested in the museum, and as a result of conversations with other people interested in it. I discussed this matter with the staffs of other museums in Canada, and have some correspondence on it. It is obvious that the state of affairs that exists in the museum is a subject for discussion in museums across Canada by people who are interested in this question, and it is also a subject for discussion by people in other countries.

In that connection I want to read a letter which I received from the director of the Instituto Interamericano dated November 13, 1963. It reads:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
We have been interested in the affairs of the national museum of Canada for some time since our organization is dedicated to the study of man and his activities, past and present, and the dissemination of knowledge thereof. We have kept in touch with the museum's stormy affairs through the Canadian press. I enclose a copy of our current newsletter that you may see how things look to us at the moment.
He then draws my attention to page 5, which is a critical analysis of the circumstances that exist in the museum.
While our area of interest is world wide, we are perhaps best informed on the U.S. and Latin America. For this reason we are curious about certain points and facts which seen uniquely Canadian.
First of all, why is it that the museum is administered by the northern affairs committee?
That question is asked by people in Canada too.
It would seem more logical for it to be administered by the secretary of public education as in Latin America or by an autonomous board of directors subject directly to the prime minister or the parliament. I admit my unfamiliarity with Canada's internal affairs.
We have received a considerable amount of printed material regarding the location of the site of the battle of the Long Sault where Dollard des Ormeaux gained fame. Our material may have been somewhat biased but it appears to us that the evidence is overwhelmingly on the side of the site excavated by Thomas E. Lee. Yet we understand that officially the site is located elsewhere. Is this a political matter as one of our sources said?
That too has been asked by a number of persons in Canada.
A third point involves the museum staff. It is rather odd that twice within four years there should be wholesale resignations either voluntary or forcibly. Is this due to internal stresses or is it also a matter of politics as also has been suggested by published articles?
I suppose that all of this is really none of our affair but we are intensely interested and greatly involved in anthropology in the Americas and this museum matter affects Canadian anthropology gravely. Moreover, we have always had a very warm feeling for Canada and her people.
Sincerely yours,
Carl B. Compton, director.
There have also been articles in the French Canadian press dealing with certain aspects of the museum's operations and organization, and numerous articles in professional publications that would be read by people interested in museums. There has been a lot of questioning as to the type of organization that exists and as to the most unfortunate circumstances that exist between various members of the staff. I have heard the most amazing stories about people who are well 28902-5-370J
Supply-Northern Affairs paid by the government of Canada, arriving at the museum at eleven o'clock and doing an hour's work. I do not know whether they are true or not, but I had dozens of letters written to me in Ottawa, and something has been brought to my attention recently that shakes my belief in the validity of information given to this house by the officials.
I have definite proof that one publication filed by Mr. Taylor as a professional publication, a publication to which a man could lay claim because it was part of his professional publications, was nothing more than a commercial pamphlet distributed in this country and in Great Britain for the purpose of selling tents and camping equipment. This well paid official had one paragraph in this commercial pamphlet, which we were informed in this house, in reply to questions asked by the hon. member for Port Arthur was a publication.
This gives rise to lack of confidence, Mr. Chairman. In fairness to those who are doing their duty, those who are unfairly criticized, and so on, I am of the opinion that this situation requires a thorough investigation. It would be too much to expect the minister to rise in his place and give the answers to all these problems immediately. He must have time to thoroughly investigate the situation. I suggest there should be an investigation into the organization of the museum, after the minister has taken the advice of the best persons available, as to the functions of the staff, the duties they perform, their hours of work, publications, and things of that sort; in fact, all things related to the organization and operation of the museum. I think the minister must have time to organize his inquiry, as it were.
I suggest, in conclusion, that it might be a good idea to have the estimates of the museum referred next session-there is not time this session-to the committee on mines, forests and waters, where the officials could be examined and the committee would have the opportunity to call qualified persons from other museums. Then we would be in a position to treat the matter properly, to be fair to the staff concerned and sift out, shall I say, the weaknesses. This committee could then do something as the result of advice from qualified persons. They could make some recommendations to clear up this situation once and for all, so that in the future Canadians can be proud of their national museum, its operations and the way it is carried on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been listening with interest to the discussion on this item, vote No. 120, and it seems to me most of the discussion thus far has been concerned with a period in the museum's development that goes back to the years 1956-57

Supply-Northern Affairs when, as hon. members have indicated, there was a series of difficulties which finally had to be aired in the House of Commons. Some mention has been made of the fact that there has been continuing interference by the politicians with the activities of the museum. I believe this came from the statement reported in the press the other day which purported to come from the former director, Dr. Loris Russell.
I should like to introduce another note into this discussion. This has nothing to do with interference by politicians as being germane to the difficulties of the museum. That is another difficulty. I refer to the problems of housing the national museum. Over the past few years there has been a chronic shortage of space and at least attempts to formulate plans that would overcome this difficulty. Hon. members will recall that following the evacuation of the old Victoria building by the national gallery and the Canadian geological survey it was felt that at long last the old building would be adequate to meet the reasonable needs of an expanding museum. Unfortunately that decision had no sooner been reached than it was discovered that the Victoria building was unstable and not suitable for the purposes that fall to the development of a national museum.
I happened to be the responsible minister when this further crisis arose. At that time the departmental officials immediately tackled the problem of finding suitable and adequate housing accommodation. At the time of the change of government I think hon. members will recall there was legislation before the house to provide for a completely new plant facility to be built in time to coincide with the observance of Canada's one hundredth birthday in 1967. It seems to me this is one of the essential problems to be overcome in creating in Canada a museum that is worthy of a nation like Canada. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the sooner we in this house get on with the legislation that was proposed last year to provide for adequate facilities, the sooner we can come to grips with some of the other problems of the Canadian national museum.
During the three years I was responsible for the national museum I believe I enjoyed reasonably warm and cordial relationships with the dedicated personnel there, particularly the director and assistant director. Once the decision had been reached to establish adequate facilities it seemed that many of the major difficulties had been overcome. It was disturbing to me to find that once again difficulties-and this was information I gleaned from the press-had occurred amongst the very competent personnel engaged in museum work. What is at the basis of those difficulties

I cannot say, but I repeat that we must move with all haste toward the passing of legislation that will make it possible for the parliament of Canada to provide adequate facilities to house Canada's national museum.
There have been expansions in recent years on what might be called an ad hoc basis. The national aviation museum was officially opened in 1960. I am sure anyone who has had the opportunity of visiting that museum, which is housed at the present time in the terminal building at Uplands airport, will come to the conclusion that here is a display of Canadian aviation history which is worthy of our nation. I am sure that once we have provided through legislation for the type of accommodation that is necessary, there will be a further unification of the various aspects of museology. The aviation museum, for example, will be brought under the same roof as the museum of natural history and human history. The accommodation that was contemplated at the time of the change in government had this in view. The aviation museum would have become the nucleus for a museum of science, something that is entirely lacking in the present organizational set-up. Under discussion as well was the possibility, or the probability, of bringing the war museum under the one roof that would be provided. This might again be one aspect of the museum of science to which I have already referred.
I do believe it is essential, if the organizational structure of the Canadian national museum is to be rational-if it is to be organized in the best interests of efficiency- to have an over-all director with separate heads of staff for the various branches that would be required to provide leadership in the various areas of Canadian history.
I would be interested in hearing the minister's comments about the present state of the legislation which was contemplated last year, and how soon we might anticipate its being brought before this house so that it might be dealt with by parliament as a whole. As has been pointed out in the letter quoted by the hon. member for Kootenay West, it is not in the best interests of Canada to have these periodic explosions amongst the highly trained scientific personnel which, of necessity, must be the kind of people employed in museums, disturbances which receive considerable airing in the public press and the type of critical comment which has been placed on the record by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
Just by way of a further thought on this matter, the hon. member who has just spoken raised a point, which is of some significance, about the department of northern affairs being the most suitable branch of government

to have supervisory and administrative responsibility for the museum. We all know that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources came into being in 1954 and under its wing were included all kinds of interesting activities, which found a home in the department because they were largely orphans in other departments. As an example of this kind I refer to the Canadian government travel bureau, which for a number of years came under the purview of the minister of northern affairs and which a year ago was returned to the Department of Trade and Commerce because it was thought that this was a more suitable department to handle these activities. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that some thought might be given by the government and by the very competent officials who have worked with the government on these matters as to whether northern affairs is the most suitable departmental home for an activity of this kind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the previous speaker, and I must say it had not occurred to me that there was anything inappropriate in the national museum being within the purview of the department of national resources, which I have always felt was the wing under which such a repository or record of our national resources, human and otherwise, should properly come. I should like to hear the present minister make some comment on this matter of museum accommodation referred to by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. I think this is a very important question in the consideration of some of the matters raised in this discussion.
One point I should like to make is this. I am not at all sure that our national museum, with much interest focused on it, should be accommodated in the city of Ottawa or its environs. Such little real association as I have had with the museum as a member has arisen out of the desire of some of the people on the west coast of Canada to have brought back to the west coast some of the items which years ago were taken to Ottawa. A great many of our Indian peoples would like to have back some of their potlatch regalia which was removed from them; they say it was confiscated, although I have understood from time to time that the authorities in Ottawa tend to claim they were in fact paid for it.
In view of some of the discussion which has taken place regarding some of the unhappy aspects of the affairs of our national museum, I should like to say that in course of dealing with this question I had occasion to discuss it both with Dr. Rousseau and Dr. Russell. If there were any differences of
Supply-Northern Affairs outlook or any disturbances within the inner workings of the museum I should like to mention, so as to introduce a more cheerful note into the discussion, that as far as dealing with me on this particular question was concerned they concealed those things very well, and I found my dealings with them very satisfactory.
I should also like to say that as far as I was able to determine their outlooks on this particular question were similar. I met with a good deal of sympathetic consideration for the idea that there was a place for the functioning of our national museum outside the boundaries of our capital city of Ottawa. I put forward this point of view at this time in the hope that the present minister will deal sympathetically as a matter of policy with the suggestion that provision be made to assist the growth and development in other centres of the country of an interest in museum affairs, and that a national museum, centred in Ottawa and operating under wing of the minister of national resources, should consider as one of its functions the stimulation of the growth and development of interest in museum displays in a smaller way in many centres of the country.
One idea which appeals to me and which I explored in discussions with both the gentlemen to whom I referred a moment ago was the idea of providing small displays for some of the smaller centres, the title to which might well remain with the national museum but which could be placed on loan in such centres for a period of time. I hope, no matter what changes may be made in the organization and structure of the museum, that this idea will be kept in mind and that the policies which are developed, in addition to providing adequate accommodation for central displays here in Ottawa, will be such as to encourage opportunities for Canadians in other parts of the country to have a sense of proprietary interest in some of our national heritage which properly belongs to museums both national and local.

Supply-Northern Affairs
This amount is allocated to the administration, operation and maintenance of the national museum of Canada. That is why we are of the opinion that the Canadian people, not only in Ottawa but throughout Canada, should know about the national museum and what it should mean to them. The national museum should be an attraction for visitors from this country and elsewhere.
As for visitors from outside, I am under the impression that, the moment they get to Ottawa, they think the federal parliament is the national museum. That is just because they cannot tell what the national museum is all about. They do not know what is going on there. As a matter of fact, there are many who ask themselves whether the national museum is not to be found in the other place.
Mr. Chairman, it is all very well to speak of the history of the war and of aviation, but I think the history of Canada should also have its exhibits in the museum. There, one should be able to go over all the history of our country, from the beginning of the colony, in 1534, to this day. Something attractive should be set up, considering the amount of money devoted to this item and which the Canadian people is required to pay.
I heard a while ago a member from the official opposition state that politicians must not interfere in any way with the national museum. Mr. Chairman, I have full confidence in the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) because I feel he is not himself a politician and will not interfere with the administration of the national museum.
On the other hand, I repeat my view so that this museum will have great significance for visitors and the Canadian people as a whole.
And if some day the national museum has to be expanded we might then suggest to the minister to find room there for the orthodox economists and sociologists who are still advocating the maintenance of an obsolete system in Canada. When that happens, visitors will be extremely interested to see those people mummified at the national museum.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It might be the wish of the hon. members that I endeavour to make some reply on each main item as we go along rather than leave all my observations to the end. I want to say at once that I appreciate very much the interventions which have been made by hon. members, the criticisms which has been expressed and the advice which has been given me for my direction in the future.
I would like to say to the hon. member for Port Arthur that I thought he was more
[Mr. Caouette.l
prone to point at the flat tire than to push on the wrench. That, however, is his responsibility and I am quite prepared to take the observations he made. I am going to admit at once that the museum has been the most unhappy part of a department which otherwise, I believe, has been a very happy ship.
This is a situation which has existed over a number of years. Like the hon. member for Calgary North, I do not wish to thrash old straw, although I would have no objection to doing so if there were more grain in it. I think probably his suggestion that we must have some strong central direction of the museum is very sound. I think some of our troubles have arisen from the fact that there was more than one skipper on the ship. I think we shall probably need to make an investigation of whether an exceedingly competent scientist is always an exceedingly competent administrator. I am rather of the opinion that the reverse may be the case, and I think in the arrangements we shall have to make our first responsibility will be to find a competent administrator. I think a competent administrator, one who has a knowledge of human beings, will attract to him people who are extremely well qualified in the work of the various branches which are required within a museum.
With respect to this work, I should like to impress upon members of the committee that these are no longer just dusty studies of bygone days. They have a real application to the times in which we live. These things are not all in the attic. Many of them are in our living rooms and could be the source of worth while developments from a number of viewpoints.
I wonder how many members of the committee have been to our museum recently. I would like to suggest that it be a required visitation on their part; because in these years when we have had all these troubles, the last five or six years, a tremendous amount of magnificent work has been done by the men there. I could mention the displays in the Eskimo hall, the hall of mammals, the marvellous collection of Indian masks and the Lord Bossom collection, all of which are a tremendous asset to our museum.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And the mineral collection.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, and the mineral collection. The suggestion was made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that we should send parts of our exhibitions around the country. I think that is a splendid idea and one which could be worked out. We did this when part of the Baddeck exhibition was sent to the Vancouver Pacific international exhibition early this year, and it would seem to me that from

time to time we should consider taking portions of these splendid exhibits and sending them to various parts of the country.
I do not want to revive the animosities and distress surrounding the severances and departures of recent years, because I do not think it would improve the position of those who have left. But I do accept the situation as being a serious one. Others including Dr. Russell-I think six or seven men with doctorates-have left us in recent years. I return to the belief that we must have a unified central administration in the hands of a competent administrator, and I think we shall start from there. So I can promise those members who have contributed beneficially to this discussion that I intend to pay particular attention myself, as minister, to the affairs of this branch. I have studied book after book on the history of the museum in recent years, and they make a doleful tale.
As I say, I intend to pay particular attention in my capacity as minister to trying to establish some peace there and to provide for some progressive work to be done. I can assure hon. members that the days of surgery are over but the days of medication are about to begin. That is a promise I can make to the committee, and I think it will work. I suggest to hon. members that they can hold me responsible a year from now, by which time I think we shall have made some progress.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I just have one question. Some years ago the museum housed a Kootenay canoe, a type of canoe not found anywhere else in North America. That canoe collapsed. The officials of the day having responsibility ordered another one to be built by one or two of the surviving Indians who could build such a canoe and $400 was paid for it. I have paid several visits to the museum to try to find the canoe but without success to date. Can the minister tell us where it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will find out for the hon. member where his canoe is. I think he has implied that he supports the view of my predecessor in office, that we simply have to get a new building and new accommodation and the sooner we do that the better. I want to remind the committee that from 1916, when the fire took place in the central building here and when some of the functions of parliament were removed to the museum building as it now exists, until the year 1960 we did not have sole occupation of that building for our own purposes. We have a great number of excellent things that should be on display to the Canadian public, items that would attract scholars from other parts of Canada to make
Supply-Northern Affairs studies of them in this atmosphere, but they are hidden away and will remain hidden away until we get a new building. I want to tell my predecessor that the general plans for the building are all drawn. We require only some detailed plans. I am informed by my officers that the building can still be ready to be opened in late 1966 or 1967, and that will be our objective.
Item agreed to.
