maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize that everyone is quite anxious to get some of these estimates through but I should like to say a few words particularly about Banff national park, which is situated in my constituency of Bow River. This year more than a million people visited Banff national park, I believe, and one of the problems that no doubt troubles the departmental administrators and will trouble the new minister as it has troubled other ministers arises from the premise spelled out in the National Parks Act in relation to what goes on in the parks.
I do not think I could refer to two better authorities than the Glassco royal commission report, volume 2, page 37, and page 2 of the Oberlander report entitled "Urban Development Plan". I wish to ask the minister some particular questions, but before doing so may I say to him seriously and with the greatest respect that there is some uneasiness among the people in the parks with regard to statements that have been made that they feel are not correct. I have asked the present minister certain questions on the orders of the day. On some occasions he has denied the reports that have appeared in the newspapers as to statements made by himself, and on other occasions he has left the matter up in the air. In view of these facts I say to him seriously that there is some uneasiness among the people who serve the tourist trade, which is probably the second major industry in Canada.
Before dealing with this question I think it is interesting to put on the record the basic problem that frustrates me as a member of parliament representing Bow River, and other members representing constituencies where there are national parks. It is a problem that must frustrate the administrators and the minister as well. I read now from page 37 of volume 2 of the Glassco report:
The National Parks Act declares that these lands are "dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment" and further



Supply-Northern Affairs
stipulates that they be maintained "so as to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations".
If I may interject there, Banff national park is not a small area of land. It contains more than 87 square miles. I believe I read somewhere some months ago, possibly in the Glassco report, that the park is the size of Prince Edward Island. So it is not a small area of land. The few acres that are taken up by the Banff townsite are so small that they are like a pinprick on mount Rundle. Therefore when we are realing with Banff townsite and Banff national park we must realize they are two distinct things, one being the townsite that serves tourists and the other the park itself.
This is what the Glassco report says, and this is the whole crux of the problem and why there has been friction from time to time between members of parliament and the minister, and between members of parliament and the administrators. I see the officials are in their places this afternoon. Probably the new minister will have a similar experience with regard to members who represent park areas because the problem is difficult. The report goes on to say:
This is somewhat of a contradiction in terms, and the provision of amenities and recreational facilities for the five million people annually visiting the parks has, of necessity, brought about physical changes in the countryside which rob it, in part, of its virgin character.
In other words, if we are going to have the world Olympics at Banff national park we have got to make up our minds what we are going to do. An island is being rebuilt for the world's fair, and some very definite changes are going to have to be made quickly with regard to Banff town-site and also the skiing site.
Are we going to run slam bang into the proposition set forth in the National Parks Act that these lands are dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment? What that means I am not just sure. I know there is no judicial interpretation, and the administrators have interpreted these words as they have seen fit, as their ambitions and visions have dictated from time to time.
Let us take a look at what the Oberlander report has to say on page 2:
Established primarily for the preservation of the natural landscape and for the protection of native wildlife, they are to be "maintained and made use of so as to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations".
I do not think that the fact that we allow some development of the townsite in order to serve tourists is going to run afoul of the preamble and intention of the act. In fact, I do not think the act says what some people
[Mr. Woolliams.l
believe it says. In my opinion it is being interpreted very narrowly, and from reading the Calgary Albertan recently I am inclined to think that the new minister agrees with me in that regard. But there is somewhat of a contradiction, because if you are going to attract tourists you must provide some facilities.
The extreme interpretation of the act is that the park should be fenced off so as to preserve those funny bears with their queer posteriors. Hon. members will recall when that came up in the house. That is the extreme viewpoint. The other viewpoint is that the park should be kept in its natural state as far as possible but that motel, swimming, camping and other facilities should be provided for tourists at certain places.
Even at the time when the minister of the department was a Conservative I said that when the Rogers pass road was opened there would be more people coming to Banff each year. The fact that more people visited Banff national park this year was not because there was a world's fair last year in Seattle. The fact is that people come to the parks of Canada for three reasons. First, they like Canada. Second, they like our parks. Third, they come because the dollar is pegged at 92J cents and they have more money to spend.
I think the administrators have a big say in the operation of the parks and I do not want to be unkind to them, but if I was critical at all it was because they lacked the vision that all these people were going to come to our parks. I do not want to give my source of information, but I have been told by a person who has lived in the parks for years, a person who is not in the restaurant business, the hotel business, the motel business or any other business whereby money is made out of tourists, but is in a capacity of some authority, that at one time people had to sleep in their cars in the park.
They could not find camp facilities because the camp grounds are crowded. I want to pay the former minister a compliment. There was a large development took place in connection with camp grounds under the previous administration. However, I must go this far and be fair by saying there is still not sufficient space provided to satisfy the number of visitors coming to Banff national park each year. Surely, after people drive 300 miles or 400 miles from the United States, after they have read these attractive ads that are costing the taxpayers of this country money, it is not fair to make them drive another 80 miles to the city of Banff to get accommodation.
This is a problem that was mentioned in the Glassco commission report. There seems to be a conflict as between some people as to

what the act means. Once we clear up that conflict, then we are on the road to getting satisfaction in these parts. I think that is the major problem. I will go this far: I know that everyone in the department is doing the things he honestly believes are correct. However, I say with the greatest respect that some individuals seem to have lacked vision in considering this matter.
I should like to take this opportunity to ask a few questions. I said there was some uneasiness in the parks with regard to the statements the minister has been making in the Albertan and the Calgary Herald. These statements have scared the people in the parks, and they have scared people like Mr. Bruce who has several times tried to get the Liberal nomination in that riding. It is not just the Conservatives who are scared, but the Liberals as well. Why are these people scared? Let me tell the minister this: For some time the department used to give 20 or 21 leases. Then, these leases were extended to 40 years or longer. This was the security of tenure on lands of persons who had invested in motels, restaurants and other facilities to look after the tourists. They made their investment in buildings, and they would have the security of tenure provided by these leases.
Now, recently, the minister stated that there was some question of the elimination of these leases. I do not know whether or not the minister made that statement, but it was reported in a Liberal newspaper, and because it was reported in a Liberal newspaper the Liberals believed it and so did the Tories. First of all, I think the minister should clarify that situation. Then, in that same article there was reference to the fact that people might have to pay land taxes. They have never paid land taxes in this area. These statements have unnerved the people. They expect an answer from the minister.
There is one matter that is sub judice, and I do not want to get into a court case. However, I do want to say that there is freehold land in the parks, and a large amount of it is owned by the Canadian Pacific-I do not know how many hundreds or thousands of acres. I want to say now that the Canadian Pacific does an excellent job of serving people from the United States and other parts of Canada who go to the parks. I am not being critical in that regard. However, there are other people who own land in the parks. I do not expect the minister to make a statement on this now because it is a big subject; but at some time I would like to hear from him an explanation of why it is that, over the years, land was expropriated from individuals. They were discriminated against, and 28902-5-371
Supply-Northern Affairs yet the land of the Canadian Pacific, that big corporation in this country, was not expropriated. I know it is said these decisions are made at the minister's level. I believe they are made at the administrative level and laid on the minister's desk.
Do you know how you expropriate land? You do not even notify the owner; you merely file an order in council. One group of individuals did not know they had lost their land until they wanted to make a transfer to somebody. They searched the land titles in the office at Calgary and they found a certain order in council. I can go further. When they came to me, I called the Canadian Pacific and they referred me to the head office. They did not know their oil rights were expropriated, and they are now very concerned. The previous government had suggested, and properly so, some changes in the law connected with expropriation. I was looking for such legislation. I would say this situation should be looked into by the new government. I want to say, too, that more and more individuals are being discriminated against but the Canadian Pacific holds its land on a freehold basis. I am not against freehold, and I want to make that point clear. I am against discrimination. I am against the method by which expropriation was accomplished.
I am not saying there were politics involved, but I know a man who was a friend of the late R. B. Bennett. He owned some 60-odd acres of land in the park and it was expropriated by the previous Liberal government. I do not say it was a coincidence, but I do say that if you leave the law of expropriation in this condition, whether it is a Conservative government or a Liberal government, you are going to find politics being played with land transfers in the park. It is time there was a clearcut policy from the minister and the department. This is a serious matter. The minister has not been too long in this portfolio, but this situation has continued for a long time. I might say that, at long last, like the Duke of Windsor, I can say a few words on my own. For five years I have wanted to say what I have said this afternoon. I am laying it right on the table. Here is a terrible situation. I want to say once again that individuals are being discriminated against. Why is it that the Canadian Pacific is allowed to hold land under freehold? If there should be a decision of the government approving the expropriation of freehold land in parks, then let us have it. I am against it because I believe that free enterprise can do a better job in the parks. I am certainly against any discrimination.

Supply-Northern Affairs
Now, that is point No. 1. Point No. 2 concerns a smaller matter, but it is an aggravating matter. For a number of years I have been asking that this be changed. It may be changed now, I am not sure. I wish the minister would assure the people it has been changed. People come into the parks and park their cars. They come to spend money, to see the mountains and live with nature.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, and some of them live with nature. They park their cars. Maybe they park them too long and they get a ticket. Normally, in any city you can go down to the police station and pay $2 or $3, whatever it is and settle the matter. What have you got to do in the parks? You have to stay over. You are charged with an offence, almost as if you committed a murder, and you have to appear before a magistrate. Please get that regulation fixed up. If you do that for me, Mr. Minister, I can assure you that when your estimates come up next year I will be most kind. People have been asking for this change for a number of years.
I just want to say a few more words about the school of fine arts. There is even a recommendation in the Oberlander report in that regard, that the school of fine arts should not be allowed to develop any further because it might spoil the look of the mountains. This is a big area, as big as Prince Edward Island. I think there are bears in the park that have not been seen by a human and vice versa, it is that large. I may say that the hon. Senator Cameron, if I may refer to him in a most courteous way, has done a tremendous job in developing the school of fine arts at Banff national park. Why was it developed there? Well, certainly the senator could give this information far better than I, because I am not a student of the fine arts. The fact is that a school of fine arts should surely be in Banff national park, the most beautiful place in the world, in that mountain atmosphere. Surely buildings which fit into the trees and mountains, in a space covering 8,700 acres, will not ruin the park? They are not going to scare the little animals and they are not going to hurt those great, big mountains. Let us take a broader look at this thing.
I want to be complimentary to the minister in this regard, because I go along with some of the things he has said. He has grasped the situation that there is a definite conflict-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: But neither of us want to scare Claude Brewster.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, we do not; but I am just going to show you how ridiculous this is. When Premier Manning of Alberta decided to build two art centres, one in Edmonton and

the other in Calgary, he wanted to use some of the stone that is found on mount Rundle. Now, mount Rundle is a fairly large hill. It is a pretty large place, and I am certain that somewhere on that mountain a little rock could have been taken out to build one building in Canada. But what happened? The premier could not get the rock. It could not be moved from the park, even with a truck, and so they shipped the stuff in from the United States, which doubled or tripled the cost. I may add that these two beautiful buildings in Calgary and Edmonton are a credit to the provincial administration, but surely the example I have given is carrying things too far.
There is a conflict between keeping all this place for nature and making use of it for other purposes. When one talks like this, especially around Calgary, people write editorials, and they are dirty editorials. They say you want dancing girls, pool halls, and everything else; but no one is suggesting that. I hope I make myself clear this afternoon. I am suggesting facilities suitable for the million and more people who visit the parks, and that these facilities should be extended to take care of more and more people who will come to visit the parks, and that this be done with real co-operation between the federal department and the provincial governments.
There is a little spot up in the north where a mine extends only a few feet into the national park, but if anyone were to put his hands across the dividing line he would have his fingers removed. This is carrying things a little too far. Again, the animals are not going to be scared by that little bit of encroachment.
It may be said that this will establish a precedent. In fact a lot of people criticize lawyers because they believe in precedents, but I have never seen a precedent that could not be changed, distinguished, or done away with by a court. Therefore I tell the minister not to be afraid, in dealing with the parks officials, if they tell him he is going to establish a precedent. The average person who thinks about the development of our parks is not concerned about that.
I congratulate the administrators; that is their job, to keep the parks in their natural state. But if we are going to have tourists we must have some development, and let us make it a reasonable development, and not a monopolistic development either. There was some suggestion, and I do not know whether this is correct or not, that the department was going to get into the building of motels. For goodness sake, it does not matter how socialistic a government may think we should become, freedom of enterprise does do a

better job when there is competition, and we can make certain that tourists from the United States and all over Canada can be provided with proper facilities without having the government getting into this kind of business.
There are three things I would say. This conflict must be straightened out. Second, for goodness sake take a look at the way expropriation is going on for the parks, and whether there is any discrimination. Under the present act there certainly could be. We should also determine whether it is fair to have certain forms of traffic regulations throughout Alberta, that encourage tourists to come to our parks, and then have other regulations that are medieval.
How many years does it take to make these changes? If the minister does the things I suggest, he will do a good job for the tourists, for the parks and for Canada. One of the most beautiful places anywhere for skiing is at lake Louise and Banff, and when the world Olympics come we will sell our parks as they are and develop good will all over the world. Look at what has been done in that connection in European countries. What has been done in Europe can be done in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I was listening to the hon. member for Bow River I remembered that the first time I came to this house I was seated immediately behind his predecessor, and I have come to the conclusion that, regardless of party affiliation, the hon. members for Bow River seem to show an almost obsessive concentration on the problems of Banff. I used to tell the former member that when one was travelling west, after spending a few weeks or months in eastern Canada, those mountains around Banff did not look too bad; but of course when one was travelling east, after having spent some time in British Columbia, those little pimples were hardly noticeable.
I have one or two suggestions for the minister which may help him solve some of his problems with the hon. member for Bow River, concerning the overcrowding of Banff.
I would point out that in my constituency we have some ice fields that would make the Columbia ice fields look pretty small. The hon. member for Bow River also talked about another vast expansion of park, but in the mount Waddington region there is mountain scenery that would make that at Banff rather pale in comparison, and which I hope will be made one of the great wilderness parks of Canada. However, I am not seriously proposing at the moment that this should be done immediately; but while we are discussing this item I would like to know how the 28902-5-371J
Supply-Northern Affairs minister is getting along in the discussions he has been having with the British Columbia provincial authorities in respect to national park development in the coastal areas of that province.
Earlier this session there were several references to Garibaldi park, and I would like to tell the minister that I have been receiving increasing representation from Vancouver island as to the desirability of Strathcona park and the Forbidden plateau area being developed as a national park. I have replied that the initiative for any such development would have to come from Victoria, because Strathcona park is a provincial park and comes within the jurisdiction of the province. But I have expressed the hope that if such a development would be within the wishes of the provincial authorities, then perhaps the matter would receive a favourable reception here in Ottawa, and I have indicated I would do everything I could to persuade the federal authorities of that desirability.
As I have said before in this house, it is a matter of great regret that while we do have these beautiful national parks in the eastern part of British Columbia, and in the adjacent area of Alberta, we have no federal park development in some of the beautiful park areas on the west coast. I would like the minister to tell us if there is any greater likelihood of his being able to make such proposals than there has been on various other occasions when this matter received discussion and attention here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just a very brief question to ask the minister. He might reply to it when he replies on the item concerning national parks. My question concerns the proposal for the establishment of a national park in the Yukon. As he knows- or may not know-there are two views in the Yukon with respect to the establishment of a national park. All the groundwork has been done, of course, through the efforts of parks branch officials who have very thoroughly investigated areas in the Yukon which might be suitable for the establishment of a park. The matter has come before the legislative council of the Yukon on more than one occasion for discussion, and I believe the minister will find in his departmental files certain submissions made by the Yukon chamber of mines, and other organizations in the Yukon.
One point of view is that we should have a park because tourism is essential to the growth of any economy, and certainly it is an important segment of the economy of the Yukon. In opposition to this view is that of the mining community, which is against the

Supply-Northern Affairs establishment of a national park because of the existing restrictions which would prevent geological exploration and development with any park boundaries which might be established. The Yukon has perhaps the largest area of nature in the raw of any area in Canada, with over 207,000 square miles available for the establishment of a park. One of the objections of the legislative council in the Yukon to the proposed location of the park was that it was to be located in an area of promising potential development adjacent to, for instance, the holdings of Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, where substantial low grade nickel deposits have been established.
All I would like the minister to do is tell us what the intentions are, in so far as the government is concerned, in connection with the establishment of the park. When he was in Whitehorse he spoke on the subject-it may not have been in Whitehorse, but certainly in one of the locations in the Yukon; perhaps Dawson City-of the establishment of a park. That might be a suitable area;
I do not know. Certainly the parks branch officials are much more capable than I to suggest the factors which should be present in the establishment of any park. But my understanding of the minister's remarks there was that such a park would be established, and just as quickly as possible. With those few brief remarks, Mr. Chairman, and the request to the minister to state the intentions of the government, I have nothing further to say on the item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister did state his intention was to reply to each item as it was raised. If he would follow that procedure, it would be very acceptable to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Yukon, I would say I assume we would be forced to regard the territorial government in the same light as we would a provincial government. Therefore I would very much hesitate to announce that we were going to place a national park in the Yukon without an agreement with or request from the territorial council of the Yukon. I know, as the hon. member knows, that this matter is under way up there. I think all it requires is a determination and agreement on their part that they are setting aside a piece of property with regard to which they can overlook the expression that "there's gold in them thar hills". I think it is a matter of deciding on a property which the mining interests agree is not worth working. I am quite certain that if an application were made by

the territorial council on that basis, the government of Canada is desirous of seeing to it now, particularly in the light of the coming centennial celebrations, that there be set aside such property for preservation in the future. That would be the attitude as far as the Yukon is concerned.
As far as my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni is concerned, we have latterly had indicated to us that there is a minute piece of property in the general region of cape Beale, on the west coast, which is available to us. I do not think this would interest us because of its size and location. I have not given up hope entirely in respect to Garibaldi. I have spoken to some of the ministers of the province of British Columbia and I would hope there is some chance yet of our having the government of British Columbia agree to turning that property over to us. I am quite convinced that as there are four or five national parks on the Atlantic coast, and not one of the Pacific coast, it is in the interests of the provincial administration that we have a national park on the Pacific coast. I am quite certain it would net the province of British Columbia $4 million or $5 million a year in holding back that great number of tourists coming into that province from the south, making a bee line toward Banff, because Banff is a historic name they have in their heads, and then using the ultra modern highways to get out of British Columbia as fast as they can. I am told by men who are familiar with areas which people enjoy in Europe that there is no comparable area anywhere in the European Alps with what can be developed in the Garibaldi area. I want to thank my hon. friend for mentioning Forbidden plateau. It too is a very considerable and renowned area in British Columbia and I think it should be given a great deal of attention as either provincial or federal parks are developed in the future.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the hon. member for Bow River. I enjoyed him very much and I am quite certain he enjoyed himself. I think all the estimates he ought to discuss should be in this department, because he was indeed humorous and at the same time gave us something to think about. I want to assure him that I made the statement that we are searching for a different and more equitable basis than the present one on long term leases in the park.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What does the minister mean by "more equitable"?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Well, a fair basis. I am thinking in terms of what might be called a business tax, rather than the situation that now exists.

My hon. friend dealt with the tremendous increase in the number of people. Historically the western parks attracted some wealthy Canadians and a great number of wealthy Americans, as he knows, who came through in trains in the old days. They set up in C.P.R. or Canadian National hotels, where all facilities were provided, and their holidays were very expensive over several weeks. There is a new torrent of trade now, which is due to the automobile, rubber tires, good highways and a number of other factors, including probably the 92 cents dollar, but also the relatively buoyant conditions of the economy of Canada, and statutory holidays with pay. Therefore Canadians who hitherto did not have the money with which to see Canada now have that money. It is a very fine thing that they do. We have to take care of the accommodation that they require in our parks. I agree in general with my hon. friend from Bow River that our parks are large enough, the topography there is of such a nature that we can put these tenting and camping locations and the requirements for trailers in areas where they will not deface the general landscape. This is what we are going to do.
The hon. member talked about historic leases. I have studied this question and have been astounded and amazed at what I found. There are leases for tiny sums of money that have been built up through the years, partly as a result of the monopolistic situation created by the establishment of the parks by a national government, into tradeable items of many thousands of dollars-and I do not like it. I am referring to leases of $7 or $9 a year, and I hear reliably that those leases are being traded for ten, twelve and fourteen thousand dollars. I suggested that we should arrive, over a period, at a position where we could establish what I call a business tax in place of these long-term leases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Does that mean that the leases would remain the same, the tenure and so on? What you say is, tax the enterprises which are getting rich in the tourist trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not want to be unfair or scare anybody, but I am told that one or more provinces in Canada have given notice over a period of years that long-term leases are out. I have not decided that we should do that nationally, but we are making a concerted study to see whether more equity as well as fairness can obtain. Because we have a situation, as my hon. friend knows, where some grandchildren are today in the position where their grandfathers took the original lease of land in a national park and have been living in the park, but now that right is
Supply-Northern Affairs denied other Canadians because we do not lease them any more. In the interests of equity and in the interests of participation on the basis of the accruing value from the monopolistic position of the parks branch here, I would like to see something better than that which we are doing at the present time. I appreciate very much the advice given today by hon. members who have spoken on this item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the minister say something about the remarks I made-made not in a political way-about the method of expropriation of land? I say this with great respect to the C.P.R., who have done a tremendous job of building up the tourist trade, not only with their trains but also with their beautiful hotels. I should like to know what the minister's plans are for the future, or whether he has discussed this question with the Department of Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not know, without notice, about expropriations such as the hon. member describes. Any attempts we have made to buy property have been made strictly by negotiation. I think that is the case in every instance since I have been with the department. Some of the attempts we have made along the line of negotiations have frightened me to death, again because of the apparently monopolistic position. We are spending tremendous sums of money, and some of them I have set aside currently for this reason.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to develop this for one minute. A lot of these things have been cleared up, and in this I pay regard to the former minister. When I first became a member of parliament for Bow River in 1957, Mr. Edward McCormick, Q.C., of Calgary, had various cases in his office where all the government does-and I have checked the procedure; I know the procedure and have done research into it-is to pass an order in council, file it in the land titles office, and there is no notice to the landowner at all. He may or may not know about it. The land titles office may inform him, but otherwise there is no notice.
On top of that, five, six or seven years go by. I am now referring to one of the cases which the minister and his officials may have in mind. It has now got to the stage where I do not know whether they will compromise or not. I am talking about ordinary cases in Banff and I could name dozens. I have a file full of cases which were finally settled. We begged the minister and his officials from 1957 on, and finally they settled. I am not saying this was because the Conservatives came into power, but because pressure built up. Although I give the minister credit for cleaning these cases up in his time, I am sure

Supply-Northern Affairs that if he had been the previous minister he would have cleaned them up. The fact is that I hope the minister looks into it, because there is a lot of freehold in our parks land. One lady came to me when I was in Calgary with a letter from the department. She knows what happened to her other relatives. This letter said: "Will you sell your land?" If she does not answer the letter and does not negotiate at a price with a gun at her head, what happens? At some time in the near future there will be an order in council passed and there is only one solution. They say: "You can go to the exchequer court".
Why should a landowner have to go into court? Why does not the department in three or four weeks, if they cannot settle it at a price, after proper valuation take the matter to court and pay the costs? Much of this land in Banff is only worth $100, $200 or $300. If they did go to legal counsel and fight over it, it would not be worth their while. That is how it is done and it is wrong. That is why the Expropriation Act of Canada should be changed. I know the minister cannot do it today, but I ask him to take a hard look at this. I have a case-when it is settled, or tried and passed through the exchequer court-that will be a national scandal. It dragged along for four or five years before they started an action. Why should people have to start an action? Why are they not notified? Why does not the department sit down and negotiate with them? If they cannot agree to a reasonable price let the exchequer court decide. But the fact is that it costs that person money. He has to go and hire a lawyer. He is put in all these difficulties. But it is so easy for the department; they sterilize development. That is what the department does, and it is a national scandal. You can own land and put your life's savings into it. Then the government expropriate it, and if you do not take their price they sterilize development till they get it in their hands, and then develop it. Is that fair to the individual? What about the civil pronerty rights of the people of this country: That is what I am complaining about. It is a national scandal.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not think any of the conditions portrayed by the hon. member in the bad old days of which he was a part persist at the present time. I do not think we have picked up any person's property at all without attempting to negotiate. If we have been unable to negotiate-and I am talking after eight months' experience-we have not expropriated the property in question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Since the minister took over many of these things have been cleared up, and I would say that is correct; but in

the past, under former Liberal administrations it has happened. I am not saying it was because a Liberal administration was in power but that is what took place. It is at a halt at the moment, but I can show you letters where freehold landowners have written to me, maybe unknown to the minister, saying: "We do not believe in any freeholds in the parks; we want your land". But the C.P.R. does not get a letter like that. You can deny it, but give me the chance and I will bring in files of evidence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Only one question for the minister. Has he received a request from the government of the province of Quebec to create national parks in that province? Because I do not think we have one park.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I understand that the government of the province of Quebec is engaged in some studies. We have had no request from them to establish a national park in Quebec. However, I am told some studies in respect of two areas are under way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I take a few minutes of the committee's time to make a few remarks. I am wondering why there is one very important deficiency in our national parks program, namely a lack of proper and adequate park facilities close to our two major metropolitan centres of Montreal and Toronto. I think there is a growing recognition at all levels of government that as the full force of the technological change which is called automation strikes industry and our working population, a shorter work week will result and it will be necessary to provide recreational facilities to meet the increase of leisure time. The full effects of this automation will first be felt in the metropolitan areas. I suggest that the need for park facilities within a reasonable driving distance of Montreal and Toronto is urgent. I suggest that wherever possible and with full cooperation from the municipal and provincial authorities, a survey be made in the river area along the St. Lawrence, in the Montreal region, and in the lake area around Toronto, with a view to establishing park areas around the many historic sites which mark the route of voyageurs up the St. Lawrence and the paths of the early settlers around the lake in the Toronto area.
I have a specific suggestion to make, and it is that the historic site of the battle of Chateauguay at Allens Corners in the county of Chateauguay should be properly established as a park under the jurisdiction of the department. This site is located only 25 miles from the island of Montreal and it commemorates, as I am sure any historian today would agree, one of the most significant

events in Canadian history-the repulse of an invading American army as it approached Montreal in October, 1813. This victory over the Americans on October 26th, 1813, was a French Canadian victory. Had it not been for the unity of all the elements of society in Lower Canada in 1812 and 1813 it is very likely that Montreal would have fallen to the invaders and, with the link with Upper Canada cut, that the whole of Canada would have fallen to the Americans. I suggest that this battle is worthy of proper commemoration.
At the present time there are two stone cairns commemorating the event. These are situated on plots of land, one of which measures about 25 feet square, and the other approximately 40 feet by 150 feet. Since there is a great deal of land available in this area -it is not an urbanized area-I hope the hon. gentleman will give every consideration to further development of the site commemorating the battle of Chateauguay.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest that along the St. Lawrence river a number of historic sites exist which are neither marked nor commemorated, and I hope the appropriate branch of the department will in the near future investigate the possibility of commemorating these important reminders of our history.
In closing, I should like to say that if we are ever to establish any sort of Canadian identity it seems to me it will have to come from our identification, as Canadians, with the vast wilderness heritage which has fallen to us. When we consider the space we have available, I think Canadians should be the greatest outdoor people in the world. Yet they are not. I feel, as I know the minister does, that his department has a most important role to play in instilling an appreciation of this Canadian heritage in our youth.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was interested in the observations which have been made with respect to the possibility of establishing a national park in the Garibaldi area of British Columbia.
I know that on a number of occasions suggestions have been made in this regard. I do not know if the idea has been regarded too favourably by the province of British Columbia. It may be they are leary of the intentions of the federal government in this field, because on several occasions in the past they have been faced with efforts on the part of the federal government to gain a little more control over British Columbia and its resources. I look back a number of years to a bill called Bill 3 which proposed to take over the Columbia river area and declare it to be in the national interest. Then, more recently, the federal government proposed to
Supply-Northern Affairs lay claim to the offshore mineral rights of British Columbia, and this question has not been settle as yet.
So, with regard to this possibility of acquiring land for a federal park in the Garibaldi area there is a question of just what might be involved in the way of provincial natural resources. I would like to ask the minister if in any consideration he has given to this project he found himself in agreement with the former minister, that there is room for two developments in this section, one, provincial, taking in the Golden Ears area, and the other federal, to include the northern alpine area as a national park. I wonder whether the minister is of the same opinion as his predecessor was in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That might well be so, but I would prefer to have our technical men make an inspection of the area and report upon it before I make any judgment. So far, the premier of British Columbia has not agreed to let our technical men enter the property.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have only a word to say at this point and it is with reference to the minister's assurance that no decision will be taken with regard to the establishment of a national park in the Yukon until the Yukon legislative concil has made application. I wish to thank the hon. gentleman for that assurance, since it was on my suggestion that the previous administration established this policy. I am sure the people of the Yukon, through their council, will be happy to hear what the minister has said in this regard.

Item agreed to.
SO. Canadian wildlife service-Wildlife resources, conservation and development including administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, $979,700.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have a few comments to make under this heading. The problem I wish to raise concerns the natural migration in the fall of large birds called sandhill cranes which do great damage to the crops of farmers in one area of my constituency. This is the area around Govan, Nokomis and Hatfield at the northern end of Last Long lake-an important lake which enters into the naming of my constituency, Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.
To outline the problem very briefly which I wish to present, I should like to read a few comments from an article which appeared in the Semans Gazette, a newspaper in my constituency. The article reads in part as follows:
-the breeding range-
Of the sandhill crane.
-is in the far unsettled north, from Siberia to Baffin island.

Supply-Northern Affairs
This is the part I am concerned about:
In August the cranes start funnelling down from the Arctic toward their wintering range around Texas, Louisiana and Mexico. Last Mountain lake... is a sojourning region where the cranes gather in thousands and live well for a few weeks before continuing the journey.
With regard to the damage to crops done by the sandhill cranes the article says:
It is not the amount of grain the birds eat, although this can be considerable, but the damage they do to the swathed grain with their large feet that brings most complaints from farmers. The birds will literally take a field apart. What grain they do not eat they scratch out of the heads and pound into the ground.
The article also brings out an item which should be of interest to the minister and probably to the house. It refers to the number of sandhill cranes in this particular area and says:
On August 1 less than 300 of these cranes were in their usual roosting ground on the lake. By August 31 their numbers had increased to 30,000.
The problem I am trying to bring out is put in these words in the article:
It is one of trying to fit the crane migratory pattern into the local farming industry so both may survive and flourish.
Naturally the farmers who suffer severe crop losses want some way of controlling the birds. The former minister of northern affairs and national resources, whom I am glad to see in his seat, took definite action on the problem in 1961 and 1962. His department planted what were called lure crops to attract the birds from the grain fields. I think this plan was at least partially successful and I believe additional land was seeded to lure crops this year.
I have had considerable correspondence about this problem and I think the minister has too. I should like to refer briefly to some of it. I have here a letter from the secretary of the rural municipality of Wre-ford, No. 280, in my riding. He says in part in his letter:
We would recommend.. .If these cranes must be protected, that a couple of sections of lure crop might keep cranes off the farmers' crops which might be sufficient, under favourable weather conditions in the fall, to allow farmers to harvest their crops and not suffer too much damage, but in addition to this, exploders and shooting to scare practice should be used, outside the lure crop area, in order to herd them onto the lure crops.
I have another letter containing a resolution adopted at a meeting in Govan, Saskatchewan, of the Saskatchewan farmers union. This resolution was passed on March 21, 1963. It suggests that some plan be worked out under which the federal and provincial governments would pay all losses caused by sandhill cranes. I am sure the minister received a copy of that resolution. I think these
[Mr. Pascoe.l
resolutions demonstrate that the farmers in the district are ready to co-operate in any effective program of crane control. I find the residents around Last Mountain lake just as interested as any other group in preserving the whooping crane. To a great extent the whooping crane resembles the sandhill crane and the odd specimen of the whooping crane is found among the sandhill cranes. That is why the farmers are loath to shoot them. I do not believe they have permits to shoot them anyway.
It might be of interest to the committee to know that a small bird sanctuary, the first one on the North American continent for birds, was established in the area around Last Mountain lake in 1887, and I am pleased that it was established under the Conservative government of Sir John A. Macdonald. I suggest to the minister that this wildfowl sanctuary should be expanded by purchasing additional land, some of which can be seeded to lure crops and the rest left as marshy feeding grounds. I also think that the sight of
30,000	large sandhill cranes, each about three feet tall, feeding in one sanctuary would be a great tourist attraction. There would also be the possibility of tourists seeing one or more of the rare whooping cranes.
I understand that the minister's department has agreed to allow certain farmers in designated areas to shoot cranes threatening their crops. I realize that some of the farmers might be provoked into shooting the birds because of the damage to their crops, but I think it would be a mistake to allow indiscriminate shooting in view of the danger that one of the rare whooping cranes might be killed.
Most people would agree that an adequate bird sanctuary is a better solution. As I said earlier, the first bird sanctuary on the North American continent was established in this area in 1887. The enlargement of this sanctuary by 1967, 80 years later, would be a very fine centennial project. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources might be able to call on his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, to help secure the necessary land under the ARDA program, and I am sure the farmers in the area would co-operate in any project that is planned.

speechtext:
I should like the minister, just briefly, to inform the committee what, if any, developments are taking place in the field of federal-provincial co-operation in respect of wildlife services. I have had certain representations made to me by fish and game organizations to the effect that there should be developed a federal-provincial cost-sharing program in this field, one which would probably lead to even greater integration and co-operation in this field.
Now, I should like to know whether or not this has been the subject of discussion at the resources ministers conference, and also whether there was any discussion of this matter during the recent federal-provincial conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member I may say that there are a number of fields in which co-operation is being advanced between the federal government and the provincial governments, notably under the resources program in respect of wildlife on the Canadian prairies. We have set up so-called "wet spaces", particularly for the duck population. We are in the process of making arrangements, over an extended period of years, to do considerable of this work which will plan the efficacy or fail to plan the efficacy of doing this on a large scale. We are finding a great deal more information about ducks all the time. We want to put some of this knowledge to use on a fairly extended scale, involving quite a sum of money in the various provinces.
The closest possible relations also are beginning to exist between the provinces and the federal government in the acknowledgement of the fact that here we have a resource of tremendous value, not only for the enjoyment of the people who live in Canada but for tourists as well. I can assure my friend that real progress is being made in that direction.
While I am on my feet I should like to say a word to the hon. gentleman who brought up the problem of the sandhill crane. He dealt with the technical aspects from begin-ing to end. I may say we have arranged with the United States authorities to, what my scientific people call, harvest a crop. The United States authorities have undertaken,, after separation of any whoopers that come up in the crop of sandhill cranes, to bash the cranes down. Whether or not that will work, I do not know.

Yes, some work can be done in that regard. Apparently, these birds can be attracted to one place, and they damage the

crops on farmlands. I do not believe anyone should snicker at this. I believe these cranes congregate in three places only; and when they do so in such numbers, millions of dollars of crop damage can result. In any event, we are undertaking, in co-operation with the United States authorities to annihilate them when they are down south.

1. Departmental administration including grants and contributions as detailed in the estimates, $1,378,100.

I will be very brief in my remarks on this item because I do not feel the estimates should be dragged out. However, when the first item was up for discussion a week ago, most of the remarks centred around security changes. Speeches were made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. I do want to make one or two perfunctory remarks.
It has been customary, when the departments are first called and when the estimates were prepared by a former government, for the minister to say that criticism would be limited. At times former ministers have paid tributes to the different civil servants with whom they have been associated. I cannot do that job adequately, but since I was parliamentary secretary to the former minister of justice, Mr. Fulton, as well as Mr. Fleming, I do want to take a moment to say a few words. I am sure we all recognize the good record Mr. Fulton had when he was minister of justice. His energies and his capacities were known to all of us. He had a good record as a parliamentarian and I am sure he will be remembered as a good cabinet minister. In so far as his work in the Department of Justice is concerned, he will be remembered particularly for his reorganization and modernization of the federal penal system and the change to medium security and minimum security prisons, as well as for instituting a program of staff training and industrial training for inmates.
I should like to pay tribute at this time also to the press who were so co-operative during my time in the department in attempting to explain and sell this new idea of penal
[Mr. Laing.l
reform to the people. Some of the other matters that came under reform in the department during Mr. Fulton's time were the national parole board, narcotics control, capital murder, sexual psychopaths, anticombines legislation and R.C.M.P. reform. I merely mention these things for the record, Mr. Chairman. I had some extensive notes, but hon. members will be pleased to know I seem to have lost them since the estimates were first presented.
I want to mention two other subjects which were of particular interest to me, namely the R.C.M.P. and juvenile delinquency. I want to pay tribute to the former commissioner, Mr. Harvison and to his successor, Mr. McClelland. I am sure that their records are known to us all. We wish them both success in their new endeavours and their responsibilities, respectively. The R.C.M.P. have suffered a certain loss of prestige in the eyes of some people in the country. We hear of criticism of them in their performance of the many arduous duties assigned to them, such as traffic control, policing yachts, boats and matters of that type. I think we should take a hard look at that because it is we, in society, who assign these very difficult tasks to them. There have also been communist activities which have needed investigation, and we have been perhaps overzealous in our criticism of them there.
I think, Mr. Chairman, a new look is needed at this problem. It may be that social contact between the R.C.M.P. and individuals in our society will help this problem. It could be that a full campaign of national publicity and a youth program would help make this better understood. There were some figures I saw recently which quite surprised me. I noted that out of 1,538,000 investigations within a full year, the R.C.M.P. had only received 103 complaints and of those only six needed disciplinary action. This is one matter we will be watching from the opposition standpoint. The various activities of the R.C.M.P. do seem to be very close to our daily lives in this modem world.
Now, juvenile delinquency is another favourite subject of mine. A short while ago I asked the minister a question about the juvenile delinquency report, and he answered in some detail on November 20. That answer is in Hansard and I do not intend to go through it. It was to the effect that the committee, which was set up by Mr. Fulton, is continuing its work. There were some difficulties due to staff changes and the like, but it is hoped that the complete report will be available in 1964. I hope the work will go forward and that there will not be any delay.

I want to stress the importance of it. I am sure the new minister is interested in this too, and I would hope that in some way part of the report could be made available, after it has been seen by various responsible persons, so that those of us who are interested can go through the statistics and the information, and try to assist in making final recommendations that will result in new legislation.
Some of the figures on juvenile delinquency are very startling. I recall reading a report in the October 21 issue of "U.S. News and World Report" dealing with crime in Washington. I am not suggesting it is the same in Ottawa, but here are two capital cities that have similar conditions. What was amazing was that some 50 per cent of the juveniles who ended up in the hands of the police in Washington had come from broken homes, and in one particular area 90 per cent of the older persons with records had previously been charged as juveniles. I leave those figures with the committee for consideration, and I hope they will interest us to make these very necessary changes in our society.
There is, of course, a great link between the two subjects I have mentioned, the R.C.M.P. and juvenile delinquency. It might be that the responsibilities of the R.C.M.P. could be directed, even more than they are now, to problems of our youth, and in this way a more favourable image of the R.C.M.P. would be created. That force would then be dealing with one of the great challenges of today.
I do not have anything more to say. I wish the new minister well in his endeavours, and I hope he will carry on some of the very important reforms that were made by Mr. Fulton when he was minister of justice.

It is not my intention today to discuss the question which I, and a number of other members in this group, have discussed on a number of occasions, namely the measures taken by the government in connection with security investigations. It is not that we do not think this is an important question. It is not that we do not think much discussion is required, but we have the statements made recently by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Justice that a new look is being taken at this important question, and that new policies and new regulations will be worked out. We are prepared to wait a reasonable time, to give the government a chance to work out a policy and report to the house, before we discuss the problem further.
I have just one more thing to say on this subject. So far as I am concerned, and I think I can speak for other members of this group, despite what the last speaker seemed
Supply-Justice
to intimate, our criticisms have never been primarily with the R.C.M.P. I have said it before, and I will say it again, that successive governments have given the R.C.M.P. an impossible job in the field of security. They have not defined clearly enough what they want from the R.C.M.P. so that they could do the job that is required and still protect the rights of the individual citizens concerned. This is something we will be dealing with at the next session of parliament. Meantime I wish to tell the minister we expect to have a pretty clear, detailed explanation rather than the fairly good but rather vague and general statements recently made by the Prime Minister and himself.
This evening I want to discuss what I think is the completely inadequate rate of progress we are making in correctional programs. In 1950 the United Nations made a survey of correctional programs in its member countries, and Canada was listed fiftieth among those countries in the standard of service which was provided to unfortunate people who pass through correctional systems. We have had progress reports since then, but I do not think the improvements we have made will have boosted us very much in the scale, and I would be very surprised if we were in much higher than fiftieth position.
This is not surprising, if we realize that at any one time in Canada, in the prisons, penitentiaries and jails operated by the federal and provincial governments, there are probably over 17,000 people behind bars. Of those in the federal penitentiaries, 75 per cent of the inmates are repeating sentences, and in the provincial institutions somewhere between 60 per cent and 75 per cent are repeating sentences.
Stuart Jaffary, who is a professor of social work at the University of Toronto, in a book published this year gives comparison rates of prison populations in Canada and Great Britain. He uses the year 1955, which apparently was the last year for which he could get figures, and these figures ought to shock and cause a great deal of concern to us.
Great Britain in 1955, which had three times the population of Canada, only had a few thousand more people in prison than we had. We had 13,500 people in prison, the rate being 87 per 100,000 population; while Great Britain had only 18,500 people in prison with the corresponding rate less than half of ours, or 42 per 100,000 population. Of those convicted of indictable offences in Canada, 45 per cent were in prison, while in England and Wales only 17 per cent were in prison. For indictable and non-indictable offences 122,000 people went to jail or prison in Canada in 1955, a rate of 781 per 100,000 population;

while the number in England and Wales was only 39,000 people, a rate of just 90 per
100,000	population.
This is not surprising because the British have had a system of probation for a long number of years, while we are really only beginning such a system, and it is not much thanks to the federal government that we have any kind of probation system at all.
The last report, the last of many studies made of our correctional system, the Fauteux report, suggested that in a modern correctional system the first principle is to keep as many offenders out of prison as possible. I suggest that something be done to get this idea across to the public.
