Mr. Chairman, I hope the Minister of Justice can do something to convince the judges of this country that they ought to pay some attention to this recommendation in the Fauteux commission report. In this morning's Montreal Gazette there is a story that yesterday a judge hearing a case of a man being tried for robbery, I think, ignored the recommendation of both defence counsel and crown prosecutor-who agreed that the sentence for this man, who was guilty, should be only one year-and imposed a sentence of seven years in the penitentiary. The judge is quoted in the news story as saying, in explanation of having done this, that his first inclination was to impose a sentence of one year for each charge. There were 17 charges, so this man could have

been sentenced to 17 years in the penitentiary, but the judge was very generous in sentencing him to only seven years. Obviously that judge has not paid much attention to the Fauteux report.
Last year in the city of Toronto a man came forward and admitted he had been guilty of arson. This man was obviously seriously ill and needed intensive psychiatric treatment. The judge again completely ignored the recommendation of the Fauteux commission report and imposed a sentence- I am speaking from memory-of well over 29 years. There was quite a storm about this and a committee of very prominent lawyers was established to work on the case, but this did not help much with regard to the original sentence. We had a case a few years ago in the city of Winnipeg-

Mr. Chairman, before the hon. gentleman continues he ought to complete this matter. The matter came before the court, did it not, and was not the sentence reduced? I think that should be clarified. My recollection is that the matter was considered in the nature of an appeal and the sentence was cut in two; is that not right?

I thank the right hon. gentleman for his addition. I think he is correct. However, speaking from recollection, even after the appeal the sentence was a very substantial number of years. In the city of Winnipeg just a few years ago we had a case involving a married man with a family, a railway worker, who had never previously been in trouble with the law. It was this time of the year, shortly before Christmas. This man was going to work; he was working the evening shift, as I remember. His wife was somewhat critical because they did not have much money for Christmas presents for the children. Unfortunately for him he left his house early and stopped at the local beer parlour, as they call them in Winnipeg. He had a few beers too many. I do not excuse what he did, but he went to the cashier of the largest theatre in Winnipeg and asked for the money. He had no gun, but he told her he had a gun and asked her to give him the money. He did not wait long enough to get the money; he ran away.
When he was apprehended he was charged with armed robbery, because of course he had threatened her and said he had a gun. The police who put him in jail asked if he wanted his wife to be notified. He said this would only frighten her, so she was not notified. He appeared before the magistrate the next morning. Everything that should have been done under the law was done, technically. He was asked whether he wanted to have counsel, but he said he was guilty

after all so there was no point in having counsel. He pleaded guilty and the magistrate imposed a sentence of four years. I am speaking from memory, but I do not think I am wrong. The first his wife knew about the case was when she turned on the radio and heard that her husband was on his way to the penitentiary to serve a four-year term of imprisonment.
Again I suggest to the minister it is time the judges of this country got into the twentieth century way of thinking about this problem of correction, instead of being better suited, as I think some of them are, to the days of the inquisition. Even if our judges were using more common sense-and I think some of them are-we would not achieve the results that have been achieved in Great Britain, because in that country they have an active and aggressive program of probation which is designed to keep offenders, and particularly young offenders, out of prison. We have a situation here where police chiefs, and indeed judges sometimes, are quoted as saying things which are not true and certainly do not help this situation. Just a couple of weeks ago the chief of police of Ottawa was quoted in both newspapers of this city as saying that the reason for the crime wave in Ottawa was that we are being too soft; that too many people who are out on parole are committing crimes. Of course, the records are clear; this is not true at all. But this is the kind of impression which people who ought to know better are still conveying. It seems to me that if we are to achieve the kind of results which have been achieved in Great Britain we must actively promote a probation system such as that proposed in the Fauteux report.
We have a large number of shared programs with the provinces. I suggest to the minister it is time we looked at the possibility of sharing with the provinces a program of really successful probation. If we do not do it on the basis of humanitarianism, I suggest we do it on the basis of the cold, hard saving of cash. I think the minister knows it costs somewhere between $1,500 and $2,500 a year to keep a person in one of our jails or penitentiaries, while the cost of probation runs somewhere between $50 and $200 a year. Unfortunately we have been too prone, too ready to pay for another building, another extension to a prison or jail in which to lock up people. We have not been ready to pay for the kind of thing that would really bring results; that is, a probation system. So we have the anomalous, ridiculous situation in which several provinces, such as Ontario and British Columbia, have no effective system of probation, while other provinces-
Supply-Justice
Quebec, for example-have no probation system. To my knowledge the province of Quebec has no such system. Then in other provinces, such as Manitoba, they have what is called a probation system, but they lack the properly trained staff to do the job that I think is required. I would suggest to the minister it is time we got on with this very important task of establishing a proper probation system. Even if we had such a system we could not keep everybody out of our correctional institutions.
The last time these estimates were before the committee the hon. member for Vancouver East spoke about our institutions, about the buildings. We have made some progress, but I would suggest to the minister that if he really means business, if he really wants the support of the members of this house in getting the money required to modernize our correctional institutions, he should arrange for hon. members to spend a day, as some of us have, going through St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. I do not think there is any hon. member of this house who would not be shocked at the conditions in that institution. All hon. members should spend a day there and see how these people live. They may have committed crimes, but they are human beings. I do not think there is a member in the house who, on seeing the conditions in St. Vincent de Paul, would suggest for a moment any reduction in proposed expenditure that the minister would want to make next year.
St. Vincent de Paul is the worst case, but it is not the only one. We have made some beginnings but really the beginnings we have made are infinitesimal. Our institutions are overcrowded. Because they are overcrowded we have no real system of segregation as proposed by every investigating commission which has ever looked into the correctional system in Canada. So you find, Mr. Chairman, in the prisons of Canada drug addicts, embezzlers, forgers, bank robbers, alcoholics, sex deviates, petty thieves and murderers all in the same institution and all sharing the same cell blocks. How can you do anything under those conditions? We cannot blame the staff. We ought to blame ourselves. The staff are doing the best they can in the conditions under which we expect them to work.
The Fauteux report recommended that the federal government take care of all prisoners whose sentence is more than one year, and that the provinces look after prisoners who have sentences of less than six months. But the federal government, although endorsing the report in principle, has so far refused not only to adopt this principle but to set the date when they will adopt it. The result is

Supply-Justice
that provinces which want to do the job say they cannot plan their programs until they know what the federal government intends to do and when it intends to put this kind of provision into action. Some provinces which have not been very enthusiastic about taking on the job, and I include my own province of Manitoba in that category, have found this to be the perfect excuse. The attorney general of Manitoba has said on a number of occasions that we were not going to go into any expensive building program until that province knows when the federal government will take on the job, and when the responsibility for it is clarified. Despite the fact that we are a long way from meeting the present needs, I suggest that the federal government should set a date when it intends to go ahead with this recommendation of the Fauteux report.
No system of correction can really be any better than the staff. You can have the best building in the world, but if the staff is untrained and is thinking in terms of incarceration and punishment instead of rehabilitation and correction we will never turn the corner and begin to solve the problem. We will never reduce the number of inmates in our institutions as they have in Great Britain and other countries. It is an amazing thing to me that this country can find the money to hire trained engineers to build the buildings we need and the roads to our resource developments; we can find experts in agriculture and do research into how to get better hogs, a better grade of wheat and how to get better fruit. I am not being critical of these things because they are required. But when it comes to finding people who are trained in the much more important field of how to rehabilitate people and improve people, we have almost been completely remiss. And of course we have no money for this.
If anyone doubts this, let him look at the answers which the minister has given this session and last session with regard to questions which have been put down regarding staff in our institutions. We have 26 penitentiaries. I put down a question not long ago asking for the names of the wardens. After all, a warden is the key man in any penitentiary. I asked how long they had had their jobs, what were their qualifications. I am not going to read a long list into the record, although I think it would be worth while to do so, but of the 26 wardens in Canada, according to the minister's reply two of them have a B.A. degree, one an M.A. degree, one a teacher's diploma and one a diploma in agriculture. According to my total, 21 have no formal training at all, or no better training than that which I have

mentioned. After looking at the qualifications of these 21 wardens, what does the minister say about them? They have had army training or they have had police training. I do not want to be critical of the training that a man gets in the army or in the police. If our correctional institutions are merely institutions of punishment, merely institutions for incarceration, I agree that a person who has had army training and training in police work would probably make a very good warden. I am not criticizing these people individually, I am sure they are doing the best they can. But if we are really thinking in terms of rehabilitation as suggested by the Fauteux report, I suggest that people with this kind of background, education and training who staff our penitentiaries simply cannot do the job.
I asked the minister the question whether all custodial officers in our correctional institutions receive training in the behavioural sciences by qualified professional staff, and the answer was very simple, with no argument about it. It was one word-"No"; that they do not. We have nothing in the estimates concerning training grants or bursaries in the field of correctional training, so even the people now on the staff or doing social work, or work in psychology or sociology, who want to go into the field could only get the training, paid partly by the federal government, on condition that they came to work in our institutions when they finished their training. This is a step which various provincial governments have taken, but we have done nothing in this direction.
Of 19 positions for psychologists in the establishment, only nine are filled according to the answer the minister gave me some time ago. Of those nine, five of them had only a B.A., three an M.A. and one a Ph.D. I want to suggest that the number is much too low and the training they have is completely inadequate to do the kind of job that people much better qualified than anyone in this house have said over and over again is required, if we are to have a modern correctional program. We have only eight psychiatrists on the establishment. I do not know how many they concede there are, but to the best of my knowledge not one of them is full time.
At the present time a murder trial is going on in the city of Quebec. On trial is a man named Dion. I have just been told he was sentenced to death today. I do not want to say anything about his guilt or the crime he committed, but I think it is significant that this was not the first time he had pleaded guilty to that type of offence. It was not the first time he had been in a penitentiary. The

reports which our vastly understaffed psychiatric departments had given on previous occasions were that this man was a very severely disturbed and ill person. How much psychiatric treatment did this man have, may I ask, before the parole board recommended his release?
I am not being critical of the parole board. I want to make that clear. I am not being critical of the psychiatrists. I have met the man who is on the staff of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, Dr. Cormier, and he is a really competent psychiatrist. But he works, I believe, only three mornings a week. How much can he do on this basis in an institution of that size? I want to suggest that if anyone is guilty of the murder of these boys it is the governments of Canada, the parliament of Canada and the people of Canada who have refused, in the past, and who have refused until this day to provide the specialist scientific staff which is required in a system such as ours.
The Fauteux report stated that the cornerstone of a modern correctional system is the classification staff. I want to read examples of the kind of classification staff we have recruited to do this work. It is true, we have made a beginning. We have the beginnings of a classification staff, the beginnings of a new system. The minister answered some questions which I put to him some time ago and I want to read some examples of what has been done. I am not being critical of these people. We get the people we ask for. The qualifications are those we set and, what is more important, we are getting the kind of people we are prepared to pay for. Obviously, we are not paying very much. Here they are. At Dorchester, the classification officer spent one year at university plus attendance at classification staff college. At Dorchester farm camp the classification officer is a high school graduate. These are the kind of people we are putting on the job, though the Fauteux report says classification is the cornerstone of the system. At the Blue Mountain institution the classification officer has almost completed his studies for the degree of B.A. At St. Vincent de Paul the classification officer has grade 12 plus university courses in criminology. Another has grade 10 plus some university courses.
At Kingston penitentiary the classification officer has three years attendance at university plus courses under the penitentiary program. A classification assistant has grade 12, plus courses at the penitentiary. Two classification assistants have senior matriculation, plus courses, and another classification assistant has grade 10. At Collins Bay the classification officer has two years attendance at university plus courses; at Landry Crossing correctional

camp the classification officer has junior matriculation; at Joyceville institution the classification officer has senior matriculation; at Manitoba penitentiary the classification officer has two years attendance at university, and at the Manitoba farm camp the classification officer has grade 11. At the Saskatchewan penitentiary the classification officer has a grade 10 education, at the William Head institution he has senior matriculation, and at the Agassiz correctional camp the classification officer has a high school education-I assume that phrase means he did not even graduate from high school.
Once again, let me say that I am not being critical of these people. We are responsible for the kind of people we have working for us in these institutions. I suggest that while we have a situation of this kind we have not even begun to nibble at the edge of the problem which faces us.
The Fauteux commission recommended that there be a presentence report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
It is not my intention to delay the committee for any length of time and I have taken this attitude in all cases with regard to the balance of these estimates, but a situation has arisen since last April with regard to my constituency with which I feel obliged to deal, and I am sure the minister will know whereof I speak. In the concluding minutes of my contribution it may seem as if I am being somewhat irrelevant but I trust you will bear with me, Mr. Chairman, because my remarks will have a definite relationship to the balance of my words.
First of all, let me say there is a considerable degree of agreement everywhere in Canada that a greater degree of fundamental progress and reform took place in the general field of justice under the Conservative government than in any period of Canada's history prior to that time. Under the capable and aggressive administration of the former minister of justice, the Hon. Davie Fulton, stimulated by the well-known interest taken in this field by the former prime minister himself, the important and long overdue steps then taken included improvements in the administration of justice in Canada, reorganization and modernization of the federal penitentiary system and the correctional program, a new and effective approach to the problem of narcotic drug addiction and the traffic in barbiturates, a new law on capital murder, and several important amendments in the field of criminal law generally.

Supply-Justice
I have the details here before me, but I shall desist from taking the time of the committee by referring to them at greater length for the reasons I have previously mentioned. I wish, however, to make a brief reference to the advance which was made under the direction of the former minister in the field of prison work camps. The value of this work has been proven many times since it was undertaken, and it is the result of the policy which was so vigorously followed by the minister of that day. I also have before me a number of well documented articles and editorials by various organizations, and others interested in this work, acknowledging the tremendous steps forward which were taken under the direction of the minister of that day.
I also have a copy of the speech which was delivered by the former minister of justice, Mr. Fulton, on the occasion of the opening of the Joyceville institution. In the course of this speech Mr. Fulton indicated that the work of prison reform involved not only the officials of a penitentiary but the public as a whole. The rehabilitation program which the minister sought to bring about at that time was, in effect, made possible as a result of the change in the thinking brought about by the Fauteux report. I refer particularly to the section in which it is stated that federal and provincial governments should proceed as quickly as possible with the establishment and maintenance of special types of institutions for the treatment of various types of offenders. The minister of that day initiated action in this regard by setting up a committee to study the problem and bring in recommendations. I believe it was determined that the inmates of our institutions would be regarded in a somewhat different light; that there would be a change in the attitude taken toward them. The minister of that day tended to favour a program of lessened security. I believe the program, generally speaking, favoured medium security institutions, or institutions where security was even less, and he proceeded quickly in this regard. I believe he indicated in that speech at Joyceville that this type of reform in the treatment of inmates was long overdue and that it had been proven that these people could be rehabilitated in a much more sensible and satisfactory manner if they were handled in this way.
In order to save the time of the committee I will not refer in too much detail to the remarks of the minister of that day, but I should like to point out that he did state this at Joyceville:
By far the largest part of our penitentiary population does not require detention in a maxi-

mum security institution, yet the vast majority of our prisoners are kept in just such conditions. We do not need that type of accommodation. We do need more medium and minimum security institutions into which we can send carefully selected inmates to undergo carefully planned treatment and training.
Further on he stated:
It is here that our new parole system has its principal role.
As hon. members know, of course, he moved quickly in that direction. In the course of his tenure of office he made certain announcements that were indicative of the progress he intended to make. His thinking and the thinking of the departmental officials were based on two main premises. The first was to arouse in the people of Canada themselves an interest in this long neglected branch of government and to make Canadians aware of their responsibilities in this respect and of their continuing fight against crime. The second was to implement reforms and provide new facilities and programs which had been worked out during the same period.
Accordingly, Mr. Chairman, about the time of the election campaign of 1962 the minister visited my constituency and announced the construction of a project somewhere in the area of the villages of Markdale, Flesherton and Dundalk. I hold in my hand a copy of the Flesherton paper of Wednesday, May 16, 1962 in which is reported the announcement by the minister of the construction of a $4 million project with a yearly payroll of approximately $1 million. That project was to be built in that particular area.
Because of the necessity of proceeding with this project at that time my Liberal opponent also thought he should endorse it. Accordingly, in an advertisement in the issue of June 13 of the same paper he assured the people of that area that if they were interested in the construction of such an institution their wishes would surely be fulfilled when he was elected. Obviously that was the thinking of the people in the Liberal party at that time.
I come to an area now where my remarks may possibly be slightly irrelevant, but I would ask hon. members to bear with me because what I am about to say has a definite bearing on the program that is being followed. As the minister knows, I have discussed this matter with him personally and I honour the privilege of interviews with him for the purpose of discussing it. You will know, Mr. Chairman, as will other members of the committee, that at that time several medium security institutions of this nature were planned, one for the constituency of the hon.

member for Bow River, one for the constituency of the hon. member for St. Hya-cinthe-Bagot and another one which I believe has actually proceeded. It is my understanding that as of the present time the others have been terminated, after some expenditure of money.
The important factor is whether the thinking of the department has now changed. Have they returned to the thinking that such a program is not the type of program to be followed? Are the institutions now in the planning stage to be maximum security prisons and is this the reason for the cancellation of the institution for my constituency? When I think of all the acts of patronage that have taken place, I wonder whether patronage is not creeping into the Department of Justice. I have very good reason for saying this.
As the minister knows, my Liberal opponent in the last campaign was down here pleading for the construction of this institution in my constituency. Therefore he agreed with the thinking of the minister of that day and with my own desires. Not only did he come to Ottawa but he brought the Liberal organization with him. In addition to the plea of the Liberal candidate, I understand that the provincial Liberal member for the constituency north of mine has also been pleading for this institution. I believe that the present leader of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario was also here pleading for this institution.
This is a very peculiar state of affairs. I believe the reason for the withdrawal lies in the fact that the minister has intimated that such an institution must be a maximum security prison, and therefore cannot be constructed in that part of the country because the lines of communication are too far removed, and as these criminals are hardened types they must be kept under tigher security. If this is the case, I suggest that the present minister review some of the thinking advanced by the minister of that day, and he will find that his thoughts on the matter are very basic, directly relevant to the findings of the Fauteux report and should be carried out, I believe. I think it is not too far fetched to say that the fresh air in my riding would do such people a lot of good, rather than keeping them in some area of southern Ontario where the lines of communication may be a little shorter but where traffic is heavy. So far as hardened criminals are concerned, I think my area would be a very good one in which to rehabilitate them, rather than putting them in the large and overcrowded institutions which exist today.
I have mentioned people who have made representations in this regard. It may be a
Supply-Justice
peculiar thing, but I remember the present leader of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario saying how kind and considerate the Conservative government had been to him. I must say he was probably referring to the provincial government, but thank God he has to deal with an organization like the Conservative government in the province of Ontario because he knows, as does everyone else who has beaten a path to the minister's door, that there is no use coming to Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to say a few words about the estimates of the Department of Justice now under consideration.
First, I would like to extend well deserved congratulations to the head of that department, because the minister is a man who fulfils his duties with great dignity and honesty; he is a very distinguished parliamentary figure and it is not too much to say that we are very proud of him.
Mr. Chairman, the matter I want to deal with as briefly as possible is the famous Coffin case, which is creating quite a stir in the province of Quebec. The matter was raised for the first time in the house last week, if I am not mistaken, when I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) if he intended to take special measures following the publication of a very contentious book, not to say slanderous, about some persons of rank. The minister answered me quite properly that this matter came under provincial jurisdiction.
Mr. Chairman, this famous case, now known as the Coffin case, causes as much turmoil as the Dreyfus case which happened many years ago but is still referred to. I wonder whether the federal government would not be well advised to institute an inquiry into this matter, even if it comes under provincial jurisdiction, because it would not be infringing in any way the provinces' prerogatives, since the following provision can be found in the Canadian Bill of Rights which is federal legislation:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada, there has existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely:
(a) the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person-
Mr. Chairman, if there was a miscarriage of justice as stated forcibly and violently by Mr. Jacques Hebert, it means that an attempt was made on the life of a man and that his life was even taken wrongfully which is a violation of section 1 of the bill of rights and consequently, it concerns the central government.

Supply-Justice
On the other hand, Coffin's conviction was maintained by the Supreme Court of Canada, our court of last instance, which exists by virtue of a federal act, the Supreme Court Act.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the persons involved in that case are treated by the author, not as guilty people, but as murderers: "I accuse the murderers of Wilbert Coffin", he says, and there cannot be any stronger title; among those murderers accused by Jacques Hebert there is a respectable and honest judge of the Quebec court of appeal who was appointed by the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, all those reasons, in my humble opinion, call for action by the federal government.
I think it is most important that the whole population have unswerving confidence in all our institutions, whatever the authority [DOT]concerned. If the general public has no trust in the value and the efficiency of our judicial institutions, then I say that order, peace and good administration are jeopardized in Canada; and order, peace and good administration in Canada come under the jurisdiction of the federal authorities.
Those are the reasons why I humbly and earnestly submit that the central government should institute an inquiry in the Coffin case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply on vote No. 1 of the Department of Justice.

Mr. Chairman, before recess, I was reviewing the main reasons for the increase in juvenile delinquency. I mentioned in particular the social and economic conditions which make families, as well as the press, radio, television and films, refuse to assume their responsibilities.

Supply-Justice
I leave this subject by underlining a major factor which, in my opinion, is responsible for the situation that exists now: I mean our economic system which does not hold any hope for our young people who see their future darkening because we, who are now entrusted with the nation's business, keep on increasing the public debt which they will have to bear and reimburse later.
I think that this economic situation in which we live is to a great extent-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member for Lake St. John, but it seems to me that he is straying quite far from the subject matter of the resolution now under consideration by the committee when he talks about the country's economic situation.

I agree with you, Mr. Chairman, but I think that a certain link can be found between the responsibilities of the Department of Justice with regard to juvenile delinquency and the reasons for it. I feel that the Department of Justice can, in its own field, point out to the economic and administrative sectors, the reasons for the problems it has to deal with at the present time.
In my opinion, the present economy of this country does not offer to our young people the advantages they are entitled to expect; that is the reason for this problem we now experience: juvenile delinquency.
To conclude, I should also like to mention that judges, when they met in Quebec city, admitted the weakness of our system as far as institutions where sentences can be served are concerned. In my opinion, judges have no choice when they have to pass a sentence. As a matter of fact, they must sentence offenders to a term in a penitentiary or in a prison. I suggest that the government should generalize in Canada, as it had been undertaken, the setting up of those institutions that make it possible to rehabilitate the young and not so young people who, in fact, constitute not only a burden for society but also a loss, since we deprive ourselves of the services they might render if they were rehabilitated.

Mr. Chairman, we begin consideration of the estimates of the Department of Justice. They amount to a total of $30,748,000 for a department with 3,559 employees-I believe that the bench, at all levels, is included.
Although the incumbent of the Department of Justice and myself are politically in complete disagreement, I must admit that he is competent as far as the administration of the Department of Justice in our country is concerned.

This afternoon we heard several members successively and I would be remiss if I did not mention, for instance, the member who spoke on behalf of the N.D.P. about our penitentiaries, because it is important to reorganize them so that the directors of these institutions be, not professional executioners but educators.
We must by all means see, above all, to the rehabilitation of our young people who, for one reason or another, have to spend some time in those penitentiaries, in whatever province it may be.
We have received, on many occasions complaints concerning the treatment given to some prisoners, chiefly young people, as one must admit that inmates in those penitentiaries are mostly young people from 20 to 30 years old.
Mr. Chairman, I call upon the Minister of Justice to consider this question of prime importance most carefully. The staff of those penitentiaries must include educators, as I said, men and women of great ability who can come to an understanding and communicate with other human beings.
Very often in the past parolees became habitual criminals. Why? Because they had no chance to rehabilitate themselves and because, instead of being taught moral principles during their term in the penitentiary, their morale was undermined by the sombre perspective they were shown of going back to a society where there was no place for them.
I should also like to say a word about a point which the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) raised this afternoon, that is the Wilbert Coffin case which puzzled and still puzzles the average Canadian citizen.
The accusations in Jacques Hebert's book constitute an attack against the judicial organization in our country. The judicial organization of Canada finds itself today, if not undermined, at least badly damaged by violent statements and attacks against the administration of justice in one of this country's regions.
That is why I endorse the request of the hon. member for Lotbiniere when he asks the Minister of Justice to institute a royal commission to inquire into this particular case. I suggest that, in the present circumstances, such an inquiry is in order and is becoming increasingly so. Our whole judicial structure is attacked, dragged through the mire, and there is a point beyond which we should not allow things to go.
If Mr. Hebert is right, let the government find the evidence. If he is not right, then Mr. Hebert becomes himself a sort of moral assassin of our judicial structure in Canada.

I feel that the Canadian Minister of Justice does not have the right to tolerate or put up with a book which directs fantastic accusations againt judges and lawyers.
Therefore, that royal commission should be set up, so that the Canadian public does not lose confidence in our judicial structure and the administration of justice, not only in the province of Quebec but in the country as a whole.
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to deal with the parole of prisoners. It will cost the Department of Justice $701,500 to administer the Parole Act.
On many occasions, complaints have been made about paroles being granted too easily in some cases. As a matter of fact, the Dion case was brought up before supper and I believe this criminal was sentenced today to be hanged. Dion was paroled once or twice, if I am not mistaken. Finally, after being charged with the murder of youngsters of 11, 12 and 13 years-there were four, but we mentioned only a few-Dion is now sentenced to hang after succeeding in evading, so to speak, the law of the province and of the country.
Now, occasionally some young people are condemned to six months, a year or two, young people who were arrested following a burglary, car theft, armed robbery, theft committed wearing a mask. Among them are young repeaters who in several cases were led astray when they were quite young. While habitual criminals sometimes manage to obtain their parole, some of those young people can hardly manage to do so, even when favourable reports are given by the judge who heard their case, by the parish priest, by clergymen of some municipalities or districts, by relatives or employers who are willing to hire them.
It appears to me that we should examine more thoroughly and carefully the requests for parole which are submitted to us or to the Minister of Justice in the case of many of our young people who are now in jail. This does not mean that we should give our blessing to the vandalism of those young convicts. Not at all. But I am of the opinion that after a stay of a few months in prison, many of those young people change their mind and become honourable citizens afterwards, citizens who understand the implications of their actions. I maintain that most of them have committed thoughtless deeds because they had joined a gang or a group of young people of their age, which was often dominated and led by elders-and it is in this manner that those young people have become involved.
Now, the parents must be taken into consideration and also the family circle where
Supply-Justice
those young people evolve. If the possibility of an easy rehabilitation is seen for them, if they seem to show regret as sincere as possible and a desire not to repeat the same actions, it seems to me that they should get better consideration from the Minister of Justice.
Mr. Chairman, in the estimates of the Department of Justice, there is also an item concerning the administration of the R.C.M.P. On that score, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Justice on a fact which happened in Quebec city some ten days ago. A certain Mr. Jos. Gignac had secured a $5,000 loan from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and he was paying it back at the rate of $100 a month. He experienced financial difficulties and undertook to pay back the corporation at the rate of $30 a month, and that, for the last five or six months. However, some ten days ago, while the balance due by Mr. Gignac was $507, an R.C.M.P. officer from the Quebec division, under the direction of a Mr. Poirier, arrested Mr. Gignac and put him in a cell, ordering him to pay the total amount of $507, otherwise he would remain in jail.
Apparently, the individual named Poirier, a very zealous member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, uttered threats against Mr. Gignac, saying that he would serve several months in jail should he not pay the amount of $507. Fortunately, somebody came to Mr. Gignac's rescue and paid the total amount, thus allowing him to recover his freedom.
I wonder under what section of what legislation a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police can arrest and imprison a man simply because he does not discharge the monthly $100 payments he undertook to make to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I have the greatest respect for the R.C.M.P. I imagine it is the most famous police force in the world since it is given as example in the whole world, but among its members may creep some zealous people of Mr. Poirier's type, who threaten the people they meet or rub shoulders with behind bars.
I point out this case to the attention of the Minister of Justice to let him know that Mr. Gignac was imprisoned because he had not paid the monthly $100 he owed Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Mr. Chairman, it was said a while ago that Canadian penitentiaries should be rehabilitation centres rather than correction centres. I agree with that. It happens that small thieves are condemned to one or two years in jail because they broke down a store door. They are given a good talking to and urged not to commit again the offences for which they were condemned. On the other

Supply-Justice
hand, there are others who should be the subject of a very special attention from the Minister of Justice and be put behind bars too, especially when there is evidence that they did not steal only from stores, taxi drivers or banks but from all the population.
1	refer to the sugar trust.
It was suggested this afternoon that a fine be imposed on those cartels, those "controllers", those cartel and "trust" owners. A letter received by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) was also read to us which proved beyond any doubt that exorbitant prices were being imposed on sugar, whichever trust was involved. But the trouble is that, should the Minister of Justice decide to prosecute those people, make them pay a fine of $25,000 or $50,000, then they would go back to where they came from as if nothing had happened. A fine of $250,000 or $25,000 means nothing to them because, upon their return, all they would have to do would be to raise the price of sugar by one half cent, one quarter cent or
2	cents per pound.
Because, then, it is $1,000,000 which goes into their bank. Therefore, it is no punishment for them. However, there is a way to prevent trusts and cartels from exploiting the Canadian people. When we are confronted with the man responsible for a trust on sugar or some other commodity-let us amend the legislation so as to put him behind bars for 10 years. I assure you that once behind bars, the "controller" in question will think about it twice before exploiting the people again when he goes back to his usual business, whether selling sugar or engaging in any other sector of the Canadian economy.
Mr. Chairman, we have little thieves, but we also have public thieves. They are the ones who jeopardize the economic security of this country. They are the ones who prevent the poor from shaking off their poverty and impose hardships to human persons who do not deserve them. As it was demonstrated, the price of sugar is twice as much in Canada as in the United States. This situation is certainly not normal. We have been discussing the sugar situation in this house for three months, and the more we discuss it the more the people who control the sugar trust go on raising their prices, in order to take more unfair advantage of the people.
That is the reason why I ask the Minister of Justice to amend the legislation, so that those trust controllers might be sent to jail. Then we would enjoy greater freedom.
I understand that some trusts may help support election coffers. In all likelihood, this support to election coffers prevents the present Minister of Justice, as was also the

case for past ministers, to take action, but we, in our group, are not backed by the same coffers. We enjoy a greater freedom and this is why we denounce these swindlers and these trusts throughout Canada.
I appeal then to the Minister of Justice who, I believe, wants greater justice for all Canadians. We have a responsibility to help the oppressed and to safeguard them from the attacks of financiers and of trusts that prevent the human person from knowing self-achievement in a country like ours.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say just a few words, so as not to delay the passing of the minister's estimates.
I may have made somewhat bitter remarks in the past against the minister, but I am pleased to avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate him for his appointment, which is well deserved on account of the services he has given the country for a little more than 25 years.
I wish to tell him that he has chosen a very efficient staff. I had the occasion to seek information from his two executive assistants, Mr. Lord and Mr. Denis, lawyers both, and I have always been answered in a courteous and conscientious way.
I would also like to ask the minister whether he intends to amend the Criminal Code in 1964, so as to allow the provinces to establish lotteries if they wish to. I know that there are provinces which do not agree about such a thing at the present time, but the federal government often assumes positions which do not require the provinces' unanimous consent.
My second question is this. At a recent meeting in Banff, Alberta, the minister announced that the government was considering the convening of a conference, in 1964, to amend the British North America Act. I should appreciate it if the minister would tell the house what he means by the word "amend". Will the objective be the strengthening of national unity? What amendments does he have in mind?
I wonder also whether it would be possible for the Department of Justice to examine a problem which exists throughout Canada concerning the C.B.C. Indeed, certain provinces complain because they have no right of censorship over the films shown on television.
In fact, I remember that on one occasion the C.B.C. presented a film on its network shortly after the authorities of a western province had forbidden its showing in theatres.
I would also like to ask the minister if it would not be possible to amend the legislation soon, in order to stop this great number of n.s.f. cheques the payment of which is

refused by the bank owing to insufficient funds. Those cheques are a plague at this time everywhere in the country. I wonder if there would not be some means of passing legislation similar to that now in force in Switzerland. In fact, under the provisions of that legislation, whoever writes a cheque without sufficient funds is immediately placed under arrest and brought to court. I believe that the adoption of such legislation would prove beneficial to society.
Mr. Chairman, as far as Mr. Jacques Hebert's book is concerned, I do not think that we should give it too much attention, because this author specializes mainly in sensationalism. One must not let oneself be carried away by whatever he writes, because this is an existentialist author, and he delights especially in writing sensational material and in trying to revive old stories.
In my opinion, the minister was wise to ask the experts of his department to examine the book instead of setting up immediately a royal commission of inquiry. In fact, if he feels that the question is doubtful, it might be advisable to have competent lawyers study the Coffin case, before an investigation is launched, to prevent boosting the sale of Jacques Hebert's book by excessive publicity. Indeed that is the author's objective. Afterwards, the file could be closed if the experts so recommend. I would like it very much if the minister would answer those few questions.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm allow me a question? Does he not find the question serious enough-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have recognized the hon. member for Skeena and given him the floor.

Mr. Chairman, when a minister introduces his estimates for the first time, it is customary to congratulate him on his appointment. Right now, I do not quite know whether I should do just that by congratulating the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) or whether I should wish him farewell.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At any rate, it is well said. [Text]

Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that that is the extent of my knowledge of the language in which the minister is so proficient, because I will have to wait until I see the translation to discover what he said in rejoinder.
When the hon. member for Winnipeg North spoke he outlined the views of the members
Supply-Justice
of the New Democratic Party very ably and well, and I simply want to say in passing that I endorse them. He indicated that the emphasis within penitentiaries should be on rehabilitation or reform, rather than on dispensing justice and carrying out sentences merely for the sake of carrying them out. It seems to me still, as it did a few years ago, that the penitentiaries branch is perhaps more interested in the soul of the inmate in prison than in what he will do when he gets back into society again. We spend more money for and employ more clergy than psychologists. I understand there are some nine full time psychologists on the staff of the penitentiaries branch and not a single full time psychiatrist, but there are 22 full time ministers or priests to minister to the needs of inmates. If we would alter that situation a bit and spend more money on psychologists and rehabilitation, those gentlemen and ladies who are now inmates of prisons would have a better chance to get to that place where the members of the clergy want them to go after they leave this earth.
In my view there is not too strong a desire on the part of members of parliament to pay more than passing attention to affairs within the penitentiaries, or to penological matters. In that regard I am reminded of the fact that since our native Indian people have been given the right to vote in federal elections there has been a marked increase in the interest by political parties and candidates and members of parliament in Indian affairs, because the Indians are a group of voters now. This has been beneficial, because it means that parliament and members of parliament are better informed about Indian affairs. It seems to me that we might expand this idea and perhaps give the inmates of prisons the right to vote in federal elections. If such were the case, I am sure the prisons would be filled with members of parliament wanting to find out how these people were going to vote, and in the process members of parliament would discover some of the problems within prisons. The result might be a better attitude toward prison matters than exists at the present time.
I should like to deal with only one aspect of the activities of the Department of Justice, which has to do with two sections of the Criminal Code. There is one section which I think is a most shocking invasion of the rights of the people of this country. I refer to section 660, the so-called habitual criminal section providing for the imposition of a sentence of preventive detention, which is in effect a life sentence.
A person may be charged, if that is the proper expression, under section 660 of the

Supply-Justice
code if he has been convicted on three separate occasions since the age of 18 years of indictable offences for which he has received a sentence of five years or more. If this can be proved to the court he can then be sentenced to life imprisonment, or as a so-called habitual criminal receive a sentence of preventive detention.
Even though this provision has been on the statute books for some 13 or 14 years, I submit this is wrong in principle because in fact it is a process by which an individual may be sentenced twice for the same crime. He may receive a sentence which in fact is the third of a series of sentences he has received since the age of 18 and then find he is subject to being charged as a habitual criminal and may be so charged and found guilty under that section. I am not sure of the legal terminology used with regard to this section. I do not know whether the individual is charged, found guilty and sentenced or whether there is merely an application to the court for the imposition of such a sentence. However, in essence the individual may find himself sentenced to a certain number of years on a specific charge and then find later that an application has been made to the court to sentence him again for exactly the same charge, plus two or more other charges for which he has already been sentenced and with regard to which he has already paid his penalty.
I submit this is sentencing the individual twice for the same offences; and in addition the sentence of preventive detention is based to an extent on future crimes that might be committed, because reference is also made in the statute to the individual habitually associating with other criminals or normally leading that sort of life. This section of the code is not confined to crimes of violence such as sexual offences or crimes of violence such as armed robbery or assault. It covers the whole field of indictable offences, and because it does its impact falls more heavily upon certain sections of our so-called criminal society than it does upon others.
I am thinking primarily about the impact of the status of habitual criminal as described in the code upon those unfortunate people who are narcotic addicts. These people, because they are narcotics addicts and because of the rather stupid policy adopted in the past towards narcotic addiction, are pretty well doomed to a life of narcotic addiction, whether they are in prison or out of it. Under this section a person may well find that he could receive, for one indictable offence, a sentence of five years if the crime with which he is charged carried a sentence of five years. Then, he could discover later that, even

though he had been sentenced to the maximum for the particular offence with which he was charged, he was confronted with a life sentence under the habitual criminal section of the code. He might, on the other hand, find himself having been charged with an offence which, for the sake of argument, carried a life sentence, such as trafficking in narcotics, and the presiding judge, in view of the circumstances of the case, may only sentence him to two, three or five years. Then, that individual may find himself faced with an application by the attorney general under the habitual criminal section of the code.
I submit that inherent in this section there is the principle that a person may be sentenced twice for the same crime. He may be sentenced once for the crime itself, and then under the habitual criminal section of the code which carries with it a sentence of life imprisonment if in fact, he has had other convictions which carried with them possible sentences of five years or more.
Normally, I gather there is a period of 30 days during which an individual may appeal his sentence. It can happen, and often has happened, that an individual who has been sentenced does not appeal within the 30 days. Then, he finds, after his last resort has gone, that he may be imprisoned for life if a charge is laid under this section. However, if an indication were given to him before that this charge might be laid, he might have appealed his sentence. There are a variety of reasons why a person might not appeal a sentence, such as a lack of money and so on. He might then, having the knowledge that he might be faced with life imprisonment under the habitual criminal section, take steps to save himself from that fate.
It is submitted that some people plead guilty or, in effect, take steps to prove their guilt under section 660 of the code without actually knowing what they are doing. Perhaps I could best illustrate this point by quoting from a letter sent to me by an inmate in one of the penitentiaries in Canada. I do not believe it would be correct for me to put the name of this individual on the public records. Any hon. member desiring to see the letter to ascertain that an inmate did write to me, may do so. The letter reads in part as follows, in respect of this question of pleading guilty or proving your guilt under the habitual criminal section:
There's one other thing that bothers me very much and that is the way the officials of the court allow you to plead guilty, without your knowledge, to what amounts to life imprisonment. By that X mean they first, with no warning after they have found you guilty or you may plead guilty, which I did, they then ask you if a document is your criminal record which, in fact it is. When you reply that it is, not knowing you are about to be charged as an habitual criminal 80 or 90 days later,

they use this admission in your habitual proceedings, which of course makes it very easy for conviction.
This, coupled with the practice which allows the 30 day period for appeal to lapse before an application is made, is a most unfair way of using what I think is a shocking section of the code in any event. The chairman of the national parole board, Mr. Street, is a person for whom I have great admiration. Incidentally, I think he is doing a remarkable job of administering the act under his jurisdiction and assisting in providing a mechanism whereby people may be rehabilitated. A few years ago Mr. Street made a statement to the effect that the habitual criminal section could be used more often so that individuals would be placed under his jurisdiction for potential parole of life sentences. Then, they would have control of these individuals on parole, with all the administrative facilities available to them, and that individual would be subject to their control for the rest of his natural life.
As a result, there was a marked increase in applications for preventive detention under section 660 of the Criminal Code. This has resulted in what I believe are some anomalous and rather ridiculous situations. If we look, for instance, at the question of the age of people who have been sentenced under this section, we find that in the city of Vancouver a 68 year old man, a narcotics addict, was sentenced to life imprisonment. We all, of course, have a feeling of pity and sorrow for narcotics addicts. I believe everybody in this house regrets the fact that past governments, this government and provincial governments, have not found an effective and sensible way of dealing with narcotics addiction. Here we have a person 68 years of age, a narcotics addict and he is sentenced to life imprisonment as a habitual criminal. This is a rather ridiculous situation. The statistics printed in Hansard for July 17 of this year reveal that of the 68 people who are serving sentences of preventive detention, eight were 58 years of age or over. As I have said, this seems to be a rather ridiculous situation.
In British Columbia, the primary effect of this section of the Criminal Code falls upon people who have a history of narcotic addiction. We all know how the R.C.M.P. hounds people who have a history of narcotics addiction, almost day and night, for the purpose of trapping them and charging them with possession or trafficking in narcotics. Automatically, they are sentenced to the penitentiary. I have a great wealth of correspondence from one individual in the British Columbia penitentiary, and have visited and spoken to others who have found themselves in this position.

The minister, his department and the government should review very carefully and seriously the section of the Criminal Code which sets up the machinery for preventive detention and take steps to eliminate it as it is presently constituted, because I submit it is a violation of the right of an individual, namely the right not to be sentenced more than once for the same crime.
There are other matters in which this party is extremely interested. I shall not go into them at this time, except to say that other members of the party have an interest in these fields also, and will put their points of view to the minister. We will attentively watch and listen to the responses of the minister to the various points we raise, and we hope the words we use will somehow or other have a beneficial effect.

I should first like to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena, on his efforts in French tonight. I notice he has been carrying on some correspondence with the minister of natural resources in Quebec, and it seems Mr. Levesque has had some influence upon him.
Other hon. members this evening have spoken about people who are in prison and who may have been dealt with harshly. I am going to speak of some people who perhaps should be in prison and who have not been dealt with at all harshly. I want to say something about the anti-combines act and the activities of the government in the past few years in enforcing it. I have had a feeling for some time that for a great many years really not very much has been done in Canada in this particular field, and my feeling is shared by many people. It is only rarely^ that we see any successful prosecutions in the field of monopolistic practices, and usually these are followed by what seem to be very small fines.
Many members of the public are skeptical about this whole affair, and the vague feelings they and I have had, have been substantiated in a recent major criticism of Canadian anti-combines legislation and the enforcement of it, in a book published earlier this year entitled "Canadian Anti-Combines Administration, 1952-60." This was written by Gideon Rosenbluth, professor of economics at the University of British Columbia, and Mr. Hugh Thorburn, an assistant professor of political science at Queen's University.
Before dealing with the period under study, 1952-60, the authors give a short history of combines legislation in Canada. They deal with the early days, with the views of Mr. Mackenzie King on this subject, and with the work of Mr. McGregor who was commissioner until his resignation in 1949. They then go

Supply-Justice
into the dispute which arose, I believe around 1948 or 1949, between some members of the cabinet, between Mr. C. D. Howe and Mr. McGregor, a dispute which arose out of an investigation of the flour milling industry.
Following the resignation of Mr. McGregor a royal commission was established to investigate the legislation, and this commission was generally known as the MacQuarrie commission. I note that the President of the Privy Council was a member of that royal commission, and it made some recommendations, some of which were implemented by the government of that day.
It was at that time that the functions were separated, and there was established the restrictive trade practices commission, and the office of investigation and research. Incidentally, I notice that one of the original members of the first restrictive trade practices commission is the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, so that within the cabinet there is no lack of experts on this particular subject.
In 1960-61 other changes were made in the legislation. Over the years Mr. Fulton had gained some bouquets for the job he did as minister of justice, particularly in the field of penal reform, but I do not think he has any awards coming to him for what he did in the field of restrictive trade practices, because the changes made at that time seem to me, and to the authors of this book, to have weakened the act. However, it is the enforcement of the act with which we are primarily concerned.
The authors point out that the importance of a government department or agency can be measured by the amount of budget it receives. They point out that the amount of budget available to the combines investigation branch has been rather small throughout the years. In 1960 it had a budget of approximately half a million dollars, and at page 44 of their book they give some comparisons for other government departments. The Canadian government travel bureau in that year had $2.3 million, while the Newfoundland bait service had the same amount of money, half a million dollars. I am not knocking the Newfoundland bait service, but it seems to me the combines investigation service ought to be a more important field of activity.
In that same year the administration of the Immigration Act cost $1.2 million, and defence research and development $39.2 million. In any case, the amount of money allocated to combines investigation has been quite small, and on looking at the estimates for this year I was disappointed to note that there are very minor increases for the office of the director of investigation and research, and the restrictive trade practices commission.

I know the minister may answer that this budget was prepared by the previous administration. Perhaps that can be accepted for the moment, but I would point out that, even though our gross national product has grown year by year, and at present is around $37 billion, the total amount for combines investigation has not grown in any comparable manner.
The authors of this book made quite a thorough search and analysis of the administration of the act between 1952 and 1960. They analysed the fields of business that were investigated. They have made lists where successful investigations have taken place, where prosecutions have followed, and they have also listed those fields of business where the investigations were unsuccessful or were not followed up. The important thing is that the total amount of successful anti-combine work, the successful completion of investigations, followed by prosecutions in some cases and by no prosecutions in others, is a very small part of the total business activity in Canada.
It does not seem to me that there has been very much increased activity in this field since we had a change of administration last spring. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North, has at present a series of questions on the order paper concerning recommendations of the restrictive trade practices commission, recommendations which have not yet been acted upon. During the past several months I have, on two or three occasions, asked about a report filed by the commission concerning tied sales, that is, the practice of petroleum companies forcing service stations to buy and handle certain products.
This practice was recommended against by the commission some two years ago, and the minister has replied that the recommendation is under study by an interdepartmental committee. I hope that in the new year we can see some action on this point.
What year?

1964. However, Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied from my own observation, and this has been verified by the authors of this book, that there has not been a very vigorous enforcement of the combine laws which we have. A number of years ago one hon. member of this house had this to say, and I am quoting from page 13 of the book:
A law can be full of teeth, but if the teeth are not used to bite with it becomes a mere sham on the statute books.
That member is now the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. Again, Mr. Chairman, the authors point out the dilemma that faces a Canadian government in this field. They say

the government has a choice between alienating important business groups in the country on the one hand, or keeping satisfied certain other groups on the other hand-the small businessmen, the consumers, labour, agriculture, and so on. They say also that in this balancing which is supposed to take place, the other groups-the consumers, the small businessmen-usually lose out. Again, Mr. Chairman, they pose this very important question:
Does anti-combines activity in Canada represent a serious attempt to influence the structure and functioning of the Canadian economy, or is it essentially a political gesture designed to meet the demands of voters while leaving the structure and practices of business substantially unaffected?
I get the impression that this is what has happened in the past, that it has been left unaffected. It seems that our governments in the past have acted on the assumption that combinations, monopolistic practices, are not the usual thing; this is something out of the ordinary; somebody may commit a crime and should be punished for it. I suggest this is the wrong approach, and that in the type of economy we have the tendency to eliminate competition is there at all times. Indeed, people in business may be forced to do this. Nevertheless the tendency to eliminate competition, to form larger firms, to get the market under the control of fewer and fewer companies, is built into our economy. It is not something unusual that has to be watched at all times.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that this is much truer in Canada than perhaps in the United States. An earlier study by one of the authors of this book, Professor Rosen-bluth, "Concentration in Canadian Manufacturing Industries", points out that we have a relatively greater concentration here than in the United States, so that we should watch this particular field of activity more than they do in the United States. I hope this subject is under study by the government at the present time. I see the parliamentary secretary to the minister has the same book in his hand, so at least he is studying it. I hope someone else is also. When the new estimates are presented for the next fiscal year I hope we will see an increase in the budget for this very important department.
I should like to conclude, Mr. Chairman, by reminding the minister of this. I quote again from the text:
However, in more than a technical sense, ultimate responsibility for the scope of anti-combines activity rests with the cabinet. It selects the director and the commission, determines heir budgets, and can issue directives that govern their work. It selects prosecuting counsel and is responsible for their instructions. It can initiate changes in the legislation to meet needs revealed by judicial interpretation. If the application of the
