I trust, Mr. Chairman, we will see a change in the future in this particular field.

Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege to rise in my place and speak on the estimates of the Department of Justice, particularly in view of the fact that this department is responsible for the estimates of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is just 90 years ago that Sir John A. Macdonald introduced a bill into the House of Commons to set up this world famous force. We have always had good leadership in the force, which has contributed in a marked degree to their world wide reputation in the maintenance of justice and freedom in our country. It is a painful thing to have to sit here sometimes and hear members of parliament, who should know better, pick on the mounted police and their role in our national life as if they were some kind of hoodlum gang from Chicago, and not the world famous force which it is and which we so rightly admire.
To say that the R.C.M.P. hound people in the matter of narcotics is just sheer nonsense. If you knew, as I know and as the members of the mounted police know, how difficult it is to pin down the traffickers in narcotics in Canada, and how our boys go out and risk life and limb to track these people down, I do not think you would say they are hounding them at all. They are performing a most difficult task. Having found the fellows who peddle it, it is even more difficult to track down the source of these drugs. I would recommend to the minister through you, sir, that the mounted police be taken more into his and the people's confidence. I think those who have to administer the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act know better than anybody else the best long term plan for putting down this trafficking. I personally am convinced that if we gave drugs free to the people who are subject to this dreadful habit and took the profit out of drug trafficking, we would have some chance of putting down this nefarious business. It is the enormous profit which causes drug trafficking, even in Canada where we have the services of the mounted police to try and keep it down.
Some hon. members may not know that in certain countries these dangerous drugs can be bought for $2 or $3 a pound. When they get here and are watered down, thinned out, and sold on the market to the individual, sometimes one packet of dope costs as much as $30 or $40. This means a pound of dope can be worth $55,000 to $75,000. Do not say the

Supply-Justice
mounted police hound people. Let us get behind them, not only outside the house but inside, and appreciate the service they are giving us.
It has also been said that they hound people who are suspected of subversive activities. Hon. members know how difficult it is to track down subversive activities. These activities range from open sabotage to the undermining of the morale and the national spirit of our young people. It is not an easy task to pin it down. The R.C.M.P. are seized with this job. None of us like it; but they are doing the job and yet it is said they are spying on their neighbours. That is a harsh word to apply to the work of security. This is done in the United States by the F.B.I. We are very proud of the work they do down there. Our force, in plain clothes, are seized with this job in Canada. They are not hounding any Canadian, but are looking out for the security of our country. I am tired of hearing this carping criticism which I think is only dreamed up to get notoriety in picking on a famous organization which is doing its best.
I think the role of the R.C.M.P. should be reviewed with regard to their contracts with the provinces. On several occasions within my memory the R.C.M.P. have been in difficulty. Their leadership has been in difficulty because the duties of the force have not been clearly defined, when it comes to maintaining law and order. There are three circumstances in which the force might be called in. In the first place, if there is a man breaking the law, openly stealing or drunk in a public place, their duty is plain, where they are seized with this duty. It is to arrest the man and bring him before the magistrate at the proper time, see that the proper evidence is produced, and so forth. The role of the force is plain. It might be called out in time of open strife, perhaps even to co-operate with our armed forces in an emergency. Naturally if a submarine was seen coasting along the Cape Breton coast a patrolling officer would contact the military authorities, who would alert the army, the navy and the air force. Then they would retire to their proper role of civilian police. I do not think there is any difficulty there; they could be used as a warning device to let the proper authorities know.
Then there is a third situation, in which they are called upon in the role of what civilians perhaps call strikebreakers. Where are they then? I say that their duty in this situation has never been clearly defined. Where and when is it the responsibility of the individual policeman or the mounted police, as led by their officers, to maintain law and order, which in a sense is a kind of political war? I think these roles should be clearly defined and then never again will

the commissioner and the mounted police find themselves at loggerheads with the Minister of Justice.
Some years ago the R.C.M.P. were used actively in what we called the youth and police program. There are statistics in the records to show that when this youth and police program was in full operation juvenile delinquency suffered a dramatic decline. We used to call juvenile delinquency "being a bad boy," but, call it what you like, when the mounted police were actively engaged in this great program there was a dramatic drop in juvenile delinquency. I think many of the members felt at the time that this was an imposition. Some of them did it willingly, some under a certain amount of pressure from above; but nevertheless, if the record is looked up it will be found that the mounted policeman was proving himself to be in his finest role when he was interested and active in this preventive police work among our youngsters. I would recommend to the department, through you, sir, that this very important and valuable use of the mounted police be considered for revival.
Another matter to which I wish to bring attention, having been a policeman myself, is the great difficulty in the public mind, and sometimes even in the minds of the police, of the lack of uniformity of provincial laws. We have at least ten traffic acts in Canada, not to mention the bylaws in all the different cities. I know that that is not anything new, but I would again stress that I think it is of prime importance that at the next provincial conference perhaps the heads of the municipal police, the heads of the mounted police, and the heads of the various justice departments, the attorneys general, might well accompany their premiers, straighten out the situation once and for all, and agree upon a sensible traffic law which would be acceptable all across Canada. I do not think we need run into constitutional difficulties here. As long as we have uniformity in our thinking it would not be difficult to get uniformity in our laws. To travel across our great country touring and trying to keep in mind ten, 12 or 14 different traffic laws is certainly difficult for someone who has had personal experience in the matter; for the uninitiated driver of an automobile I am sure it causes many accidents and a great deal of grief and pain.
May I close by saying that during this 90 years we have always had leadership in the mounted police which has been a credit to that force and to our country. I must say that we can look forward to the future with confidence in these fine men who care for our national security, and the Queen's peace.

Mr. Chairman, I shall take just a few minutes of the committee's time since I only wish to outline one point in connection with the estimates of the Department of Justice.
I should like to call the minister's attention to the necessity, indeed, the urgency of amending the Bankruptcy Act so that the rights of Canadian citizens are better protected and more respected.
Mr. Chairman, I am not a jurist and that may be why I do not understand much of that legislation. However, on the basis of what I have been told by members of the legal profession, I do not hesitate to say that the Bankruptcy Act is probably the most complicated and ambiguous piece of legislation in our statutes.
Besides, numerous bankruptcies are merely daring and clever financial operations to succeed in business in defiance of all honesty and fairness.
And yet, those operations are effected under the act and seem to comply, if not with the spirit, at least with the letter of the law.
I have just gone through a rather painful experience during which 30 odd workers of my city have lost almost $20,000 in salaries following a bankruptcy that has been before the court for more than two years.
Yet, those workers acted in good faith and relied on people regarded as competent to help them to recover their salaries.
In this case, of course, I am not accusing anybody of incompetence nor of dishonesty, but I am still convinced that if the Bankruptcy Act had been worded in a clear, accurate and concise way, those workers would have been able to recover what rightly belongs to them.
For several of them, the losses exceeded $1,000, an amount which represents several months' salary. I am not trying to be emotional over this, but try to understand, Mr. Chairman, what such an amount means to families having to manage on an annual budget of $2,000 or $2,500.
It is urgently required that the Bankruptcy Act be thoroughly reviewed so as to protect the public against unscrupulous and ambitious crooks.
I am thinking not only of workers, but also of suppliers and subcontractors who, more than once, have suffered at the hands of those sharks.
If they have not done so already, I hope that the officials of the Department of Justice will start planning a revision of the act, not to cover and shield questionable transactions, but to protect the rights of Canadian citizens who, in their vast majority, are honest and conscientious people.
Supply-Justice
The present act gives rise to judicial conflicts, which are always very expensive for those who bear the costs.
I quite understand that it is difficult, not to say impossible, to draft legislation which would put an end to lawsuits in cases of bankruptcy; but I am confident that the departmental experts will at least be able to improve matters considerably in that field.

Mr. Chairman, I only need a few minutes to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to some of the problems with which my constituency is confronted.
However, before doing so, I wish to congratulate on his excellent French, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who spoke a moment ago. He should indeed be congratulated for this commendable effort, and I suggest that the other members might follow his example.
Mr. Chairman, I am coming now to the substance of my remarks. I wish to point out to the Minister of Justice that, in my constituency, there is no bankruptcy court.
As I pointed out to the Minister of Justice a few days ago, we must go to Sherbrooke, that is some 60 miles from Granby, the centre of the constituency of Shefford, to settle bankruptcy cases.
There is a court at Sweetsburg, in the district of Bedford but at the present time there is no bankruptcy court there. Such a condition is far from being practical for lawyers or interested parties who have bankruptcy cases to settle.
In addition, I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that the city of Granby in my constituency of Shefford has quite a large population now but is still without a court house or a court; we have to go to Sweetsburg to settle our legal problems.
I am therefore wondering whether it would be possible to establish in the main city of my constituency a court where our problems could be settled. It is our most important problem at the present time. As the bar association of Bedford pointed out some three weeks ago in a resolution, it wishes to settle this problem as soon as possible. Consequently, I hope that the Minister of Justice will attend to this matter.
In addition, I wish to point out to the Minister of Justice the problems of the judges, especially in the Quebec, Montreal and St. Hyacinthe districts. Looking over the list of cases, we note that thousands are waiting to come before the court. It is also noted that in some cases, they will have to wait for three and maybe four years before they can be heard.

Supply-Justice
I think the Minister of Justice is aware of the problem.
At present, in the city of Montreal, there is a backlog of thousands of unheard cases or cases heard several years ago and still awaiting a judgment. Besides, a great many cases have not yet been called before the court.
Mr. Chairman, I should also like to make a few comments concerning the famous Coffin case which everyone has heard of and which has been making the headlines these last few days. It does not seem normal to me at this time to allow someone to write a book- maybe hoping for a large circulation-that can only undermine justice in our country.
I am not discussing the merits of the book. But, at this time, the way things have been going, I doubt the wisdom of the questions being asked about prominent people and especially about judicial principles and mechanisms in Canada.
What strikes me most is that for several weeks now they have been reconstituting a case by means of films-and in this I ask the Minister of Justice whether the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not co-operating with the writer of this book in order to reconstitute the circumstances of the crime in the Coffin case. We have the feeling that the C.B.C. and the writer of the book in question work together, hand in hand, in order to create a scandal around an unproven theory.
In any case, what moves me the most is to see that the C.B.C. is using our money, public funds, to undermine the concept of justice in Canada.
Under the circumstances, I would ask the Minister of Justice, whose longing for justice I would in no way question, to kindly request the minister responsible for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to have an inquiry made and see to it that openly offered cooperation by socialists in the C.B.C. be stopped. In fact, for several years, everybody has been complaining that the C.B.C. is crawling with socialists; you get the feeling, especially since the alleged Coffin scandal has been stirred, that the intention is to promote certain well known socialists in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I should like the Minister of Justice to settle that case as soon as possible, because the longer we wait, the more we let those things happen, the greater the harm done to the smooth operation of our judicial system.
Therefore, I suggest that the sale of that book be banned, that a royal commission be set up and that the culprits be convicted,

otherwise, the confidence of the Canadian people in the judicial system of this country will be destroyed.
Mr. Chairman, I think I have said enough to draw the minister's attention to the problems raised by the Coffin case, to which newspapers have been devoting full pages in the last few days.
We seem to want to pass the buck but if nothing is done, who will deal with the problem?
Mr. Chairman, I know that the Minister of Justice has answered a few questions on the subject, these last few days saying that he was expecting certain decisions which did not come under his department. But he ought to do everything in his power to set up an inquiry into the facts under his department, through his officials and those of the province of Quebec, so as to put an end to that scandal which, if allowed to continue, will contribute to undermine the trust of Canadian citizens in the judicial system of our country.

I want to take a few minutes of the time of the committee to pursue a subject which I have raised on the orders of the day for the last couple of days and which has been the subject of comment by several of those who have spoken in the course of this debate. I refer to the Coffin murder trial. I want, again, to urge the Minister of Justice to give some consideration to a suggestion which has been made both inside and outside this house, namely that a royal commission should be set up to investigate the situation. I understand that some of my hon. friends on this side of the house are not in favour of this suggestion-that they have suggested a committee of lawyers should look into it. This, of course, is something which has already been done. It was done in the United States, and it was done here, when the committee which reviewed the case included some of the defence lawyers as well as newspapermen, all of whom came up with grave doubts as to Coffin's guilt, and the justice of his being put to death.
It may seem strange that we should be concerning ourselves today with what happened ten years ago. In the summer of 1953, three United States hunters came to an area of the Gaspe and were killed there. Their bodies were mangled by bears. A few weeks later they were discovered and Mr. Coffin was subsequently arrested. Then there began what is surely the strangest and most complicated criminal trial in the legal history of this country. No murder case ever went through so many procedures. Perhaps no man was ever reprieved so many times. By the time he was finally executed, Coffin had been drawn back

from the brink of death no less than seven times. He started his trial with jet black hair and he went to the gallows with snow white hair. No case within my recollection has provoked so much disturbance in the minds of the legal people who have perused the evidence. From the day Coffin was arrested to the day he died a curtain of mystery descended around this trial and this veil of mystery has persisted until this very day.
Recent disclosures have resurrected the events of the trial and revived doubts as to the validity of the sentence. Let us consider the trial itself. The mangling of the bodies meant there was no real evidence of the way in which they had died. Coffin was convicted on circumstantial evidence, and there is considerable doubt as to the strength of that chain of evidence. It is a well known rule of law that circumstantial evidence must not be just consistent with guilt; it must be inconsistent with any other reasonable conclusion. This is the question which has troubled the lawyers who have been concerned about this case. It has troubled the counsel who acted for him, the people who knew him in the penitentiary and the priest who sat with him and knew him for some five months. This was a case in which there was no murder weapon ever produced, no mark on the body, no killing bullet ever found. Only one charge was laid and that was in the death of the Lindsay boy. The only evidence of a bullet wound was a hole in his jersey. The medico-legal expert at the trial testified that he could not say with certainty that the rifle Coffin was alleged to have used would have caused such a hole.
So much at the trial was not done. One hesitates to criticize counsel. It is always easy to be wise after the event. But an examination of the trial itself makes me wonder. Witnesses were not cross-examined. No defence at all was put in. Not a single witness was called in Mr. Coffin's defence. Mr. Coffin himself was not permitted to take the stand to testify, although throughout the period before he was executed he insisted he had always wanted to. As I said, the only evidence of a bullet hole in the body was a hole in the jersey and the medical evidence was very doubtful in that sphere.
Some of the bodies were found five miles apart in the bush. Maps were presented to the jury, for example, that did not show the multiplicity of roads that permeated the area and the ease with which other individuals could have arrived at the scene of the murder. The goods of the murdered hunters were strewn along the road leading from the scene of the murder and evidence was given this could not have been done by one man but that, for example, it would require two
Supply-Justice
or three men driving a moving vehicle. No investigation was made in this regard.
Coffin had stated, and he maintained until his death, that when he left these men in the bush there were two Americans with them and that the Americans had driven up in a jeep which Coffin described in great detail and with great particularity. We have no evidence that any search was made to find this jeep though after his death, as I will show in a moment, witnesses came forward with affidavit evidence that they had met these men and seen them in the area.
Coffin denied having a rifle and no rifle was ever produced at the trial. Yet it was alleged he had used a rifle. The only evidence against Coffin at the trial as to a rifle was that of a Mr. McGregor, I believe, who said he had seen Mr. Coffin coming out of the bush and in the truck he saw what he thought was a rifle. The man was never cross-examined to ascertain if it could have been anything else. After Coffin's death this man came forward and made an affidavit stating that he wished to change his evidence, that he now wished to say he thought it was an iron bar that had been in the truck. Again, no investigation was made of this statement.
The trial was the longest and most expensive criminal trial in the history of the county. It would have bankrupted the county to pay for it, but the entire expenses were very kindly paid by the province of Quebec which seemed to have a very keen interest in the trial at that time. The defence had stated throughout that they were going to call 100 witnesses, but when the crown rested its case the defence got up and said: "We are not going to put in any evidence at all; Mr. Coffin is not going to take the stand in his own defence".
Coffin until his death, as I say, persisted in his story. He never changed it one iota. He always claimed that he had wanted to get on the stand and tell the one story that could have saved his life, namely that he had been in the bush, that he had seen the truck of the hunters, that he had stolen the goods that were later found in his possession but that he did not murder these hunters. This was the one defence which, if believed, could have saved Coffin's life but he was not given the opportunity to present it.
I am not being critical of the people who conducted the trial, but the trial itself raises very grave doubts in the minds of a lot of people as to the validity or otherwise of his conviction. However, Mr. Coffin was found guilty. Perhaps on the evidence presented this was the only conclusion the jury could reach. Certainly with no defence presented it must have been difficult for the jury.

But the real mystery of the Coffin case starts from the day of his conviction, because after his conviction and before his death a whole series of bits of evidence developed which cumulatively began to increase the doubt which everyone felt. For example, the crown had charged that Coffin had murdered these people for their money and had stolen $650 from them. After his death people came forward with sworn affidavits that they had paid Mr. Coffin $580 to go out and stake mining claims for them. This was never followed up and investigated further.
Coffin always maintained there was a jeep with American hunters at the scene of the murder. Sergeant Doyon, who testified at the trial, said that he had seen marks of a jeep on the scene but had not mentioned it at the trial because nobody had asked him. This was not brought out in cross-examination. Dr. Wilson, a young Toronto physician, swore an affidavit with his wife that in June of 1953 they met two American hunters crossing on a ferryboat going toward the area. They described the coats the men wore and the plywood covering, and so on, on the jeep, which was similar to the jeep that Coffin had described. Maddern River, a Lome Patterson service station operator, remembered seeing the same jeep and that the occupants had asked for the Lindsays, who were the murdered men. Again this was in the general vicinity.
A Dr. Charles Attendu of Montreal gave evidence that he had seen a jeep in the area near the murder. A Mr. Tapp, who was a police constable, recalled meeting an American at a cocktail party who was going to go to Gaspe to hunt, and in this book by Beli-veau he recites how the American was picked up by another man in a jeep and they drove off to go hunting.
The whole mystery of the rifle that committed the murder has never been resolved. I have already placed on the record the statement of Wilson McGregor who was a witness as to the rifle, and who first thought it was a rifle and later wanted to change his evidence, and made an affidavit that he thought it was an iron bar.
Because of these doubts the pressures mounted and the government of the day then referred the case to the Supreme Court of Canada and asked the court to give it guidance as to what it would have done if it had heard the appeal. The case was argued extensively. I believe the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration represented the government at that hearing and is no doubt familiar with the case. At the conclusion of the case the court ruled five to two that if

it had heard the case it would not have quashed the conviction and would not have granted a retrial.
No one is quarrelling with that, because the real significance of the Supreme Court of Canada case is that the court did not have before it all of the new evidence that came to light after Coffin's conviction. The Supreme Court of Canada, and rightly so under our rules, is limited to the court record at the trial and at this hearing it did not have access to all of the new evidence I have alleged tonight. To my knowledge this evidence has never been presented to a court of law considering this matter.
Therefore, while the Supreme Court of Canada did rule five to two, I think the significant point is that there was dissent, that a judge of the eminence of Mr. Justice Cartwright said on the basis of the evidence at the trial that, had he been dealing with the matter "it would have been my opinion the appeal should have been allowed, the conviction quashed and a new trial directed". I would have thought that the fact of a dissenting judgment by two eminent judges would have raised doubts in the hearts of the members of the cabinet. The new evidence I have mentioned tonight was not available to the court, of course, but it was available to the government of the day and representations were made to the government, first for a new trial, which was declined and, second, for commutation of the sentence to life imprisonment.
We do not know what consideration took place. The records indicate that considerable discussion took place in the cabinet and the matter was thoroughly investigated, but the tragedy is that by that time the Coffin case had developed political overtones in the province of Quebec. The then premier of the province, the late Mr. Duplessis, seemed to regard any action by the federal government as an infringement of provincial rights, and he began making very strong statements as to what view he would take should the federal cabinet ever grant a new trial or commute the sentence to life imprisonment. Indeed, Mr. Coffin's tragedy may have been that he was convicted of murder at a time when provincial rights were very dominant in the minds of Quebec politicians. There has never been any overt evidence of this, but it was significant that when the refusal to commute the sentence was announced Mr. Coffin then asked if he could marry his common-law wife and legitimize his little son. Mr. Duplessis, in all charity, refused. Mr. Coffin was hanged, I believe, the day after the cabinet declined to commute his sentence.
These, briefly, are some of the facts that surround this mysterious case. Over the years,

Mr. Chairman, the members of the legal profession, at least the ones I know, have had a secret doubt in their hearts. I do not know whether or not Coffin was guilty. I would have thought, in the face of the new evidence, in the face of the dissent by two eminent justices, there ought to have been enough doubt to have permitted Mr. Coffin to live under a sentence of life imprisonment. The tragedy today is that, even if we got a royal commission, even if we were able to prove Mr. Coffin innocent, he is not alive to be released. If ever there was a case which supported abolition of capital punishment, it is the case of Wilbert Coffin. Here was a case where there was doubt, I think, in the hearts of most honest men, a doubt which should have been resolved in his favour. For reasons good or bad, it was not so resolved.
After his death his counsel were so convinced of his innocence that they did not let the matter rest there. They formed a committee in Toronto, the Canadian Coffin committee, and invited newspapermen to serve on it. These people investigated further, reassessed the evidence and still there was this doubt. The well-known court of last resort in the United States, for the first time in its history, took up a capital case after the accused had been executed. They, too, investigated. As I have said, down through the years there has always been a doubt in the hearts of many people as to Mr. Coffin's guilt. Certainly, there was enough doubt that a new trial should have been granted. Certainly, there was enough doubt that he ought to have lived, so that if his name were ever cleared he would be able to be released. This avenue is no longer open to us and that is why we have raised this matter.
It is true that even if we were to investigate the case now, it would not help Coffin. We have always said that under our jurisdiction it is almost impossible for an innocent man to be convicted. The presumption of innocence is so strong, the necessity to prove his guilt beyond all reasonable doubt is so strong, that it is clearly impossible for an innocent man to be convicted. The question we now ask in our hearts is, is it possible for an innocent man to be executed? Until the mysteries of the Coffin case are resolved, I am not sure that we can ever say that under our jurisdiction it is impossible for an innocent man to be convicted and executed.
I am not too concerned with the recent book that has been written, although I think these charges are unprecedented and disturbing. The writer of the book seems to be alleging what almost amounts to a conspiracy of the parties to convict Coffin and have him executed. He makes what appear on the surface to be rather wild charges. They are 28902-5-373

sensational, and because they are sensational they are receiving very wide attention. I want to assure the Minister of Justice and his parliamentary secretary, for whom I have a very high regard, that interest in this case is not going to die down. If you think that by postponing or neglecting it you are, in some way, going to ride out the storm, the forces that have again been set in motion by this recent book and by the sensational charges, the resurrection of all the evidence that no court ever heard, I can tell you that most of the interest in this case is going to continue. For my part, I will do what I can to see that this is the case. I think it would be a wise move on the part of the Minister of Justice to appoint this royal commission. Let us go into the facts of the case and if, in fact, an innocent man was convicted and executed, then let that be known. Until you clear away the clouds of mystery that surround this case there will always be a cloud on the integrity of our jurisprudence, and for that reason I urge the minister to give favourable consideration to this request.

I had hoped the minister would reply before the item carried. There have been many problems that have been raised, but certainly none of them have been raised as eloquently as the last appeal by the hon. member for Danforth. I think it is a classic. If it does not move the Department of Justice to some consideration of this matter, then of course there is no point in anyone else speaking. I hoped the minister would reply immediately to the hon. member's remarks, because the problem I have is not quite as serious.
The problem I should like to raise, Mr. Chairman, is one in which I have been interested for a long time, but it affects only those who are getting out of prison or about to get out of prison. We have heard today many complaints about the manner in which we treat criminals. Certainly one of the problems that faces every inmate of a prison is the fact that some day he is expected to walk out the gate and live again in society. I think this is one of the most difficult problems that faces a prisoner, especially after many years in jail. In speaking to the officials of the Department of Justice, I have been told that cost is a factor in remedying the treatment of prisoners. They say that they know St. Vincent de Paul is in terrible shape and they would like to get prisons of a new type constructed. They would like a system under which an inmate might be given more freedom, under which he would be allowed to engage in useful activity in a community under supervision. These things would be very good, but we have not got the money for

Supply-Justice
them. Mr. Chairman, should we not have reached the stage where we try to treat our prisoners within our penal institutions in such a way as to indicate that we want to reclaim them in society? If we believe that the only purpose of putting a man in jail is for the protection of society, then I believe we have an obligation to make sure that a prison sentence is not necessarily considered as a punishment.
If this is true, then rehabilitation should be the prime consideration. It is very interesting sometimes to read what the prisoners themselves have to say. I should like to quote from an article written by a man who is certainly highly qualified in this field, the director of remission services, Mr. A. J. MacLeod. The article is entitled, "The Citizen and the Correctional System", and the author refers to a prisoner coming out of prison. He has this to say:
The prison experience is bound to have left its mark upon him, and this is especially so where the period of confinement has been eight, ten, 12 or 15 years. By this time he has forgotten most of the social graces that he ever knew. To him the simple operation of buying a package of cigarettes or ordering a cup of coffee in a restaurant is fraught with difficulty. He is highly conscious of his table manners-or rather the lack of them. He has forgotten how to go about buying his own clothing. He is nervous about meeting strangers.
I think that this is something most of us cannot understand. Just think, Mr. Chairman, how this must be in other fields, in particular emotional fields, rather than in social fields. The man who has been in jail for a considerable length of time has only met his family through a glass partition. He has not been able to talk with them in privacy, and he must have suffered untold emotional damage which he would have to be very strong to overcome.
I am sure some hon. members have visited prisons. No doubt a few of them have gone on junkets where they were shown around prisons, but I am sure others have gone to prisons to visit a particular inmate at the request of that inmate. He certainly has a problem or he would not invite a member of parliament to visit him; but when a member goes to see him a guard sits behind and the talk is through a partition. There is an emotional restriction that prevents free discussion.
By contrast, I am always very pleased when I visit any of the provincial jails. I do not know whether this is because I have no business being there, but when I go to visit prisoners in my own district the officials give me the doctor's office and we sit in easy chairs, with the guard outside the door, and we can talk about whatever we wish. It is much easier for a prisoner to discuss his

problems in that atmosphere rather than in the normal prison visiting atmosphere. I am quite happy to go into a room, have the door locked, and talk with one or two prisoners for a half an hour. They would not ask me to visit them unless they wanted to talk to me, and I am sure they would not cut my throat. Now, members of parliament certainly have more privileges than other prison visitors, but even so in federal prisons the atmosphere could be better.
There are many emotional problems that may develop between a prisoner, his wife and his children when they visit him, and there are many emotional problems for the family at home. We put the offender into prison and we say we do this because he has offended against society; but have we not really convicted his family as well, and is their penalty not even greater than the prisoner's? It has been said that once a door closes on a prisoner he knows he is convicted, what sentence he must serve, and the reason for it. But is this true for the family left at home who may not have been aware of the circumstances surrounding the offence which ended in the imprisonment? They may be completely unaware of it until, as some hon. member said this afternoon, the wife picks up a newspaper or listens to the radio and hears that her husband has been sentenced to four years in prison. What are we really sentencing such a family to, when they do not know what the circumstances were?
It is for this reason we should take advantage of some of the developments in other parts of the world. I know perfectly well that because we have not sufficient room to house all the prisoners in jail, we will have great difficulty in providing space for their wives to visit them in privacy. But I have been surprised to learn that in one of the most backward areas on this continent, the southern states, the state of Mississippi allows the wives and families of prisoners to visit them every Sunday. We should be able to do something like that. I do not know too much about penal institutions down there, but I have heard of the chain gangs. However, the authorities do not make these conjugal visits dependant on the good behaviour of a prisoner. It does not matter whether a prisoner has been on good behaviour or not; he is entitled to these visits. For three Sundays in succession his family can visit him from one o'clock in the afternoon until three, and on the fourth Sunday they can visit him from one o'clock until five o'clock.
In Alaska, which some say should be part of Canada, and which is the youngest of the American states, there is a law allowing families to visit prisoners for 24 hours, every three weeks, provided the prisoners have

been well behaved. This is even more far reaching than the system in Mississippi.
There are also cases where houses have been built in which families can visit with the prisoners. A wife can cook for her husband and the children can get to know their father. Such visits last for a week end, and when the prison gates open and the prisoner returns to society he does not find the transition so strange. Many countries have more farsighted laws in this regard than we have. I am not suggesting this will solve all the problems of rehabilitation, but it will solve some of them.
How many times have members of parliament sought parole on behalf of prisoners only to find that once that a parolee has been released he finds himself in trouble with his family? He no longer knows his wife. Maybe he did not know her too well before he went to jail, and the children left behind are now older. During the period he has been in jail the wife has been both mother and father to the children, has been the sole authority in the house, and when she punishes the children an argument develops with her husband. The man then does what he has always done, certainly what he has done when he has been in jail. He dodges responsibility, because he has not had to carry it for a long time. He goes downtown, gets drunk, his parole is rescinded, and he goes back to jail.
We do not want to talk about the homosexual practices engaged in, in all our prisons, but I think the minister will agree they have been the basis for most of the riots we have had in Canadian prisons over the past number of years. I am sure the minister is not going to stand up and go into the details of the homosexual practices that have taken place, and which have been responsible for many of these riots. But we know they exist. We know that if you take normal people out of society and put them under control, they will turn to any alternative which is available to them. With regard to those people who may not have the education, the intelligence and the background that would prohibit them doing this sort of thing, this is the type of practice in which they engage.
I think it is safe to say-and I am not making any charge against any particular penitentiary or any particular guard-that many of the guards fit into the category that allows this practice and take advantage of it, and sometimes they become quite wealthy because of it. This is a fact. This has always gone on in prisons; it has always gone on in any kind of institution where men are in close proximity for a long period of time.
There is another side to this question, Mr. Chairman. What happens to the wife? Sex is 28902-5-373J

equally important to both our sexes, and the wife also finds herself in a situation she has not been prepared to face. Her husband has not been sick; he has not died; there has been no preparation for the withdrawal, which preparation is necessary. If the minister wishes to refute my argument he will have to tell us how many prisoners have returned to their homes to find a child or two born during the period of their confinement in prison. We know this is true in many cases. I do not think you can blame the people involved, because they have been accustomed to a normal sexual life and there was no emotional preparation for this withdrawal. If there is a war and people go away, the emotional attitude makes this withdrawal possible. When a person dies there is an emotional attitude that makes it possible. In the case of the confinement that takes place in prison, this is not necessarily true.
What do prisoners themselves say about some of these matters. A year ago T. Cunningham, a prisoner, wrote in "The Telescope", the inmates' magazine of Kingston penitentiary, when speaking of visits:
Any time they sit across from their wives, a table and a mesh screen separating them, they don't think about words like reformation and rehabilitation.
They think about how nice it would be if they could just reach through the screen and hold her hand for a moment. In 30 short minutes she is gone and they find it hard to believe she has ever really been there. And some wonder if she will be back.
He points out this is not the case in some prisons, and speaks of the situation in Mississippi in this way:
"Wives are permitted to visit every Sunday afternoon between one and three, except on the third Sunday, at which time they are permitted to visit between one and five. Unless a prisoner is being punished and is confined in our maximum security unit, he is permitted to see his wife privately on any visiting day-no matter how good or bad a prisoner he is".
He is there setting out what the warden of the Mississippi state penitentiary has written about this subject. Then he says:
Adjusting to the society that banished him is a difficult task for a man released from prison. The affection and support of a wife and the responsibility he feels to his children can make the task less difficult.
No woman can be expected to endure a life devoid of physical love for a number of years because her man is in prison. Her needs are as great as his and they cannot be satisfied through a glass and mesh partition.
The communication must be more than spiritual, as has been borne out by the many broken marriages caused by imprisonment. If judges and magistrates understood that when they sentence a man to prison, they are also sentencing his wife and family, conjugal visits in Canada would be more likely to gain their support.

Mr. MacLeod, who is responsible lor this and you might say should be recommending a higher budget for it, does understand the problem and I think is very sympathetic to it. He had this to say in the address he delivered to the John Howard society on February 25, 1963:
We are concerned about the relationship of the inmate with his family. That relationship will, upon his release, usually have a profound effect on the question of his successful readjustment in society. Accordingly, we encourage visits to the inmate by members of his family and we provide as little restriction and supervision as possible during such visits, having regard to the security considerations involved. We want the inmate and his family to meet each other frequently in surroundings that are free from strain.
This may be true and it may be what we want; but it is not what we are accomplishing in most of our prisons. It may be true that we are a prudish nation and do not want to talk about these things. Very seldom, if ever, will you hear the reasons for the problems in prisons discussed. But there was a story told recently in this connection. The minister can investigate it. It concerns some of the practices that took place in Kingston penitentiary. The minister should look into this case of a young chap for whom the guards and the inmates took up a collection. They bought him a bicycle and turned him loose in the compound to learn to ride the bicycle. He was not an old man, or even a young man; he was a boy 13 years of age. I think the minister should find out for himself what happened in this case. Perhaps he would then be sympathetic to the problem we have in Canada because of our prudishness and our unwillingness to even face this situation.
I do not know whether it is wise to be too strong about these things. I do not think the minister is going to do a damned thing about this. I do not say that because he is the minister, but because this is a problem society has not faced up to, and it is a very serious one. If the minister is even going to talk about this problem, people will say, "Why in heck are you paying $2,500 a year to keep a guy in jail, if you are going to give him all the comforts of home?" Certainly they are going to say this. Many people don't give a damn whether that guy is ever rehabilitated into society. Even here we have the chief of police of Ottawa saying these people should not be out on parole, we should keep them in jail. If many of the people who are really involved with this matter understood these problems and were more sympathetic to them, more willing to bring them out into the open and ask for the help, support and consideration of the nation in general, and told people the facts of the problems, I think this nation

would be very sympathetic and would want some solution found to the problems.
We quite often cover these things up. I think we should not do this. If the minister were to get up and say, "We are going to allow conjugal visits for married prisoners who have been married over six weeks, and these visits will be allowed once a month", somebody would immediately get up and say, "What about the single man? How come you are doing this for the married man and you will not do it for the single man?" In other countries they supply prostitutes for the prisoners. I am sure this could not be tolerated in Canada and I am not suggesting it should be tolerated. But just because there are some road blocks, we do not have to go to that extreme or any of the other extremes; we can give consideration to those things which are acceptable to our society and can develop our program to meet the needs of today.
We are a long piece behind. I hear hon. members speak of the Fauteux commission. I decided to read it one time and did not get too far in my study of that document. But I hear people refer to it and I think you can take any part of it out and say, "I would like this to apply", because very little has been applied to our penal system in Canada. In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say that I think our institutions should be for the re-establishment into society of people confined therein. Even murder is acceptable to society in times of war and other situations; it is even approved, spiritually approved in many cases. It is only when it does not conform to society that it causes difficulty in the society against which the crime is committed. We should try to rehabilitate these men in our society. I will not mention the other systems of treatment which may be provided to prisoners; other hon. members have done this much better than I could. I think one of the things we should be prepared to do is this: When a prisoner goes out of a gate he should be capable of going in a normal fashion into the society from which we took him, so as to live with his family in the proper way; so that he can walk down the street carrying his lunch pail to work, coming back again to his family who understand him and can sympathize with him and give him support at the time he most needs it. If we provide the machinery, they can make it possible. If these steps are taken about one or two years before long term prisoners are released, this will be an advantage and keep many people out of prison the second time, as well as making the job of the parole officer, that of the John Howard

society and others interested in rehabilitating prisoners in society very much easier.

Mr. Chairman, I know the house is anxious, and I am sure the minister is, to end this discussion and get the estimates through, but I have a matter of a constitutional nature which I believe of some importance. Even though the matter is important I think I can sum it up very quickly.
A few weeks ago the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the validity of the labour relations amendment act (1961) of British Columbia by a majority decision of four judges to three. This legislation in effect prohibited trade unions from using about 99 per cent of their funds to support any party or candidate for office in the federal field as well as in the provincial. One of the minority judges described this decision as a grave and unwarranted extension of principle. He also described it as a matter of great constitutional and political importance.
The decision, if I may say so with very great respect, justifies an intrusion by the provincial legislature into the field of federal elections, which is surely a matter which should be within the control of parliament, not of provincial legislatures. The decision of the majority indicates-and I say this with a great deal of respect to the court-a lack of understanding of the historic rights of labour. And lastly, this decision implies the right of the provincial legislatures to restrict the political rights of every organized group in Canada, be they a trade union, a corporation, a co-operative or any other association of individuals. It is, I suggest, entirely inconsistent with the bill of rights passed by this parliament, which purports to preserve freedom of association as one of the basic constitutional rights upon which our whole system depends.
In light of these facts, Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will give careful and indeed favourable consideration to the request which I understand has been made to him to support an application for a rehearing of this matter by the full court of nine judges. The matter is of such grave importance that I respectfully suggest to the minister and his department that by supporting an application for a rehearing they will be assisting in the protection of the rights of this parliament, and the rights of the people of Canada.

Then, Mr. Chairman, in view of that I think I will accept the suggestion made and proceed at once to deal as generally as I can with the matters which did come up for discussion. Having regard to the number of years I have been in the house and to the fact that I sat on the other side for almost six years, I think I can say that these estimates have been given very careful scrutiny and study by all those hon. members who rose to discuss them both this evening and on a prior occasion. I think that is all to the good. I am grateful too for many of the suggestions which have been made, because several of them, not to say all of them, have been excellent, and I shall certainly be glad to give them my utmost consideration.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North dealt with a number of items, and he will excuse me if I do not go into all of the subjects which he brought up seriatim, and in the manner in which he did. But I should like at once to say to him that I think he has shown a tremendous interest since he has been in this house in the matters which he has discussed and in the questions he has posed from time to time. That has been evident from the trouble it has given me to find answers, with those of my officers who surround me, to the multifarious questions which he has asked. However, I might say without any hesitation that all of them have been pertinent and enlightening.
The hon. member referred to the inadequacy of progress in the field of correctional
