programs, and at once I must admit, and agree with him, and with those others who have spoken tonight, that there is inadequacy-in that field. There are reasons why this exists. I do not make any excuses for it. Unfortunately the progress should perhaps have been greater, but as my hon. friend knows, in a country such as ours there are always priorities. It is unfortunate that matters of this importance should be relegated to, I should not say the bottom rung, but to a secondary level. But none the less, unfortunately that is what happens from time to time. I can assure him that our officers are giving this matter careful consideration indeed. I might add that representations were made to me during the course of the last federal-provincial conference about this very matter and some action will be taken with reference to it.
The hon. member made comparisons between what happens in the United Kingdom and in Canada. Those comparisons were, of course, enlightening, but I should like to say to him that the constitutional position in Canada is entirely different from the position in the United Kingdom. The hon. member referred, for example, to the case of a young boy in Winnipeg whom a magistrate had sentenced to four years and compared it with what happens in the United Kingdom. I am sure the hon. member recognizes that this case, if 1 understood him aright, is one over which the federal government would have no jurisdiction. Magistrates are appointed by the provinces, except, of course, in the northern territories, and if a magistrate decides to pass a sentence such as that, even though it would appear to be severe in the circumstances, it is not a matter which falls within the jurisdiction of the federal government.
I agree with the hon. member that every member of parliament should visit the penitentiaries of our country, particularly those which are not far from the House of Commons, penitentiaries such as Kingston and St. Vincent de Paul. He knows full well that members of parliament are free to visit these institutions. He and other members have been given the fullest co-operation in visiting them, and this situation will continue.
Reference was made to the Fauteux report and the fact that many parts of it are not being put into effect. As I said earlier, this, also, is a matter which was taken up by representatives of certain of the provinces with me in my capacity as attorney general, and this question is under study.
There was a discussion, too, on the Dion case.
[Mr. Chevrier.i

Mr. Chairman, here I take the liberty to say first a few words in French on this matter which, as the hon. members of the house know, has been discussed many times in the house not exclusively, but mostly by the members of the Social Credit party and also by certain members of the Ralliement Creditistes.
I prepared a statement some time ago concerning the points raised in relation to this unfortunate case, but considering what is going on today and due to the decision of the tribunal, I believe that I should not make that statement to the house under those circumstances. Furthermore, the case is still sub judice. There will probably be an appeal; as everybody knows, it is possible to go to the supreme court in cases as important and serious as this one.
I would then ask hon. members to excuse me from making a statement today; I shall make it at another time.

The hon. member for Grey-Bruce brought up a number of matters. He referred to the penitentiary program which was inaugurated by the former government and inquired whether there had been any change with respect to that program. No, as far as 1 know there has been no change in principle. The program is the same and it is being carried out in accordance with the recommendations which have been made by the commissioner of penitentiaries. There may have been changes as far as the locations of some of these institutions are concerned, but these changes were, I believe, decided upon for obvious reasons.

The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) dealt with the Coffin case, as did the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott).

But since most of the remarks with reference to that case were in English perhaps I should deal with them in that language.
I listened very carefully to what the hon. member for Danforth said with reference to the Coffin case and I do not think there is anything useful I can add to what I said this morning on the orders of the day. I do not think the hon. member would expect me at this time to say anything more. There is a divergence of view with reference to what should be done. The hon. member for Lotbiniere suggested a royal commission should be appointed and the hon. member for Danforth did likewise. One hon. member suggested a committee of officers of the Department of

Justice. The hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm felt the accusations in the book by Mr. Hebert should not be taken too seriously.
I thank the hon. member for Danforth for the time and study he has given to this case. It is easy to see he has spent a lot of time on it. I have no hesitation in saying that he has spent far more time considering the facts, at least, than the Minister of Justice has. But he will not be offended if I say that most of the things he said tonight-not all of them, but most of them-point toward action by the provincial jurisdiction. I would remind him, as I did earlier today, that this matter was referred to the appellate court in the province of Quebec which unanimously dismissed the case. Leave to appeal was asked of the supreme court. It was refused. Thereafter, the governor in council under section 55 of the Supreme Court Act referred the case to the court in order that the convicted person might have the same rights as he would have had if the Supreme Court of Canada had heard the case on appeal. As I indicated earlier, by a decision of five to two the supreme court decided that it would not interfere with the decision of the governor in council. The hon. member is right in saying they did not hear the new evidence.

Not with the decision of the governor in council; that was not a decision of the governor in council. I think the minister is in error, there. It may only have been a slip in expression. But the Supreme Court of Canada decided that if the case had come before it by way of appeal, it would not have allowed the appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition is right in correcting me and I am glad he did. I return to the interjection made by the hon. member for Danforth, and I say it is because of this new evidence that I have asked the law officers to ascertain if there is not some aspect of the case which the federal jurisdiction should consider. As I have said, I have not closed the door but I will have to await the report of these officials.

The hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) raised the matter of sugar.
What grieves me a little is that he said that the Minister of Justice was hiding behind technicalities.
I am not in the habit of hiding because I am rather regularly present in the house, and I am sure the hon. member did not mean it that way but rather in the legal way.
It is a very serious matter, but when he deals with the sugar price, there is no need for me to remind him as well as the house
Supply-Justice
that the federal government has no jurisdiction as far as prices are concerned. Let us not forget, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) repeatedly said in the house, that if price control is what is wanted another jurisdiction than this one will have to impose it.
Unfortunately, the restrictive trade practices commission's jurisdiction is rather limited.
I have here a section which I cannot read into Hansard because it is rather long but you will find in sections 32 and 33 the powers attributed to the commission. They deal with the abolition of combines and, most of all, collusion. When there is collusion between two corporations, the government can intervene through that commission.
I appreciate that the question of sugar is of particular interest to the house because it affects every home, but the fact remains that the government is bound by the law and cannot go beyond it.
I would have liked to deal at greater length with these sections. I may have the opportunity to do so another time, because I wonder whether this is the right time.
I certainly do not want to ignore the suggestion made by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) who dealt with the organization of our penitentiaries and suggested that we hire competent officials, so as to rehabilitate these people. That is what we are trying to do.
As I tried to say a moment ago, in reply to one of the hon. members who had raised this question, unfortunately there are some priorities to which we must give greater importance-and I regret to have to say that- both in the present circumstances and at the time of the former government, which was faced with the same problems.
The hon. member for Villeneuve mentioned a case in particular, that of Mr. Gignac; I am not acquainted with the details of that case, but I will seek information from the officers in my department.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) asked many questions. He asked me if it was my intention to amend the legislation in 1964 so as to permit the establishment of lotteries. I have already answered that question in the house by saying simply that following the federal-provincial conference I would report to my colleagues and that a decision would be reached at that time-
Before the minister goes on-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I finish the sentence?
5860	HOUSE OF
Supply-Justice

-with regard to the advisability of amending the legislation.

Before the minister goes on, I should like to ask him whether he made the statement yesterday and whether he was speaking for the government when, in reply to a request by the international railway brotherhoods for an amendment to the Criminal Code to permit legal lotteries controlled and operated by the government, he said that he personally favours the establishment of lotteries under provincial jurisdiction? In saying that, was he speaking for the government? If not, how can he, in virtue of his position, separate himself from the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no hesitation in answering the question. Yes, I made that statement, and I made that statement at the federal-provincial conference. I made that statement openly. I made it before the attorneys general. I made it in the conference. I said that I personally favoured the operation of lotteries under provincial jurisdiction but that I was expressing a personal opinion and these matters had to be considered in the light of the representations that had been made by the provinces. These representations were made to me first by the attorneys general and some premiers and then later by the members of the dominion-provincial conference assembled together. I repeated again there that I would have to give consideration to the representations of the provinces, because many of the provinces were against the operation of lotteries. Several indicated quite clearly that they did not favour them. I believe that on that occasion I gave, as succinctly as I could, the reasons that certain provinces were against them. That is why I say that the matter will be submitted to-
I should like to clarify this. This is a very important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I should like to continue. Just a moment.

If the minister is turning from that matter to another point then all I can say is that if he does not want cooperation he will not get it. I want to clear up how a minister of the crown can say that this is his personal opinion, and not be representing the view of the government of which he is a part.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I apologize if I did not allow the Leader of the Opposition to raise the question, but the Leader of the Opposition will remember that I was asked to deal with


what had been said. That is what I was trying to do. If questions are forthcoming when we get down to the particular item I will have no objection to dealing with them. Again I say to the Leader of the Opposition that if he thinks I have been brusque-
No, but it is a simple question-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -I am sorry.
-of how the minister can make a statement like that and not bind the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I may go on with the other question asked by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm having to do with an amendment to the B.N.A. Act; as I indicated, that again is a matter for a conference of the attorneys general which I said at Banff I intended to call during 1964. There is machinery in the Department of Justice to deal with conferences of this nature. There have been a number of them. This matter is under careful consideration now.
The hon. member also asked about an amendment to the Criminal Code with reference to those who issue cheques without funds. I think all I need say here is that there is a committee within the department that deals with amendments to the Criminal Code and I could ask them to give consideration to such an amendment, if it has not already been done.
I commend the hon. member for Skeena upon his excellent French. In fact, I think it is remarkable that he should speak, or at least write three languages, because according to the press there is another language which he at least writes. In any event, I can tell him that his French was quite good. I join with other hon. members in telling him how well he pronounced it. The hon. member dealt particularly with section 660 of the Criminal Code which has to do with habitual criminals. He paid a compliment to one of the officers of the department, and I am delighted that he did. I should add to what has already been said on this matter, that there is a study being made of amendments to the Criminal Code. I can tell him that the officers of the department will carefully review this section relating to preventive detention.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond dealt at some length with the combines act and referred to a book entitled, "Canadian Anti-Combines Administration", which had to do with restrictive trade practices and the like. I am delighted that my parliamentary assistant has given special study to this matter and I think I shall be guided by much of the advice which he will give me.

I commend the hon. member for Athabasca for his support of the activities and actions of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I am delighted that he made the speech which he did. It is not the first time that he has intervened in this house in that respect. I think it is a good thing that members do rise from time to time, as often they do, to support the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Although some hon. members do criticize the mounted police, I believe that those who do so, criticize constructively. I was pleased to listen to the remarks which were made by the hon. member for Athabasca.

The hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Frenette) and the hon. member for Shef-ford (Mr. Rondeau) talked about amending the Bankruptcy Act. I say without any hesitation that that act should be amended. The Bankruptcy Act is getting more and more obsolete. I wish to change the word "obsolete" and replace it by the expression "ineffective in some cases".
As both hon. members and the whole house know and as I said on several occasions, we are now studying the Bankruptcy Act in all its aspects.
I hope it will be possible at the next session of parliament to submit a bill amending that act.
I take note of the suggestions which were made by the hon. members for Portneuf and Shefford.

The hon. member for Timiskaming, along with other members, raised the question of the rehabilitation of prisoners, the aftercare treatment that they should get, and the fact that we should be doing more in order to integrate them into society. I agree with him. I hope it will be possible to increase the estimates for the next fiscal year towards that end. He did refer to one particular incident which took place in Kingston, and I shall ask my officers to look into it.
The hon. member for Greenwood asked me to give consideration to the labour relations practices act, and requested a rehearing of the case. I would ask the hon. gentleman not to press me unduly on the matter because, as he knows, I have received some representations and I am going to receive additional representations on this subject. Until I do, I do not think it would be proper for me to make any statement with reference to his request. I can assure him that I listened carefully to the submissions made by him, and I shall listen carefully to the submissions that will be made.
Supply-Justice
I think I have covered, as best I can, most of the suggestions that were made in the debate.

May I be permitted to put on the record some brief background information about the sugar situation in Canada and to indicate, from my point of view, the smooth, facile and gentle way in which the minister approached this question. His approach left a great deal to be desired, so far as the people of Canada are concerned, and showed that the minister really did not tell all the facts about the sugar situation in this country.
Some years ago the B.C. Sugar Refining Company in Vancouver acquired the assets of the Alberta sugar factories and made them subsidiaries of that company. This acquisition put the company in a monopoly position in British Columbia, Alberta, and perhaps midway into Saskatchewan. A few years later the company took steps to acquire controlling interest of many Manitoba sugar factories, and made them subsidiaries also. This placed the B.C. Sugar Refining Company in a monopoly position in respect of sugar in all of western Canada to about the lakehead, which, I understand, is the break-even point on distribution costs between B.C. sugar refining companies and eastern manufacturers.
It was as a result of this acquisition by B.C. Sugar Refining Company of the Manitoba sugar factories that the combines investigation machinery was put into motion to determine whether or not the proposed acquisition was contrary to the statute. A reading of the report of the restrictive trade practices commission would be most enlightening. If hon. members think that the letter read by my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam from Mr. Rogers, about keeping things secret concerning the operations of that company was enlightening, they should read the drastic statements he had to make about the steps which should be taken to gain control of the Manitoba sugar factories.
In any event, a charge was laid under the Combines Investigation Act, the merger section of it. This action was lost in the courts. This was the second case which was lost, the first being the one against Canadian breweries. I submit that the case was lost for two reasons. One, the merger provision of the Combines Investigation Act is just about useless, as these two cases proved. Two, the then minister of justice, who has since returned to British Columbia, Mr. Fulton, by the process of prosecuting the case, in fact gave it away.
In 1960 when the minister and the present Secretary of State for External Affairs sat on this side they were most vociferous in their opposition to proposed amendments which were then introduced by Mr. Fulton to

Supply-Justice
the Combines Investigation Act. They raised a fuss day after day in this house and in the committee on banking and commerce, I believe it was, which was studying the bill, in opposition to the amendments which were proposed at that time. Those amendments became law, and out of all this we really see that the Minister of Justice is probably one of those types which the mother of the hon. member for Red Deer referred to as being able to look both fore and aft when driving a car.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought he did not get the story over.
Well, I was closer to the hon. member than the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is an interesting admission.

In this regard the minister reminds me of the Roman god Janus, who had two faces so that he could look both behind and ahead at the same time. This is the type of minister we have, one with two faces, and one face says, "we would like to do something about the sugar situation," while the other says, "We cannot." If he really had a sincere heart in this matter, the government would have long ago introduced amendments to the Combines Investigation Act so that the law enforcement officers could proceed to deal with the gouging that is taking place by B.C. Sugar Refinery.
When the minister, in his very suave and smooth way, tries to get out of all responsibility in this matter, I can only conclude he is speaking out of the other side of his face, and we will look upon it accordingly.
I was reading the Vancouver Sun and I saw where an old acquaintance of mine, one Wilfred Heffernan, a lawyer in Vancouver, is back in business as a prosecutor for the crown in drug cases. When the Conservatives came into office we discovered that they tore up the old patronage list of the Liberals with respect to lawyers to be employed in the prosecution of drug cases, and imposed their own list of Tory legal friends and firms to get the spoils of office by prosecuting in these cases. During the renegade years, as I think they are referred to, Mr. Heffernan and the other Liberal lawyers were out of the picture; but now Mr. Heffernan and other Liberal friends are back in it again, and I wonder whether the minister will tell us that he has put into effect the Liberal legal patronage list that existed prior to 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In answer to the last part of the question there is no Liberal patronage list so far as I am concerned, and I can tell the hon. member that there are a number of lawyers who were appointed by the former

government presently acting in these cases because, as the hon. member knows, some of these cases last over quite a number of years as they go from one court to another.
I would remind the hon. member also that, while he does not seem to approve of what I have said, and thinks I am smug about the manner in which this act is being administered. I am not. I am as concerned about it as he is, and I am as worried as he and some of his people are; but I have to say I am bound by what is contained in this act, and it may well be that in order to put teeth in it, it will have to be amended. I am willing to give consideration to that, because I find that most of the time when investigations are made, or when lawsuits are brought-and I think the house should know this-it is section 32 which is kept in mind, and which says what an offence is. I will not put it all on the record because it is too long, but subsection (2) says:
Subject to subsection (3), in a prosecution under subsection (1) the court shall not convict the accused it the conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement relates only to one or more of the following:
(a)	the exchange of statistics,
(b)	the defining of product standards,
(c)	the exchange of credit information,
(d)	definition of trade terms,
(e)	co-operation in research and development,
(f)	restriction of advertising, or
(g)	some other matter not enumerated in subsection (3).
Then it goes on in another subsection and gives other reasons why the court shall not convict.
What year was that particular section brought into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This section was passed in 1960. Now, I am not complaining. What I say is that the courts are bound by the law. The director of investigation and research is the one who has to put this into effect, and these are the difficulties. But I repeat what I said. I feel that we should give consideration to seeing if there is not some way to strengthen this legislation.
I do not think that we can do anything with reference to the control of prices, and I do not think the hon. gentleman, if he is serious, questions that. But I do think that we can perhaps do something to get at those who are guilty of collusion, mergers, monopolies and the like, and I say that I am willing to ask those responsible for the administration of this act if it is not possible to give consideration to amending it.

With respect to the employment of lawyers for drug prosecutions, the minister said that there are still under contract, or however it is done, lawyers who were

appointed under the previous administration. Then he went on to imply that would not be carried on very long, because he said that many drug cases take a long time to conclude, through appeals and the like. I suppose what he does not want to tell us is that he does not want to change prosecuting horses in midstream, but as soon as those particular cases are finished we will find that these lawyers are out of business or prosecutors in drug cases, and this Liberal patronage list, that he does not know about, will suddenly be discovered-just the same as the Liberal patronage list that the Postmaster General and the Secretary of State did not know about suddenly came to light.
When the minister quoted the section from the Combines Investigation Act, that the courts shall not prosecute if the combine, conspiracy, or whatever it was, related to certain things, I would point out to him that when those amendments were introduced in 1960 by the Hon. E. Davie Fulton, the present minister and his colleagues, led all the way by the person who is now Prime Minister of Canada, said at that time that they would do everything possible they could to defeat them, because they were inimical to the interests of the Canadian people.
That was three years ago. They did not do very much about it then, but I thought that since returning to office the Liberals would remember the then clarion call of their leader, and we would have had amendments introduced to bring the act back to a stable basis, and remove it from the distorted condition in which the Conservatives placed it. I hope that if the minister stays in office, by the time these estimates roll around next year we will have had these amendments before us.

I am not going to enter into any argument respecting the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act three years ago, except to say that the concept that bigness is an offence is contrary to the experience of all the nations of the world, particularly the western world. The offence must always be that of doing something to the detriment of the public as a whole. Wherever that detriment is caused, it should be an offence. But in so far as combinations are concerned that are designed for the purpose of making it possible to compete for trade in other parts of the world, and are not in any way intended to interfere with the rights of people in Canada, certainly they should not be legislated against. But I did not rise for the purpose of dealing with that matter, Mr. Chairman. I come back to a
Supply-Justice
question that I asked earlier and which the Minister of Justice answered in a rather cavalier way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought you had forgotten that.

The other day he advised the federal-provincial conference that he personally was in favour of lotteries operated under provincial jurisdiction. Furthermore, yesterday he repeated the same proposition to a group that met with him. I ask him this, and I hope to get an answer on this question. When he placed that viewpoint before the federal-provincial conference, was it the viewpoint of the government, or was he merely endeavouring to ride two horses, to be able to say, "I am in favour of this. I want to ingratiate myself with those who are in favour of this; but I do not speak for the government"? I am certain that a person with his lengthy experience would not advocate such a proposition. This is a statement made, according to the newspaper report, with regard to an amendment suggested by one or other of the provinces, which he said was acceptable to him and would be supported by him. In making that statement was he speaking only for himself? I ask the minister this simple question. When he made that statement was he speaking for the Prime Minister and the government, or was he merely flying the kite in order to ingratiate himself and establish further evidence of that smile which wipes aside so many arguments so often?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hope the smile, if I continue to have it, will wipe aside the question that my right hon. friend has put. I do not want to be offensive, but I am inclined to think he put it with his tongue in his cheek.
No; I am asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will answer it.
All right; that is what we want.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Nevertheless, I think I indicated quite clearly to the right hon. gentleman earlier what I had said on two occasions, and I am not attempting to withdraw from that position. But I am saying this. There was a discussion on the subject. No decision had been taken. I think I as an individual, whether it be as minister or in any other capacity, have the right to express my opinion. That need not be the opinion of others. It need not be the opinion of colleagues. But once the government has taken a decision on it, then my right hon. friend is right-I think there must then be collective responsibility, as he has said. If that had been the

Supply-Justice
case, I think my right hon. friend would be quite right in the position he puts forward. But that was not the case. It was an informal discussion which took place following a subcommittee meeting, and in the course of a very friendly conversation which took place with several of the premiers I made the statement. I can only say that I was expressing my own personal views.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I would like to read the press dispatch with regard to this matter, because I asked the minister whether he was speaking for the Prime Minister. In a Canadian Press dispatch dated December 13 it says this:
Mr. Chevrier made the statement Tuesday in reply to a request by the international railway brotherhood for an amendment to the Criminal Code to permit legal lotteries "controlled and operated by governments".
He was pinch-hitting for ailing Prime Minister Pearson at the annual meeting between the federal cabinet and the national legislative committee of the international railway unions-
Does the minister say that when he pinch-hit for the Prime Minister he was not exactly sure on what team he or the government was?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I doubt very much if I used that expression, even though it is in the report. I am not denying the substance of the report; I am denying the words. I doubt very much if I said I was pinch hitting. I probably said that in the absence of the Prime Minister I was acting as chairman of the meeting, and I said about the same as I had said earlier at the federal-provincial conference. This, too, was a very informal meeting with the legislative committee of the railway brotherhoods at which the greatest, I should not say unanimity-
That is what appears.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -but certainly the greatest informality existed. I do not think I need add any more to what I have said. I was not speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister; I was speaking, again, on my own behalf, but I was acting as chairman of the meeting in the absence of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, it was good to hear the minister express such interest in and support for the anti-combines legislation. Coming as I do from Winnipeg, I have had 30 years in which to read editorials in that great Liberal newspaper, the Winnipeg Free Press, about this wonderful legislation, this important legislation passed by that great Liberal Mr. Mackenzie King. The minister has mentioned the difficulties the government has had to face as a result of the amendment passed in 1961 by the former government. I express no opinion about that. But if one looks at the record of governments over the

years with respect to the anti-combines legislation, most of them Liberal years, he cannot help being struck by the complete ineffectiveness of the legislation we have had in those years.
Some members of parliament, myself included, asked last year, I think it was, for the tabling of the list of prosecutions which have been conducted over the past 15 or 20 years, I think. The list was a long one. I am speaking from memory, but there had been in the neighbourhood of 50 or 60 prosecutions. What do we find? Even when the courts found the companies guilty, they imposed penalties which were really ludicrous. If one makes a mistake and has the misfortune to commit an offence against property, commits a robbery, for example, the first time you are caught and convicted you are likely to get a relatively minor sentence. But if you are caught a second or a third time, the judge-I am not being critical of judges-makes very sure that he impresses upon you the fact that you should not be doing this again, and you are likely to wind up with a pretty severe sentence. I spoke about this earlier in connection with the kind of sentences imposed by judges. But when it comes to companies we see that in this country we have one law for the poor and one for rich; one law for the individual and another for the company-and it seems that the bigger the corporation, the better it is for them. I took the trouble to list these companies to see how many of them were convicted more than once. Speaking from memory-and if I am wrong I apologize-it seems to me that the Eddy Company were convicted four times, and certainly three times.
What are the courts doing about this? Here is a company doing millions of dollars worth of business and making fantastic profits. I do not question their right to do this if they are an efficient company. But in each case the court has imposed a fine of $25,000. In the course of eight or ten years what is a fine of $75,000 or $100,000 to the Eddy Company? That is not a penalty; it is a licence for doing business. It is a licence for stealing from the public, just as much as a man who holds up a store or a bank is stealing.
Unfortunately, these people do not go to jail. The law passed by the former government permits the court to impose a penalty of either a fine or a jail sentence. I ask the minister whether any officer or director of a company in the history of Canada has ever gone to jail for breaking the anti-combines law? I know that his answer will be no. I think the minister should look very carefully in this regard at the experience of the United States, where the officers of some electrical companies were sent to jail, it is true only

ior a month, but at least they suffered in the same way as poor people who break the law. Since we have for many years given the courts the option of making the penalty either a fine or a jail sentence, and since the courts have consistently refused to impose the more severe penalty, as they would with an ordinary citizen who breaks the law, I suggest to the minister that he give serious consideration to making the penalty of a jail sentence mandatory at the second or third offence. Because in my opinion the breaking by a corporation of the anti-combines law is just as serious as the breaking of any other law by an ordinary citizen.
In the United States of America it is optional; it is at the discretion of the court.
But our courts do not use it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is a matter for the courts.

If the courts do not use it we will have to find another method.
There is another matter which comes to my attention. I took the time to get the reports of investigations made by the anti-combines branch of the department over the last five years and was amazed at the number of investigations which were made. Some involved in the neighbourhood of 15 to 20 reports. Many of them made very specific recommendations. I wonder whether the government is going to give consideration to looking at those reports and taking steps to implement those recommendations. Because if they do not, I suggest that the government is in fact saying that the work of that investigation branch is really useless.
I have put some questions on the order paper, and although I do not want to refer to them in detail I would like to refer to some of these cases concerning drugs. In this regard the commission made a number of recommendations. One important one was that the commission made the charge very clearly that companies who keep the price of prescription drugs in Canada at the highest level anywhere in the western world should have their patent rights taken away. I suggest the government look at that recommendation and introduce legislation to give effect to it pretty quickly.
In the case of the paperboard companies, the commission recommended that the tariffs be reduced. If ever there was a party which prided itself on the establishment of free trade and low tariffs, it is the present Liberal party. Is it not about time that these recommendations, which were made not yesterday or the week before but over the last two or three years, should be put into effect? In the case
Supply-Justice
of Canada Packers the commission recommended steps should be taken in the courts to force that company to divest itself of the control it had purchased in other companies.
I ask the government whether they are considering these recommendations, or whether, like so many others, the reports will gather dust on the files of various offices in this and other buildings. I think the sentiments the minster expressed and which we were glad to hear are very fine ones, but the time is long past when pious platitudes suffice. We ought to see some action by the government in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a few remarks.
I appreciate that the minister had to deal with several subjects in reply to the many speeches made tonight, but I would like to get his or his government's views about the appointment of judges in certain judicial districts of our province in particular, where the rolls are too heavy. I believe that the minister forgot to mention this in his reply.
Does his government intend to make appointments shortly in order to relieve the backlog in several courts in our province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. member allow me to answer this question when we are dealing with the item in question?

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take too much time; I simply want to say a word to the minister before the general item passes, because I imagine the other items will not take so long. I am sure hon. members of the committee appreciated the courteous replies the minister gave to the various questions put and statements made. But the minister's replies will not do much to stir up any enthusiasm as to what is the future program of this department. When the minister brings down estimates one generally expects him to map out the programs he has in mind and to set forth the plans and objectives of his department. I appreciate the fact that the minister has been in charge of this department for only eight months and that these were estimates prepared by the previous administration; therefore I think there might be some excuse for dealing with the matter in a fairly low key. But I suggest to the minister that when the next session comes along, at which time we hope he will still be Minister of Justice, despite all the rumours to the contrary which are being circulated-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Paris is no place for him.

We would rather have him here than in Paris. But if he is still minister

Supply-Justice
we hope we shall be able to get a clear outline oi what his programs are in various fields. There is no need for me to go over them all because my colleagues have dealt with them admirably. There is, for instance, the penal system, which, in this country, is archaic. I have listened to the minister expressing his good wishes and good intentions this evening. But we have been listening to such expressions as these for over a quarter of a century.
I remember the Archambault report about which practically nothing was done. Then there was the Fauteux report about which very little has been done. I think we need from the minister a precise statement at the next session of parliament setting out the government's intentions in the field of penal reform. There is a tremendous need for the establishment of a farsighted policy in Canada in conjunction with the provinces. It is not enough for the minister to say that some of these matters come under provincial jurisdiction, that magistrates are appointed by the provinces and that there is not much we can do. The fact is that the federal government can do a lot by entering upon shared programs with the provinces to provide, for instance, probation and placement services. The provision of these services constitutes a most crying need today. Many of the provinces would respond. In fact, some of them are struggling to provide them on their own. I hope when we come to the estimates next session the minister will put before this house and the country a challenging program to bring Canada up to date in terms of its penal institutions and its penal program.
I think the same comment applies to the whole question of anti-combines legislation. This legislation is in great need of strengthening, as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North said a short time ago. Some time ago I drew the minister's attention to the fact that three of these sugar companies which had been found guilty of making an illegal profit on
80.000	tons of sugar were ordered to pay fines of $25,000 each, which was equivalent to $1 a ton or less than one twentieth of a cent per pound. At that time the minister said there was no maximum limit on the fines which could be imposed. But, equally, there is no minimum, either. This legislation needs to be amended so as to make the punishment fit the crime. To fine three companies $25,000 each after an illegal profit has been made on
80.000	tons of sugar is, as I have said before, simply issuing a licence to commit piracy. Again, we hope that by the time the house meets next session the minister will have legislation ready to introduce.
We hope, too, that he will tell us what is to be done about the various reports of the

restrictive trade practices commission-reports which have been brought down and upon which no action has been taken. For the moment I am not laying this at the door of the minister because he has only had a few months in which to deal with these things, but we did expect this session and, certainly, we will expect during the next session, some statement from the minister about what he proposes to do. He has promised to look into the matter of the sugar combines. I had hoped there would be some report from him on this subject tonight. But if he has nothing to report at this time, perhaps he will be able to make a full statement to parliament when it meets again in January or February.
Reference has been made by my hon. friend from Skeena to the B.C. Sugar Refining Company. I drew attention the other day to the fact that this company has in the past year increased its operating profit from $5,670,945 to $10,084,271. Its net profit amounted to $2,780,000, a gain of $591,519 over the profit for the previous year. This is the company which was able to say, in a letter sent out by its president to the employees, that due to the higher price obtained for sugar which had prevailed through most of the past financial year the over-all profits of the company had proven to be greater than normal. Then the company proceeded to send out bonus cheques to its em-ployeees of $12 for each year of service, and the letter ends by asking them to keep it quiet. I do not wonder that the president should have asked them to keep it quiet, because this company virtually doubled its operating profit in the course of the past year.
This is the company which got into Alberta and obtained control of three small refineries there. Now it intends to close one of them in Raymond and concentrate production in the other two. At the very time when sugar beet acreage is being increased, at the very time when we ought to be increasing domestic sugar production, this company is closing one of its refineries and then saying that the reason it has had to increase the price of sugar is because the price of the raw material has gone up on the world market.
I hope the minister's department intends to give the sugar industry a most careful examination. The fact that three of the companies this year pleaded guilty in the course of prosecutions initiated by the restrictive trade practices commission, indicates that there is good reason for further investigation.
I also want to express the hope that when parliament meets again the minister will be able to give some further answer to the request we have made so often for an appeal board to be set up, a board to which persons who have been accused of being bad security

risks can go to have their cases heard. The minister said nothing about that tonight. I think the government has taken a step in the right direction by providing some appeal machinery for employees in the government service, but the rest of the public are entitled to equal protection. I will not take the time tonight to go into this matter further, but I will be most insistent about this matter when parliament meets again because I have come across case after case of examples of people who have been discriminated against and who think they are unjustly accused of being bad security risks. They should have the right to appear before some body appointed by the government, to see the evidence and have an opportunity to clear their names.
I trust that when parliament meets again the minister will be able to give us some idea of what he intends to do about these various programs. I think the hon. gentleman has been very co-operative in listening while members of the committee have raised so many problems, but what we would like to get from him is a definite statement as to government policy on some of the questions which have been raised.

40. Bankruptcy Act administration, $166,900.

Before we pass this item, has the minister anything to say about contemplated changes in this act and its administration? There is a great deal of concern in the business world about the number of small companies which one finds going bankrupt with large involvements amounting, sometimes, to hundreds of thousands of dollars, though the assets may be only a few thousand dollars. There is a saying among some business people that you should have $100,000 in the bank after your third bankruptcy if you are any kind of a businessman. It may not be that bad. I am sure the minister has given some consideration to the abuses that are taking place in the bankruptcy field and I wonder whether there is in contemplation changes in the small bankruptcy field that will bring about much tighter controls than we have at present.
There is some problem with regard to trustees being available for the administering of bankruptcies. In many cases there is great delay in providing trustees for bankruptcies, because of the shortage of such people and the fact that the trustees have to have some experience in the particular field they are going to administer.

I think perhaps it might be better if I had a little conference tomorrow about the order of the proceedings we hope to have on Monday. I reiterate my request, for what it may be worth, that possibly we might have a frame of mind tomorrow when we reach orders of the day that hon. members would be willing to let the resolution respecting the world exhibition go through, so that the bill could be debated at the beginning of next week. But if there is not that consent there will not be the possibility. There has also been put on the order paper today a notice of motion to go into committee of ways and means with respect to a relatively minor matter that is, however, of some importance to the economy. I understand the Minister of Trade and Commerce has discussed it with representatives of all parties in the house and there is agreement to proceed with it at this session, even though it was not in the Prime Minister's list. This is something that has cropped up in the last little while. I want to explain that I appreciate very much the co-operation which was extended to the Minister of Trade and Commerce by all parties in agreeing, notwithstanding the fact it is an addition to the

list, and I appreciate this. If the house were disposed, because the bill will be absolutely identical except in form with that resolution, to go into committee and get the bill introduced, it would save us one step. This is not extremely important and I am not insisting in any way at all on these things, but it would make the order paper a little tidier for Monday.
So far as the estimates are concerned, this is to be the main business for tomorrow. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration will, by agreement, be called first. When it is completed, the minister of northern affairs, who has been available on so many occasions for so long, and who is still hopeful that the committee will be willing to ask him a few more questions and dispose of his department, will be available. My amiable and long-suffering colleague, the Minister of Public Works is very eager indeed to get a chance to hear the questions that are to be asked of him. If we could dispose of those three departments it would expedite greatly the objective I believe we all desire to reach, despite some suggestions that are sometimes made, that is the orderly conclusion of the business of this session.
